#6688. Warmth and Whimsy: The Blanket Coat Does It All

Is this fashion’s most comforting coat of all time?

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Fashion is all wrapped up in wraps, shawls, and capes. Call them what you will, but at the end of the day, they’re truly elevated blanket coats. For further proof, look at the fall/winter 2026 runways, where Colleen Allen and TWP led the charge with models dripping in comforting supersized scarf shawls turned coats. Elsewhere, at Fforme, models were decked out in huge swaths of furry fabrics that completely enveloped the wearers, as if swaddled. At Khaite, dresses were styled with large cocooning blanket-like throws trailing off the backs. Blanket-like pieces also emerged from stiff leather coats at Altuzarra and cascaded off the shoulders at Proenza Schouler.

Aside from being easy to wear and warm, the blanket coat offers a different kind of feel than your average black puffer might. In a tumultuous world, the blanket coat serves as a literal, wearable wrap of warmth and a representation of physical and metaphorical well-being. Not unlike the puffy statement scarf, a blanket coat is deeply practical but also inherently whimsical in spirit, even if not aesthetically so. It’s almost a little bit like taking your bed out the door with you. You already have the pillow by way of the puffed scarf. Why not bring the blanket too? And while you’re at it, don’t forget grandma’s couch in the form of the trending tapestry bag. It’s all about tactile touches.

Designers are clearly and intentionally leaning into the feeling of comfort: For TWP’s aforementioned fall/winter 2026 options, founder Trish Wescoat Pound referenced hot toddies, jigsaw puzzles, and fireplaces, in addition to other warm and cozy-feeling fabrics like Scottish cashmere in her show notes. In a more simplified vein, for Rachel Scott’s Proenza Schouler debut, where blanket-like shawls cascaded off the shoulders, the show notes described the pieces as clothes that “move easily between contexts. They are for a new New York woman, a global woman, who is aware of what the world asks of her but is unwilling to acquiesce to expectations.” Phoebe Philo’s recent take on the trend comes in the form of a brown and bronze houndstooth wool blanket coat with a hand-frayed hem.

Smaller brands like LilyEve also make a good business out of the blanket coat; the brand, in particular, upcycles hand-sourced vintage Hermès blankets and re-creates them into one-of-a-kind coats. “Seeing those little pieces and trying to think of what other product could come out of that, whether it’s tiny pieces of toweling or silk left from the scarves, that’s always a really fun inspiration,” she told ELLE earlier this year.

Certainly, there’s no arguing that we’re all craving comfort at the moment. Fashion’s obsession with blankets as clothing on the runway just further proves it.

#6687. What Is a Golden Retriever Boyfriend? Everything to Know About the Internet's Favorite Partner

Loyal, affectionate, and obsessed with you. What's not to love? Well, a few things, actually.

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

There are two kinds of people in the dating world: those who think waiting three hours to text back makes them mysterious, and those who would happily text you three times in a row just because they saw a dog that reminded them of you. The latter? Probably a golden retriever boyfriend.

If you've spent any time on Dating TikTok, you've likely encountered the golden retriever boyfriend (or GRBF), a term for the kind of guy who's affectionate, enthusiastic, and almost aggressively happy to be in a relationship with you. Think Travis Kelce with Taylor Swift. Subtlety isn't exactly the selling point.

“A golden retriever boyfriend is the human equivalent of a tail wagging, wide-eyed pup who lives to love you,” explains Tiff Baira, relationship expert, matchmaker, “Streethearts” host, and author of Modern Dating for Dummies. “He’s sweet, loyal, emotionally available, and basically imprinted on you after the third date.”

Which, after one too many situationships with men who consider responding to a text an act of vulnerability, sounds pretty damn appealing. But is having a boyfriend who worships the ground you walk on always as great as TikTok makes it look? Not necessarily. Here's what experts want you to know about golden retriever boyfriends, including how to spot one and why all that devotion isn't automatically a recipe for relationship bliss.

“A golden retriever boyfriend is loving, positive, energetic, loyal, and uncomplicated,” says matchmaker and dating coach Blaine Anderson, founder of Dating By Blaine.

“He remembers your coffee order, sends good morning texts unprompted, and genuinely enjoys helping you build IKEA furniture,” adds Baira. “He’s not playing games; he’s the overly nice and caring type who puts you before himself.”

Sounds like the dream, right? Mostly. While the golden retriever boyfriend is known for being easygoing and devoted, that same enthusiasm can sometimes mean he's a little too eager to please.

“There may also be an undertone of ‘nice guy,’—specifically as opposed to ‘bad boy’—perhaps implying the golden retriever boyfriend is the guy you settle with after having your heart broken by a bad boy,” Anderson adds. Still, the term is generally a compliment. “You date the golden retriever guy because you don’t want to waste time on moody losers,” says Anderson.

As for how the trend got started? “The term ‘golden retriever boyfriend’ definitely gained traction on TikTok, where women proudly showed off their partners as the ultimate romantic prize,” Baira explains. “These were the guys who happily did whatever their girlfriend said.”

And in an era of dating app burnout and doomscrolling, “golden retriever boyfriends became a symbol of hope in a dating landscape flooded with horror stories,” says Baira. “Amid all that chaos, the GRBF became a mythical figure—an aspirational fantasy. Someone who might actually treat you like the princess you are.”

“If you’re wondering whether you’re with a golden retriever boyfriend, the signs are usually wagging right in front of you,” says Baira. “He lights up when he sees you, offers to carry your bag without being asked, and says, ‘let me know when you get home’ like it’s a sacred ritual.” In short, “There are no games, no ego—just someone who wants to be near you, build with you, and see you shine.”

On the flip side: “Does he make you worry he’s cheating? Have you come to expect he won’t buy you dinner? Does he only text at 10pm?” asks Anderson. In that case, “you do not have a golden retriever boyfriend!”

Of course, not every guy who seems like a golden retriever boyfriend actually is one. Enter “the wolf in golden retriever clothing—the guy who seems endlessly kind and selfless but secretly has an agenda,” says Baira. “If his niceness comes with strings attached, like using your connections, expecting money, or subtly manipulating you, he’s not golden; he’s gold plated.”

In other words, “Sometimes the nice guy isn’t actually nice at all,” Baira adds. “If he makes you feel like you owe him for his kindness or if his affection feels performative or transactional, that’s a clear sign it’s not real golden retriever energy.”

Some other red flags signaling you may be with a fake golden retriever? “He’s only sweet in public, performs affection when people are watching, and suddenly goes cold the second you’re alone,” says Baira. “He expects praise for basic things like texting back or showing up on time. He might flood you with compliments but makes subtle jabs when you're shining too bright.”

As much as TikTok might make you think golden retriever boyfriends are the end-all, they're not necessarily the right match for everyone.

“While every relationship is nuanced and there’s no universal good or bad, it’s important to remember that golden retriever energy still needs to match your energy,” says Baira. “Just because someone is nice to you doesn’t mean they’re right for you.”

Case in point: The Sex and the City love triangle between Carrie, Big, and Aidan. “On paper, Aidan was everything: warm, loving, emotionally present, always chasing Carrie,” says Baira. “But that’s just it. She didn’t want to be chased; she wanted to be challenged. And no matter how hard she tried to make him the one, he wasn’t.”

Dating coach Grace Lee, founder of A Good First Date, adds that for some people, golden retriever energy can feel stifling. “Doting affection can breed contempt. At first, it feels amazing to be adored so completely. But over time, you might feel overwhelmed—or even guilty,” she notes. “He’s so focused on making you happy that his own needs seem to disappear.” This can create an unhealthy dynamic where one partner constantly needs space while the other feels underappreciated.

That doesn't mean golden retriever boyfriends are inherently bad partners. It just means being nice isn't the same thing as being compatible, and staying in a relationship because it feels safe isn't necessarily the same as being happy in it.

Lee also warns that the Very Online nature of the golden retriever boyfriend trend can create unrealistic expectations, encouraging people to play a specific role in their relationships rather than address their actual needs.

“The hashtag acts as a checklist—for both the boyfriend and the girlfriend,” says Lee. “If you’re a GRBF, that means you’re a ‘good boyfriend.’ And if you’re a good boyfriend, then you don’t have to worry about the relationship falling apart. You’ve met the criteria. You’re safe from rejection. On the flip side, having a GRBF is proof that you’re desirable. You must be the kind of person who deserves that level of devotion. Instead of confronting your insecurities, you point to the list.”

Ultimately, a golden retriever boyfriend can absolutely be a great partner. But a relationship doesn't automatically work just because it checks all the right boxes on TikTok. What matters is whether you're actually happy together, not whether your boyfriend fits the internet's favorite dating archetype.

#6686. The Stars Brought the Glamour to the 2026 Baby2Baby Gala Presented by Paul Mitchell

Harper’s Bazaar has exclusive snapshots from the event’s portrait studio

Every year, the Baby2Baby Gala brings together the biggest names in philanthropy, entertainment, and fashion for an evening of fundraising and celebration. And last night, the 15th edition was no exception—with the likes of Demi Moore, Andrew Garfield, Jessica Alba, Barbara Palvin and Dylan Sprouse, Kerry Washington, and Katy Perry showing up in West Hollywood to support the organization’s mission to help kids in need.

From the gala’s inception, Baby2Baby co-CEOS Norah Weinstein and Kelly Sawyer Patricof wanted to create an event that felt “less like a traditional fundraiser.” Year after year, the night has offered its star-studded guests more than just an excuse to get dressed up and a chance to make a difference with their wallets—pairing fundraising efforts with exclusive dining experiences from top chefs and intimate performances from award-winning musicians. (Last night, Carbone flew in from New York City and Cardi B took the stage.)

“We wanted to create an event that would appeal to a younger generation of donors through our approach to food, fashion, and celebrity, while making sure that nobody left the gala without understanding our mission,” Weinstein and Patricof told Harper’s Bazaar. “Fifteen years later, the gala has evolved in ways we never could have imagined, but some themes have stayed exactly the same. Every flower and fork is underwritten by our generous sponsors so that every dollar raised can go directly to Baby2Baby and the children we serve.”

Each year, the funds raised from the gala help get millions of basic essentials—from diapers to formula to clothing—to children who need them. But the organization, with an all-female board of directors, spends all year working towards the Baby2Baby mission. “The gala brings this extraordinary community together for one night, but it’s their commitment throughout the year that makes our work possible,” the CEOs shared.

#6684. Key Takeaways From Luxury’s Q3 Earnings

China’s macro environment has been a major drag on luxury’s third-quarter earnings, causing most companies to fall short of market expectations.

Analysts expected growth to slow in Q3, but conditions in China turned out worse than anticipated. The sector’s average organic sales growth ended at 4% in Q3 2026, versus 7.8% in Q2 (calculated by Goldman Sachs on the basis of a simple average of luxury companies, excluding currency impact).

Kering stock plummeted 17%, following the announcement that growth at the company had dropped to 1% in Q3 (vs +2% in Q2), including a 6% decrease at its largest brand, Gucci. (Gucci retail sales declined by 9% on a comparable basis.) Kering and LVMH stock are each down 37% year to date, while the Hermès share price has fallen 36%.

“Everyone is staying on the sidelines,” Goldman Sachs luxury analyst Erwan Rambourg says, referring to investors’ cautious stance. While he believes that Q3 marks the trough in the luxury downturn, he thinks that investors prefer to wait for tangible signs of an improvement rather than catch a falling knife.

And after a stellar performance in the first half of the year, jewelry brands began decelerating in Q3. Sales at Richemont’s jewelry maisons, including Cartier and Van Cleef & Arpels, rose 14% versus 24% in Q2. Sales at LVMH’s watches and jewelry division and Kering’s jewelry arm, the latter of which includes Boucheron and Pomellato, were up 6% and 11%, respectively (vs 11% and 18% in Q2). Sales at other Hermès sectors, including jewelry and home, were down 1% (vs 4% in Q2).

“Richemont’s jewelry maisons growing 14% in the fiscal second quarter is a slowdown, but it’s still tremendously better than pretty much anyone else in the sector,” Rambourg flags. “That gives a first-half average of just below 20% top-line growth for jewelry, which is the core profit driver of the company. For the first time in a while, margins have increased.”

Here are the rest of the key takeaways from luxury’s Q3 earnings.

China’s slowdown deepened after three years of deceleration. Growth at LVMH decreased 5% in Asia, while Kering fell 8% and Hermès came in flat. “It should be noted that the macroeconomic environment [in China] remains unfavorable,” Hermès’s VP of finance Eric du Halgouët told analysts during the company’s earnings call on October 22.

While the broader picture in China remained largely unchanged, with continued weakness in the real estate market, two additional factors weighed on bottom lines: the decline in equity market performance, and China’s new taxation of foreign assets. The law on taxation, which was announced in late July and applies to offshore trusts, a widely used vehicle among high-net-worth Chinese individuals, had a significant impact on the sentiment of affluent consumers; the rules have retroactive effect from 2023, and the deadline to declare and pay was just 90 days.

“The two growth engines of the industry for the past 20 years are the middle-income consumer and the Chinese consumer,” says Morgan Stanley managing director Édouard Aubin. These two engines are now barely running.

Using LVMH as a proxy, the Chinese cohort was flattish in Q2 and down approximately 15% in Q3. Richemont also highlighted the challenges in the mainland China market, despite seeing a positive trend in Greater China. “ If anybody thinks we’re less affected by [market conditions in] China, on the contrary,” chairman Johann Rupert told reporters during a media call on Friday.

Some soft luxury brands are still doing well, including in China. Ralph Lauren’s Asia revenue saw 28% growth in Q3. Greater China led retail growth for Burberry (+5%), and the Greater China region was up 5.7% for Zegna Group. In the private space, Chanel and Longchamp are also understood to perform well in China.

One category doing surprisingly well in China is prestige beauty. L’Oréal Group posted 7.8% growth in North Asia in Q3. “North Asia was back to high-single-digit growth for the first time since the first half of 2022. This marks a step change in L’Oréal’s growth algorithm in our view,” HSBC analysts, including Olivier Nicolaï, wrote in a note. Puig revenues rose 12.9% in Asia-Pacific. Does it suggest that Chinese customers are trading down — buying lower-ticket items like fragrances and skincare?

And is there a brighter outlook ahead for luxury brands in China? “There aren’t many hopes for things to improve in the short term,” Rambourg says. “I think China being very tough is probably going to be the case for the next two or three quarters. Visibility is quite poor. And if you leave aside bases of comparison, there’s no key underlying reason for China to do better.”

“Q3 was a continuation of the K-shaped economy we’ve seen in recent quarters — where the top end grows, but the lower end lags as the middle-income consumer has been priced out. The brands at the top of the pyramid are doing well; the rest are not,” Aubin says.

Zegna brand (+12.7% in Q3), Brunello Cucinelli (+13.5% in Q3), Loro Piana (“enjoying very strong growth,” according to LVMH CFO Cécile Cabanis) and Chanel (up double digits in Q1, Q2 and Q3, according to industry sources) are in the former category.

At LVMH, Cabanis noted that Louis Vuitton sales came in just behind the group’s fashion division at -5%, while Dior was flat. Rambourg remains bullish on Dior. “One, Dior is more exposed to China than some other brands, so that’s painful. Two, they have a men’s business, which is not doing as well as women’s. Three, I think it takes a bit more time for [creative director] Jonathan Anderson’s products to gain weight within the brand, but it’s certainly coming,” he explains.

Louis Vuitton felt the repercussions of both its legal dispute with Chinese tea brand Molly Tea and an issue with a shipping partner — the latter weighed on quarterly growth by a little over one percentage point. Add to that a tough year-on-year comparison basis: Louis Vuitton opened a boat-shaped mega-store in Shanghai in June 2025, dubbed The Louis, which generated a surge in foot traffic. The brand is undergoing a change in strategy, according to Rambourg: “They’re in the process of moving under the influence of deputy CEO Damien Bertrand, from what Louis Vuitton was 15 months ago, which was colorful, cheerful, fashion-driven, to something more institutional, more focused on the origin of the brand, which is the art of travel.”

A Shanghai Fashion Week attendee wears a full Louis Vuitton look.

Kering’s recent creative changes were on the agenda of the group’s earnings call. Shortly before its Q3 earnings, Kering announced the departures of Anthony Vaccarello from Saint Laurent and Seán McGirr from McQueen. And on November 5 and 6, the group announced the departure of Pierpaolo Piccioli from Balenciaga, with Martine Rose to succeed him.

While still outperforming the sector, Hermès’s growth decelerated in Q3 (+4.3% in Q3 vs +6.7% in Q2). “While Hermès’s leather goods category re-accelerated to nearly 11%, some investors questioned whether the weakness in other categories, such as ready-to-wear and accessories, could foreshadow a similar slowdown in leather goods,” Barclays director Carole Madjo says. Risk of [handbag market] saturation in China and the increasingly structured secondhand market could potentially weigh on demand over time.”

After years of Miu Miu outperforming Prada, the trend reversed in Q2, with Prada (6.3%) surpassing Miu Miu (2.6%), and continued into Q3, as Prada grew 1% while Miu Miu contracted 3%, likely due to a higher exposure to China and the Middle East  relative to the average of the sector.

Rambourg also stressed the important polarization across brands: “In the soft luxury space, we consider Chanel is now the biggest brand — bigger than Louis Vuitton — and growing very quickly. And so that’s taking a bit of the air from the others, notably adjacent brands like Hermès. In hard luxury, Cartier is continuing to do very well and is also taking a bit of air away from their competitors. So in both soft and hard luxury, you have one dominant brand which counterintuitively is growing very quickly.”

The US might remain a luxury growth driver, but things began to decelerate this quarter, partly because of a tougher comparison basis. Hermès was up 8.8% in the Americas in Q3 (vs 13.7% in Q2), and Kering’s North American retail revenue rose 1% (vs 10% in Q2). “Investors are questioning whether this signals the beginning of a normalization in the US, and whether it will be confirmed in Q4 and beyond,” Barclays’ Madjo says.

Goldman Sachs’s Rambourg dismissed concerns: “I do believe that the little softness in Q3 is temporary. I foresee a re-acceleration in Q4 linked to the easier comparison basis and the reality that holiday campaigns, new products and more thoughtful pricing should motivate people to buy. Not to mention that you had a lot of wealth creation from equity markets. Luxury demand has been a bit lagging, but I think it’s bound to pick up.”

It is unclear whether the US midterm elections — which saw the Democrats take control of Congress for the remainder of Trump’s presidency — impacted the third quarter. Some customers possibly adopted a wait-and-see approach to spending ahead of the results, which could now be released and influence Q4. “Midterm elections typically have less impact than presidential elections,” Madjo notes. Asked what impact the outcome might have on Richemont’s business, CFO Burkhart Grund said: “We’re just a few days after the midterm elections and we haven’t really picked up anything meaningful.”

Europe was up 4% for LVMH, down 5% for Kering’s fashion and leather goods division (including a 9% drop for Gucci), and up 7.2% for Hermès. “It is Europeans who are spending in Europe,” said Hermès’s Eric du Halgouët. Hermès’s sales in France decreased in Q3 to 3.6% from 6.2% in Q2, as the heatwave impacted footfall in the Parisian stores.

As brands began gearing up for the crucial holiday season, protests erupted across France, Italy, Spain, Belgium and Portugal. France and Italy are significant European markets. France accounted for 8% of LVMH’s total revenue in the first nine months of 2026 and 9.6% of Hermès’s nine-month revenues. “The comments on the impact of the protests in Europe were quite vague. It’s too hard to say and hard to quantify,” Madjo says.

LVMH’s earnings call took place before the so-called Act I, the day of major urban unrest on October 17. On October 22, Hermès’s du Halgouët said it was too early to assess impact on local stores’ business and tourism. (The Hermès store in Marseille was looted and store windows in Paris, Nantes and Lyon were broken.) “It’s not just a China problem. Now, you have a French-Italian problem on top of that,” Aubin notes, referring to the possible effects on Q4.

Despite the lack of visibility in China and Europe, Goldman Sachs’s Rambourg anticipates a progression in Q4 and next year. “Because we see the US re-accelerating, and importantly, we see self-help measures — product launches and better pricing — motivating consumers to come back,” he says.

#6683. Ronny Kobo Wants You to Embrace Holiday Dressing Clichés

The designer discusses the merits of tuxedo dressing and her new Brooks Brothers holiday capsule.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

For years, Ronny Kobo has turned to Brooks Brothers for one piece in particular: a white tuxedo jacket. “If you know a good white tuxedo menswear jacket, the best in the market is available at Brooks Brothers,” the designer tells ELLE. “Every couple of years I refreshed my wardrobe with a white tuxedo men’s size 50. And when I went to the store about a year ago, I started to daydream and I was thinking, wouldn’t it be amazing to collaborate with Brooks Brothers?”

That daydream wasn’t far-fetched; it became the starting point for Kobo’s holiday 2026 capsule with Brooks Brothers. Reworking the brand’s tuxedo and evening wear codes through a feminine lens, the collection gives sharp tailoring, satin lapels, and classic tartan a softer turn in fluid dresses and statement-making separates.

For Kobo, the collaboration was an opportunity to pair Brooks Brothers’ menswear heritage with tried-and-true holiday codes, from green and red tartan to silk bow details, clichés and all.

“Holiday dressing should be about the cliches,” she notes. “What’s fun is showing up to a holiday party in a cliche. That’s what makes your holiday your holiday party. Let’s create something that is so holiday in your closet that you take out every holiday for the rest of your fashion life.”

Despite those seasonal touches, many of the pieces can be worn year-round. Tailored staples, including a series of tuxedo jackets and formal trousers, work well beyond the holidays. Accessories feel just as seasonless, with cummerbunds, leather opera gloves, and a red rosette brooch bringing a touch of occasion to a look in any season.

The designer achieved that year-round appeal through pieces that can be styled more than one way. Kobo’s take on the white tuxedo jacket is elongated and nipped at the waist, doubling as a minidress; it could just as easily be layered with the high-waisted Ruby pant or worn over the sheer lace Beryl top. The collection is made for “going out,” with dressier options including a high-low skirt with a cummerbund waist, a fitted LBD with a red sash, and the Lazuli dress, a body-conscious stretch-satin number with a flouncy peplum.

The collection’s mix-and-match pieces reflect Kobo’s belief that black tie should leave room for individual expression.

“Allowing your personal style to shine through these tuxedo moments is really important,” she says. “Men get to show up in black tie and express their personality in such a quiet, elegant way, because you can’t put too much on a tuxedo jacket. With this collection, we’re just supplying the canvas. I’d love to see how everyone styles it, whether with lace stockings, velvet, or some kind of conversation piece that feels authentic to you.”

#6682. Hunter Schafer’s Blade Runner 2099 Press Tour Is Full of Vintage Finds and Colorful Statements

With custom Prada, Y2K Undercover, and straight-off-the-runway Lii

2026 has had no shortage of press tours. From The Devil Wears Prada 2 to The Odyssey to Euphoria to The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, it’s been a year of global rollouts and method dressing. And we’re not quite done yet.

Earlier this week, Hunter Schafer kicked off the Blade Runner 2099 promo at the Los Angeles premiere in a custom Prada leather micro dress and voluminous fur coat—and since then, she’s been bringing her A game to the miniseries’ press. Working with stylist Dara, the Euphoria actor has showed up in straight-off-the-runway pulls and vintage finds alike, piecing together a dynamic collection of ensembles as she counts down the days to the November 25 release date.

While the sci-fi series takes place some 73 years in the future, Schafer turned back a couple decades for the first day of her press junket. Working with Dara once again, the actor was seen wearing a full look from the Undercover Fall/Winter 2007 collection.

The Y2K ensemble was composed of a handful of neutral layers, including a turtleneck base, a long-sleeve ribbed knit top with sheer accents, and little micro shorts in chocolate brown. She wore ear muffs and her hair in pigtails, and tucked her semi-sheer thigh-high stockings into black-and-brown wedges.

Later, the star switched gears, selecting a vibrant color-blocked minidress from Zane Li’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection for Lii. The high-contrast runway piece saw a bright-teal shift dress with a square neckline and spaghetti straps, layered with an open-back coral-orange piece with a similar silhouette. (See photos here.)

Out at the end of the month, Blade Runner 2099 takes place half a century after the events of 2017’s Blade Runner 2049. The science-fiction limited series stars Schafer as Cora, a human fugitive posing as a Blade Runner, alongside Michelle Yeoh as Olwen, an aging Blade Runner facing death.

#6681. I’ve Rejected a Lot of Ballet Flats, But I Can’t Stop Thinking About These Glossy Repetto Pumps

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

Everyone is unreasonable about something, and mine happens to be ballet flats. Catch me in a one-on-one for long enough, and I will spew out my long list of grievances, most of which come down to shape. A lot of ballet flats are, to use the technical term, uggo: They cover too much of the foot or too little of it, the toe is square or stumpy or so long it enters the room before I do, and the block heel is cut at an angle when a block heel should be straight and symmetrical, as nature intended. Sometimes the body of the shoe is scrunched up like a shower cap, and sometimes someone goes and puts metal aglets on the bow. The horror!

Reader, I never claimed to be easygoing. But hear me out: Repetto's red patent Camille pumps are the rare pair that cleared the entire list. Repetto is about as iconic as ballet flats get, so the name kept coming up during the several nights I spent researching at 2 a.m. for a pair with a little more dressy oomph. What never came up was a proper deep-dive review of the Camille, so here's mine.

The toe is round and delicate without tipping into stumpy. The block heel is straight on every side. The hull of the shoe, for lack of a better word, is structured but still flexible, so it holds its shape instead of gathering around my foot like a drawstring bag. And there is no hardware anywhere, which feels laid-back and chic in a Parisian way to me and also means they go with whatever jewelry I already have on.

One disclosure: They do show some toe cleave, which I personally like. I'm aware a large portion of the population does not, and to those people I say, respectfully, you do you.

The consensus on Repettos, and the brand's own advice for this pair, is to size up. I went with a 37. For context, I wear a 6 in sneakers, and I've since learned I'm more of a 5.5 in ballet flats and loafers, which is the kind of self-knowledge that arrives exactly one pair too late. They're big on me, and I wish I had trusted my flats size.

I tried the usual fixes. I put in heel grips, then doubled up on heel grips, and they were still too big. I pulled the little drawstring to tighten them, which didn't do much besides make the edges wavy. My advice is to go by how you fit in flats specifically, not sneakers, and to buy from somewhere with a return policy you've read all the way through. (Groundbreaking advice, I know.)

The soles are thin—intentionally so. Repetto stitches the sole to the shoe inside out and then flips the whole thing right side out, a technique it has used since 1947. It's meant to make the shoe comfortable, the way a dance slipper is comfortable, soft and flexible enough to bend with your foot. What you don't get is much cushioning or support. It's also not what I'm used to, and not what most ballet pumps feel like. I can feel the ground under me, and I can feel the arch give a little when I walk. If you prefer a sturdier shoe, the Camille also comes with a rubber sole, like the grey-blue pair here. It comes in plenty of colors beyond red too.

Repetto Repetto Taupe Camille Rubber-Sole Heels

Heads up: These sell out often, especially in the red. Sizes go fast, so if yours is gone at one retailer, check a few others before giving up. SSENSE, FARFETCH, and Revolve have all carried the Camille, and some will let you sign up for an alert when your size is back in stock. It’s also worth looking at the other colors and finishes, since the less popular ones tend to hang around longer. Whatever you do, please don’t panic-buy the wrong size (see above).

I won't pretend $475 is a casual amount to spend on a pair of shoes. It's a lot, and whether it's worth it comes down to how much you'll wear them. For me, that's all the time. I mostly wear neutrals, like jeans and a baby tee or an all-black outfit with low-rise trousers, and these are classic enough to go with all of it yet fun enough to carry the whole outfit on their own. The red isn't a seasonal one, either, so they work in November the same way they will in May. That's my idea of a forever wardrobe piece, and by that math, they're worth it.

If that math doesn't work for you, there are other red ballet pumps that clear my list, and several of them cost a lot less.

Kim Duong is the Deputy Shopping Director at Cosmopolitan, overseeing shopping coverage online for all things fashion, lifestyle, beauty, and sex. When she's not musing about which products are actually worth your hard-earned cash, she's also writing (sometimes slightly unhinged) fashion content in print. You can find her previous writing in Refinery29, InStyle, Travel + Leisure, and StyleCaster. Follow her on Instagram for bottomless cute dog content and did-that-really-happen-to-me story times in her highlights.

#6680. 15 Best Colognes for Men in 2026, Staff-Tested and Reviewed

In 2026, the best colognes for men go beyond just smelling good, though first things first: They should smell incredible. A great fragrance nowadays tells a story, and if you choose wisely, can become part of your personal lore. I, for one, am a fragrance obsessive and will spritz a cologne at home with nowhere to be, purely for morale. What's more, years of testing and writing about fragrances has taught me just how effortlessly a stellar composition can lift your entire day, whether it’s a mainstream designer release, a niche luxury creation, or something decidedly indie.

My work in the fragrance field has also taught me that while some guys find one signature scent and ride with it for decades; others prefer a variety for different moods, seasons, and days where first impressions matter. To help you figure out where you stand, I tapped the GQ staffers who wear more fragrance in a year than most men do in a lifetime. Collectively, we put old-money classics, cult favorites, and new heat through their atomizers, looking for scents that feel distinctive and deserve repeat wear. The final cut includes a bevy of choices for all occasions, from heritage heavyweights like Acqua di Parma Colonia to future signatures like D.S. & Durga's I Don't Know What. Here's to the sweet smell of success.

Le Labo has no shortage of heavy hitters, from the omnipresent Santal 33 to newer standouts like Eucalyptus 20, but few recent launches have built buzz quite like Thé Matcha 26. Much of its insider appeal lies in its earthy yet fresh, smoky yet subtle, almost Zen-like character. Green fig leads the opening, paired with a calming tea accord, while bitter orange adds a bright bite. As it settles, the fragrance takes on a woodier, herbal edge, with a soft, green haze that runs throughout. A skin scent at heart and undeniably hip, it’s become a modern staple for Le Labo’s more discerning devotees.

Staff Notes: “I’ve been wearing Le Labo’s Thé Matcha for a few years now, and it has become my go-to. As someone who has a hard time finding a scent that doesn't give me a headache or feels too strong throughout the day, it’s one of those rare scents that just works. It has a clean, almost airy quality to it that immediately settles into something effortless and fresh.” —Bowen Fernie, senior visuals editor

Malin+Goetz is one of the few names that began in skincare and went on to make genuinely excellent, indie-cool fragrances, all at very accessible prices. The apothecary vibes run deep, from the formulas to those glass deco bottles that ooze medicine-cabinet chic. The brand's Leather EDP—like my favorite from the line, Cannabis—doesn’t smell exactly like its name. In classic M+G fashion, it plays more of a supporting role here, blended with pepper and clove for a bit of kick. Lily and orchid create a fresh floral heart, while violet adds a velvety depth, all grounded by creamy sandalwood and cedar. And of course, that warm, comforting leather note wears like a Perfecto. It’s a gorgeous spring-ready daily driver, with a grassy floral vibe that plays beautifully against the grain.

Staff Notes: “From the perfect broken-in leather jacket to a leather sofa that's been with you move after move, there's something about the smell of well-loved cowhide that's so damn captivating. Malin+Goetz captured that feeling in a bottle with its Leather EDP. The cologne brings in cedarwood and sandalwood with orchid just to avoid any possibilities of your scent being compared to a vintage store.” —Tyler Chin, associate commerce editor

Is there any cologne more synonymous with men’s cologne, period, than Polo Ralph Lauren? Since 1978, it has helped define what “classically good” smells like and sits firmly planted in the pantheon of modern perfumery. Anything that iconic will have its detractors, but it’s embedded in the culture for a reason, and few colognes today are as recognizable. Even with reformulations over the years, that signature woody aromatic structure still hits, with juniper berry and bergamot up top for brightness, coriander and a blend of herbs bringing spice, touches of florals, and leather for depth—along with that unmistakable pine accord humming throughout. Woody, aromatic, and classic, it’s a cologne guys will always rock.

Staff Notes: “Smelling good is paramount to success as a modern man. (Just ask my close personal friend Ralph Lauren.) Woody, aromatic, and a little spicy, this is a classic scent that's always on top of my dresser.” —Matthew Roberson, staff writer

It’s a household name, a modern icon, and still one of the most sophisticated yet approachable colognes you can wear pretty much anywhere. Created by Chanel’s famed nose, Jacques Polge, more than 15 years ago, Bleu de Chanel remains as singular and versatile today as ever. It opens bright with grapefruit and lemon, sharpened by a hint of fresh mint, before a heart of spicy ginger, warming nutmeg, and heady jasmine. Then comes the MVP lineup of woods: cedar, vetiver, sandalwood, patchouli, and labdanum, all working together in the citrus-spice harmony that defines this blue-hued gem. Flankers have followed, but the OG Bleu de Chanel is inimitable.

Staff Notes: “I keep a travel-sized bottle of this in my Dopp kit at all times. It's classic, great for every season, and super versatile when it comes to occasion—its citrus notes and woody base make it equally good for work dinners, poolside piña coladas, and stoking the fire outside your glamping cabin.” —Ian Burke, senior commerce editor

Baccarat Rouge 540 is now an olfactory cultural landmark. You’ve absolutely smelled this socialite-signature wafting through the night, whether from the backseat of an Uber Black or across a dimly lit dinner table downtown. Some fragrances get so popular they tip into fatigue territory, but 540 earned its status for a reason. First, it comes from one of the most meticulous noses in the game. Second, the scent speaks for itself: an intoxicating, sweet floral amber, with saffron adding a subtle spice, jasmine bringing warmth, and a heavy dose of amberwood creating that signature glowing aura, all balanced by soft woods. Polarizing, yes, but anything that moves the needle tends to follow its own rhythm, and 540 is a modern classic via its own design.

Staff Notes: “Francis Kurkdjian's reputation-making Baccarat Rouge might not be the buzziest scent on the market anymore, but it's definitely the ritziest. If you don't want to smell like a perpetually fapitzed Upper East Side doyenne, you, friend, should reconsider a lot more than just your scent profile.” — Avidan Grossman, senior commerce editor

YSL has no shortage of effortlessly elegant colognes, from more mainstream, accessible options to elevated releases in the Le Vestiaire Des Parfums collection, all infused with that unmistakable YSL panache. On paper, Trench reads as a citrus floral, but in wear, it’s laced with soft, musky undertones that give it an airy, slightly edgy feel. It opens with tangerine and bergamot, layered over heady iris and fresh neroli, before settling into a warm base of musk and cedar. A fig note threads through it all, adding a subtly sweet, verdant hue. Citrusy and floral but grounded in musk, with a slightly funky undertone (the good kind), it’s a chic fragrance you can wear from sun-soaked afternoons in the park straight into date night and out into the cool, tastefully debaucherous night beyond.

Staff Notes: “If you were to bottle the feeling of a perfect Parisian night, it would smell like YSL Trench: heady, sleek, and just a little dangerous.” —Tyler Sparling, contributing market editor

Eau de Minthé is one of the more distinctive entries in Diptyque’s GOAT-level catalog, a cooling blend of mint and patchouli that reads as a fresh, green fougère with a retro ’80s and ’90s edge, albeit very au courant. The mint is fresh and slightly spicy, far from anything toothpaste-adjacent, layered with warm nutmeg, sweet geranium, and a soft, velvety rose. It’s a cologne I wouldn’t have immediately associated with the house, until the drydown, anchored by that signature Diptyque patchouli, brings depth and candle-flickering craftsmanship the brand does so uniquely well. Fresh, aromatic, and with a bit of nostalgia baked in, this is a layered gem to wear for all your mint julep-fueled warm-weather soirées.

Staff Notes: "Diptyque's Eau de Minthé is what I imagine Michelin-level mixologists aspire toward when they're crafting their cocktails. At first sniff, it's garden-fresh floral notes are uplifted with subtle minty notes before settling into deep patchouli notes that give it a well-rounded experience that's equally light and grounding." —Gerald Ortiz, style commerce writer

To me, Tom Ford has four all-timers in his Private Blend canon: Oud Wood, Neroli Portofino, Tuscan Leather, and the sultry tobacco-vanilla duality that is Tobacco Vanille. When this spicy, warm gourmand landed in 2007, it helped redefine what a tobacco fragrance could smell like. The note historically skewed fringe or overtly macho, but Ford, of course, reframed it as chic and decadent, pairing rich tobacco leaf with vanilla, ginger, cocoa, woods, and dried fruits. The signature aroma is plush and addictive, with a near-edible warmth that never tips into excess, as sweet vanilla and spice slowly bloom through the drydown. It’s a masterclass in softening a once-polarizing note into something smooth, inviting, and alluring, and still one of the house’s most widely admired scents today.

Staff Notes: “What's not to love about Tobacco Vanille? It's smooth, smoky, sexy, and just the right amount of sweet. Far better than smoking an actual cigarette—and more luxurious, too.” — Trishna Rikhy, associate social media manager

Musc Ravageur has a devoted following, with fans reaching for this alluring, sultry, spiced gem as both a signature scent and for date nights alike. Released in 2000, it helped usher musk (as a note) into a broader, chicer tier of perfumery. The composition is beautifully layered, opening with herbal lavender, spicy coriander, and a hint of bright citrus before melting into clove and a heady rose, all resting on a rich base of musk, vanilla, tonka, amber, and patchouli. Besides being a benchmark for animalic gourmands, it’s one of the most intricately composed scents out there, where, if you read the pyramid, you can pick out each note as it unfolds. We fragrance fanatics love that.

Staff Notes: "This isn't called an icon by accident. I keep coming back to Musc Ravageur year after year. One spray of the warm vanilla, spiced cinnamon, perfectly balanced with clean musk is all it takes for pure chemistry. This is the kind of scent that turns heads." —Reginald Christian, commerce director

London-based Perfumer H has carved out its own unique path, from its apothecary-meets-indie-meets-luxury vibe to its often one-word, subtle creations that smell distinctive yet approachable. Ink is a case in point. As a self-proclaimed bookworm, I was already sold on its inspiration: late nights spent in dimly lit libraries. But the scent itself is an intriguing study, weaving together woods, papyrus (because paper, of course), heady rose, spice, warm ambers, and an incense-like, meditative quality. The result is an addictive, page-turning woody floral composition that feels both cerebral and wearable, the kind of fragrance you rock when you're quite possibly the coolest dude in the room—and likely the most well-read, too.

Staff Notes: “Perfumer H pretty much had me at their tagline: Making Air Visible. But then I smelled Ink, and was completely seduced. It transports me to lamp-lit reading rooms and old-world ateliers. And even better, because it's so light, I can apply it multiple times a day.” —Louis Cheslaw, contributing commerce editor

Well before skin scents became a thing, the indie aromatic heavyweights at D.S. & Durga dropped their now cult-classic I Don’t Know What Eau de Parfum in the late 2010s. It is less a traditional fragrance and more of an enhancer (though for many, it is the main aromatic event). The polar opposite of beast-mode projection, subtlety is its byword, with a verdant, woody air scent you lean in to experience rather than one that announces itself across a room. Iso E Super, a versatile synthetic aroma chemical known for its longevity and velvety skin-like texture, does most of the heavy, or rather light, lifting, blended with bergamot, vetiver, and sandalwood to create one of the best fresh skin scents of all time. Wear it on its own or use it to boost and layer with other fragrances. I don’t know what else to say; it all works.

Staff Notes: “I Don’t Know What has a gentle and clean scent that feels like a whisper compared to more bombastic fragrances out there. The light citrusy hit of bergamot is exactly what I need when layering scents during the warmer parts of the year.” —Jordan Bowman, commerce editor

One of the genre’s most renowned reference vetivers, this Guerlain classic has influenced not just every vetiver cologne, but many fragrances today, period. The composition is less the smoky, rooty side of the note and more early-morning, dewy freshness, clean and crisp, with just enough (good dirty) earthiness underneath to keep it interesting. Citrus and spice lift the opening before it settles into a grassy core, rounded out by touches of tobacco and woods. More than any grand concept, it smells like stepping outside early in the morning, when everything still feels a little cool, damp, and alive. With longevity and that timeless cologne feel, it has remained a benchmark since its 1950 debut and a signature scent for so many.

Staff Notes: “This bottle has been in my rotation for a few years, and it’s a benchmark for anyone into fresh, verdant scents. To my nose, it’s always smelled of drinking a Negroni in a five-star hotel room, or someplace equally polished. I spritz it particularly in the colder months whenever I’m set to meet new people, because I find it's an easy way to make a good first impression.” —Michael Nolledo, commerce director

So many folks whose taste I admire wear Colonia. Endlessly polished and easy to wear, it’s about as close as it gets to a perfect daily driver. First introduced in 1916, the Italian icon still feels as relevant today as it did over a century ago, built on that signature blend of citrus, herbs, and woods, wearing its subtlety and old-world refinement on its (freshly pressed) sleeve. The opening is citrus crisp, before settling into herbaceous notes of lavender, rosemary, and vetiver over a smooth base of patchouli, sandalwood, and soft amber warmth. It carries that classic barbershop fougère-meets-Italian-citrus-grove energy, a cologne your dad (and his dad) wore to work and date nights alike—but that smells just as fresh on you today.

Staff Notes: “'It's hard to pick the perfect cologne for the office’ is something I might say if I'd never smelled this bottle of Acqua di Parma. It smells like biting into a sexy tangerine, but in an inoffensive way that won't raise any eyebrows in your desk clump." —Doug Guida, social producer

Every exemplary fragrance house has a defining undercurrent. With Aesop (who's just as well known for its scents as its skincare), it's a botanical, earthy, elevated thread running through those amber-hued bottles. Rōzu Eau de Parfum is a woody, aromatic, rose-forward composition, not of the sweet or traditional variety, but for those who appreciate richer, headier takes. Rose, alongside iris, is one of my favorite floral notes, and here it's handled with nuance, pairing the dewy, velvety accord with a lift of citrus, then grounding it with sandalwood for creaminess, guaiac wood for incense-leaning flourishes, and vetiver for earthiness. A jasmine accord adds depth to the green, earthy rose aroma—another indie homerun from the Aussie house.

Staff Notes: “I thought I wasn’t a rose-cologne person, but then Aesop mixed in some shiso and jasmine, and it was love at first whiff. Rōzu (the Japanese pronunciation of the English word “rose”), is my go-to when I want a unisex scent that’ll last just a bit longer than the work day, because I don’t want to be That Cologne Wearer at the gym.” —Mari Herrema, marketing and production manager

Perhaps no cologne is as referenced, memed, reviewed, and well-known in modern mainstream fragrance culture as Sauvage. The line can get a little confusing, but it all comes back to a core DNA built on citrus, pepper, and ambroxan, just pushed in different directions. The EDT is ultra-fresh, the EDP adds warmth, and the Parfum goes denser. Then there’s Elixir, the darker, spicier, more aromatic outlier. It’s my favorite of the group, leaning into evening territory with nutmeg and cinnamon bringing gourmand warmth, grapefruit adding lift, and classic lavender giving it that fougère backbone, all resting on a heady base of amber, patchouli, sandalwood, and a subtly sweet licorice accord. Elixir is the refined, yet still slightly mischievous side of Sauvage—spicy, warm, fresh, and it smells good on pretty much everyone.

Staff Notes: “I was gifted a bottle of Dior Sauvage, I think, to give to a man in my life. But I love men's colognes so I decided to keep it for myself. When winter rolled around, I gave it a try and I noticed pretty immediately that the scent had pull. (I got the most interest from an Uber driver who was terribly into my fragrance until I told him it wasn't for women.) Somehow it gave me that fresh-out-of-the-shower burst of energy while also smelling woody, warm, and sexy—perfect for cooler days. I'm happy I didn't give it away.” —Savannah Sobrevilla, associate editor

The fragrances above are all GQ staffer favorites, and I worked closely with the team to bring to life what makes each one worthy of a spot in your olfactory arsenal. Of course, scent is wildly subjective. One person's all-time favorite daily driver might leave someone else scrunching their nose. Tomato, tomahto. That's part of the fun, after all. No universal crowd-pleaser exists, and what smells incredible on one guy might not work for the next.

Now, here's where I get to shine a light on a few personal favorites. From modern classics to under-the-radar niche gems and newer fumes, these are the colognes I love right now, along with a few I think deserve more attention, spanning a range of price points. Consider this a little extra olfactory inspiration, courtesy of yours truly.

I've smelled pretty much everything indie-luxe stalwart Byredo has put out over the years (including the new, fantastic Future Memories), but it wasn't until recently that I finally got my nose on Oud Immortel. It brings together just about every cold-weather note I adore, from oud and smoky incense to earthy patchouli, moss, and tobacco, weaving them into something sultry and almost decadent. But there's also that signature Byredo airiness, an almost skin-scent-like softness that keeps it from feeling too dense or overpowering.

When I first experienced Terre d'Hermès years ago, it immediately became a staple in my rotation. It's one of the best designer colognes ever, and I was, and still am, obsessed with its woody, citrusy elegance. But while the original is best suited to cooler months, with Eau Intense Vétiver, you've got an equally chic, warm-weather counterpart.

French grooming favorite Horace knows how to make fragrances that smell like they should cost far more. Inspired by Freddie Mercury's legendary 41st birthday bash at Ibiza's Pikes Hotel in 1987, this is one intriguing aromatic. The name sounds summery, but to my nose, it's more like a winter holiday celebration, with crisp fir balsam and cypress lending an evergreen character.

I’ve been intrigued by New York-based Vilhelm Parfumerie for years, right down to those distinctive bottles shaped like miniature decanters, and Morning Chess is so, so smooth. It’s a blend of citrus and amber you don’t come across often: fresh and bright on the surface, just like the morning, but a few swift chess moves later, it settles into a regal, leathery warmth with an earthy undercurrent. Checkmate.

I’m a big fan of buzzy Brooklyn house Rite of Way, as all three (yes, just three) of its fragrances are so wonderfully indie and cool. I’m normally not one for aquatics, but its inaugural scent, Outer Realm, won me over by pairing citrus and marine notes with incense to create a scent that’s anything but banal. Citron and grapefruit bring a sharp, juicy brightness, while sea spray and lotus lend an airy, almost otherworldly quality. Then, as it settles, amber emerges, giving the composition a warmth you don't typically associate with aquatics.

Quentin Bisch is one of the most renowned and daring perfumers working today, and to my nose, he has a way with woods, giving them a richness and depth that's become a calling card. His Bois Impérial for Essential Parfums, a niche house known for making high-quality fragrances more accessible, has become a sensation on fragrance forums, and for good reason. Built around Akigalawood, a patchouli-derived ingredient with a rich woody character, it has a spicy, peppery bite, while an invigorating freshness keeps it from veering too heavy.

Los Angeles–based Perfumehead’s exemplary Canadian Tuxedo reminds me of my childhood on Long Beach Island: Evening light dancing off the driftwood, when everything felt quiet, introspective, and creatively stirring. On paper, it sits in the amber family, but it wears like a meeting of resinous woods and coastal air, lifted by bitter orange leaf and coriander. As it settles, the fragrance takes on a warm, herbal quality with a touch of spice and a soft, musky finish that feels almost windswept.

I respect the citrus fragrance family immensely, but as a leading note, it’s never been my everyday go-to. L’Or de Louis completely reframed it for me: a citrus shaped by smoke and gourmand tones that’s become a fixture in my olfactory arsenal. Aromatic indie heavyweights Arquiste have a knack for weaving history into their fragrances, and this one takes us to Louis XIV’s Versailles, where bonfires burned near citrus trees at the Grand Orangery. The gold flecks in the bottle are another nod to its grandiose inspiration, resembling, to me, little flickers of fire suspended in the glass.

I recently watched a podcast where Sarah Sherman lamented that she could no longer get her hands on Santa Maria Novella's Patchouli. That's the kind of attachment people develop to the centuries-old Florentine house, helped also by its gorgeous bottles. I like Opoponax: a honeyed resin with a smoky, incense-like quality. Think monks in cloisters, holy water, dimly lit chapels, and quiet garden courtyards.

Even as Icelandic house Fischersund gains serious attention stateside, it still feels like the cool kid in the room, with a noir-leaning sensibility and music and art woven into its indie DNA. I adore No. 23, the flagship scent, which opens dark and smoky, almost charred, before softening into resinous woods, spice, and a hint of sweet citrus with a faint animalic undercurrent.

It's not often I get to shine a light on a gem in Creed's storied catalog that isn't one of its many heavy hitters, but Bois du Portugal is a bit of a slept-on classic that currently has me hooked. An old-school gentleman's fougère, it's fresh, woody, spicy, and above all aromatic, built from little more than bergamot, a hefty dose of lavender, and a blend of woods and patchouli—proof that a few top-quality elements, blended exceptionally well, can speak volumes. Created in 1987, it still smells every bit as relevant today.

Iberian Leather isn't for beginners; it's the kind of scent you have to vibe with to appreciate its artistry and complexity. A richly layered fragrance, it feels like wandering through a damp, historic castle as aged wood, worn leather, and the scent of nearby flower beds wafts through the night air. And the bottle is flat-out stunning, too, looking like something straight out of Game of Thrones.

Ever wondered about the difference between an “EDT” and an “EDP?” It's not actually all that complicated. The primary differentiator comes down to the percentage of perfumed oils used in the product, which dictates how brands classify their scents. These days, we tend to treat “cologne” as a catchall term for any men’s fragrance, but technically speaking, the term is just one of many you should know about. These are the rest.

The classifications above aren't an exact science, of course, but the concentration levels they allude to are a solid indicator of where to set your expectations, and how much a fragrance will cost.

Colognes right now have more personality than ever, and more and more gentlemen are moving beyond the one-bottle approach. Plenty of guys still swear by a signature scent, but many are building rotations based on budget, mood, and setting. As Jake Levy and Matt Belanger, founders of NYC fragrance shop Stéle, told us, “Today folks want variety: one to go out, one to go to work, one for date night, and even one to start a conversation.”

If you’re starting from scratch, keep it simple: start with two bottles—one clean, versatile daily driver and one with a little more edge for nights out. From there, add by season or occasion, like say, something fresh and citrusy for warm weather, something woody or spicy for when the temps drop.

Keep this in mind, too: classic fragrance families like citrus, woods, gourmand, and floral will always have a place, but modern perfumery is more wide-open than ever. As Carlos Huber of Arquiste puts it, if you love smoky oud or animalic leather, there’s no reason it can’t be your best cologne. Wear what fits your aura, not your algorithm.

As one of GQ’s regular fragrance writers, I’ve spent years testing colognes and reporting on the category, while the wider shopping team has spent an inordinate amount of time thinking about what deserves space on a shelf. Together, we cast a wide net, considering household names, indie favorites, heritage heavyweights, and artisanal imprints.

Because not every guy wears cologne the same way, or for the same reasons, we pay close attention to context and budget. We test scents on skin over full days of wear, tracking how they opened, dried down, projected, and lasted over time. Some needed to work at the office, others on date nights, others as an everyday signature. Each winning pick was judged on scent quality, longevity, versatility, and price, along with the simplest test of all: whether we actually wanted to keep spraying it.

The result is a list that reflects a range of tastes, occasions, and price points—from tried-and-true stalwarts to modern disruptors, affordable go-tos to wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) flexes.

#6679. Inside the New La Perla

La Perla’s comeback story isn’t a nostalgia play. CEO Alessio Vannetti recognizes that while people love vintage La Perla robes and bras, and past iconic brand moments like Halle Berry’s orange bikini in Die Another Day and Margot Robbie’s silk camisole in The Wolf of Wall Street, he’s on a mission to make modern-day La Perla just as famous.

“I want to do the best new lingerie ever. I want new generations looking at La Perla, not just for the vintage. I want the new generations purchasing totally brand new styles,” Vannetti says, speaking over Zoom from the brand’s Bologna, Italy, headquarters. “I think creativity should always lead.”

Vannetti, who became CEO of La Perla on September 1, is bullish on the lingerie brand’s prospects. Launched in 1954 by Ada Masotti, the brand became synonymous with luxury lingerie and was known for its handcrafted lacework, made by artisans in Bologna. By the 2010s, however, focus drifted as management changed hands. In 2023, La Perla was declared insolvent, and its factory went dormant. But its lace-trimmed lore lived on in pop culture: in the past few years, the brand got mentions in episodes of Emily in Paris and The Gentlemen, and Rosalía released a song called “La Perla” on her album Lux.

In 2025, La Perla was purchased by a white knight investor: entrepreneur and former Expedia CEO Peter Kern and his wife Kirsten swooped in to purchase the brand, its atelier and its former factory. They rehired all the artisans, and put a plan in place to bring La Perla back. That led to the hiring of Vannetti –– who has spent his career in brand and communications roles at houses like Gucci, Valentino, Zegna and Prada –– and a return to Milan Fashion Week with Collection #00 in September.

A new swimsuit collection will be shown later this month, to be available just in time for next summer. And La Perla’s e-commerce site is up and running, while Vannetti is scoping out revived wholesale partnerships with department stores and specialty boutiques, as well as potential store locations in the US, a top-priority market.

“Everything is new, and at the same time, everything is about reclaiming our original positioning,” says Vannetti. “How many times can you say that you are running a kind of startup, but with a brand equity as big as La Perla’s?

Where did La Perla go wrong? In part, Vannetti says, the company had pushed the brand to move faster than a high-luxury lingerie brand should. “My ambition is to create a profitable company, growing at the right speed, without compromising on quality or innovation,” says Vannetti. “In the first interview Ada Masotti gave when she founded the brand, she said that La Perla does not compromise on these two points. This is exactly what we are doing.”

Expansion at all costs is where compromise tends to happen. The brand is taking a slow approach: opening in new markets and with retail partners in order to contain that. Because lingerie is such a personal garment, he says, customers will immediately clock when the quality has gone down. “And they stop purchasing,” he says. “This is what happened in the past.”

La Perla’s production quality, after all, is its competitive edge. When the Kerns bought the company, they also bought the atelier and the factory, reviving the technique that Masotti created, on machines specific to La Perla. “She modified the machines in order to get a different stitch, and those modified machines are what have been preserved today,” Vannetti says. To keep that savoir-faire part of the brand’s secret sauce, La Perla will launch an academy in Bologna, where workers will train a new generation of sewers on techniques like frastaglio (where lace is inlaid on delicate silk or tulle) and macramé, as well as to maintain the machines should they need repair.

“We are not a public company, so we can really go at our speed, and our speed is not going to be extremely fast. It’s going to be La Perla speed,” Vannetti says. The brand has already designated the number of pieces it will produce for the next year, and it won’t exceed that. (He won’t say how many.) “I am 100% sure that by July, we will have the temptation. And that is the moment where I have to say, ‘OK, let’s stick to the plan.’ Because if you stick to the plan, and you build a brand on solid foundations, that’s where you’re healthy.”

Until then, the brand will test demand via its e-commerce store. Over the summer, the brand invited more than 200,000 former clients to shop the new collection on a private e-commerce platform ahead of the full dot-com relaunch in October. Bras started selling out, and Vannetti says a brand might be tempted to refill stock to capture sales that would otherwise go unfulfilled by switching production to a shorter-lead model — three weeks, say, rather than La Perla’s typical three months.

The brand is also testing the waters via one retail partnership with Harrods. The brand hosted a trunk show at Harrods for 19 clients — “the revenue generated was astonishing,” Vannetti says, though, again, he won’t disclose any figures as it’s too soon after a three-year shutdown. Now, he says, Harrods is pushing the brand to reopen its concession with the store. “We are running after that; we are trying to be as fast as we can, but that is the power of a desirable brand — the feeling that clients are missing it.”

Stores are also part of the strategic plan, though Vannetti says it will only open in specific markets, starting with New York and Los Angeles. The brand once had 135 stores at its peak. “We will never be in that situation again.”

While the history of the brand is paramount to this new phase, Vannetti is adamant the future of La Perla is not steeped in its past. “We all want to stay away from nostalgia,” he says. “When memories become nostalgia, there is the feeling that you cannot create new memories.”

What will the new cultural touchpoints for La Perla be? Vannetti says he is in conversations with Hollywood stylists and studios to get celebrities wearing La Perla or to have La Perla mentioned in more shows à la Emily in Paris. He’s also considering collaborations with other brands or designers if it feels right. Newness is part of the plan: in the next year, 60% of revenue will come from the brand’s icons, or recurring pieces, while 35% will be from new or one-off products.

The brand is also benefiting from the halo effect of the bra trend that dominated runways during the Spring/Summer 2027 season, perfectly in sync with its return. “Our mantra is inside by tradition, outside by choice, which is basically saying that we don’t want to and we will never become a ready-to-wear brand. But today, the bra is becoming the new top.”

But don’t expect La Perla to fully embrace ready-to-wear. That’s another wrong step past ownership took, Vannetti says. “They went in the direction of trying to aggressively become a ready-to-wear brand.” It worked best when it partnered with designers like Jean-Paul Gaultier or Dell’Acqua. “Those two moments were very good examples of how to preserve the brand identity. When they tried to expand to many different categories, it didn’t work. I really just want to do the best lingerie ever. It’s kind of the art of lingerie, the way we are approaching the future.”

#6678. The 13 Best-Dressed Celebrities at the 2026 Governors Awards

Zendaya, Penélope Cruz, and more offered an early look at awards-season style.

Awards season’s biggest ceremonies don’t arrive until next year, but the Governors Awards offered an early look at the red-carpet style to come. On Sunday night, Hollywood gathered at the Ray Dolby Ballroom in Los Angeles to celebrate artists whose work has shaped film, and the stars dressed aptly for the occasion.

This year, the Academy honored actor Glenn Close, animator Floyd Norman, and director Ridley Scott with Honorary Awards. Producers Christine Vachon and Pamela Koffler received the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award. But before the awards were presented, stars galore arrived on the red carpet in their finest finery.

Zendaya kick-started her Dune: Part Three press tour in a gilded amber gown from the archive of the British designer Giles Deacon. The actress paired the sculptural, hip-forward look with dazzling Chopard jewelry and a slim Rolex timepiece. Elsewhere, ELLE Women in Hollywood honorees Penélope Cruz, Julianne Moore, Florence Pugh, Carrie Coon, and Inde Navarette brought the fashion in Chanel, Bottega Veneta, Valentino, Balenciaga, and Dior, respectively. Primary hues—particularly a stark cherry red color—proved to be a popular choice among stars, most notably Charlize Theron, in Givenchy by Sarah Burton, and Lea Seydoux, who dazzled in a Louis Vuitton train gown. The evening also made room for menswear, with style gurus Pedro Pascal and Alexander Skarsgård rewriting the rules of black-tie dressing in unconventional looks by Chanel and Tom Ford.

Here, the 13 best-dressed stars at the 2026 Governors Awards.

In Giles Deacon, Chopard jewelry, and a Rolex watch.

#6676. 8 Fresh Perfumes Everyone Will love (Yes, Even Maximalists)

We may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

These dreamy scents smell like soap, fresh laundry, blooming greenery, and more.

Even though I love writing about fragrance, I don’t necessarily want to smell like perfume. Most of the time I wish the scent of my body wash lasted for hours or that my clothes eternally smelled like I just pulled them out of the dryer. But, as we all know, a majority of those wonderful clean scents disappear in an instant. That’s why I made it my mission to find the dreamiest fresh perfumes.

Fresh perfumes typically feature notes like ambroxan and aldehydes (two synthetic compounds that smell, you guessed it, clean and fresh), as well as citrus and musk. They can be aquatic, green, warm, or even floral, but of course, there’s an overarching subtlety about them that fits in this specific family. There's no better smell in the world (to me) than soap, fresh laundry, or simply skin, but "clean" means something different to everyone. That’s why we found an array of fresh perfumes to choose from. Just take a look at some of our faves...

If you want to smell shower-fresh at all times (who doesn’t?), keep reading to discover team Cosmo’s favorite fresh perfumes.

One Cosmo editor says: “Nothing compares to the scent of a mineralic sea breeze, and Jo Malone bottled the essence perfectly. If I close my eyes when I spritz Sea Salt & Bergamot, I’m transported back to the rocky Cornish coast. This perfume is simple in the best way possible. Even though it has just three notes—bergamot, sea salt, and driftwood—it’s completely unforgettable. I’ve gone through a full bottle since it launched this summer.”—MARY HONKUS, CONTRIBUTING BEAUTY EDITOR

One Cosmo editor says: “Alto Astral is simply fresh. (Fitting that it won the Best Fresh Perfume category in our Holy Grail Beauty Awards, right?) It’s clean and light thanks to aldehydes and coconut water, yet it becomes deep and complex with hints of sandalwood and salted amber. If you like to keep things simple, wear it alone. Don’t be afraid to layer with it though! It works with every scent family.”—JASMINE HYMAN, ASSISTANT BEAUTY EDITOR

One Cosmo editor says: "Sometimes I want to smell exactly like a bubble. And Replica has, ahem, replicated that fragrance. It's the epitome of squeaky clean. Somehow, this reminds me of being in the tub as a kid and using fluffy soap bubbles to turn myself into Santa Claus. That may not sound super appealing as a fragrance, but trust me, with the additions of creamy coconut and lavender, it's amazing."—JAYNE LEMIRE, EXECUTIVE ASSISTANT

One Cosmo editor says: “Just like a tall glass of water on a hot summer’s day, this perfume feels inexplicably refreshing. Light florals—including hyacinth, lotus blossom, and jasmine—are enshrouded with a unique water accord to make the notes smell dewy and wispy. Then this settles in an ambery musk for a soft yet warm finish.”—MH

One Cosmo editor says: “A nod to fresh laundry, Rinse Cycle is a fresh, clean fragrance with a bright, citrus opening. After it came out last year, I traveled everywhere with a mini size—I’m talking from Coachella to Paris to Miami to NYC. No matter where I went, this scent worked with every destination. It's also entirely season-less, making it a wonderful choice for hot summer days as well as cool winter nights.”—BETH GILLETTE, BEAUTY EDITOR

One Cosmo editor says: “I fell in love with this perfume at first spritz. Created in collaboration with Morgan Riddle, it's reminiscent of fresh tennis whites, cut grass, and breezy air. I adore how it makes my clothes smell, most of all. It’s like I used the best laundry detergent in the world. It smells incredible on skin, too!”—BG

It’s the ideal understated perfume that helps me shine a little bit brighter.”—MH

One Cosmo editor says: "There's always been something so supremely comforting about the smell of fresh, warm laundry straight out of the dryer. The only downside is that the wonderful detergent aroma fades quickly. Thankfully, Clean Reserve's Warm Cotton has miraculously managed to bottle it. If you've ever walked around NYC, you'll know there are a million different scents at any given time (many of them, truthfully, not amazing). However, one of my favorite city smells is walking past an apartment building and smelling clean laundry through one of the many vents along the sidewalk. Mary Honkus is a beauty contributor for Cosmopolitan with over eight years of experience researching, writing, and editing beauty stories.
