#6650. Less Space, More Beauty: Products That Do It All

From clutch-friendly essentials to giftable sets, these multitasking Ulta Beauty finds do double (or triple) duty, making your bag a little lighter.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Proof that good things come in small packages—and can serve more than one purpose. These beauty finds from Ulta Beauty help you pack less for the holidays. With a social calendar full of office parties, family dinners, and everything in between, the last thing you need is a makeup bag that weighs more than Santa’s sack. Enter hardworking formulas, all-in-one palettes, easy-to-use touch-up essentials, and a few pint-sized favorites that make getting ready—and staying polished—so much easier. Whether you’re looking to streamline your own evening bag or find a little something special for the beauty lover on your list, these holiday picks are worth making room for.

The secret to a holiday party glow without an overflowing makeup bag? Choosing products that offer more than one way to use them. Think customizable color combinations, multi-use formulas that work on different areas of the face, and products that deliver more than one beauty benefit.

Choose your own adventure with the about-face Ballet Beam Highlighting Pearls, which bring several shades together in one case, letting you play around with different finishes without carrying multiple products. Swirl your brush over all the pearls for a custom blend, or pick up a single pearl when you want a more focused glow.

If subtlety isn't on the agenda, Fenty Beauty Limited-Edition Midnight Diamonds Diamond Bomb All-Over Diamond Veil brings the drama with a diamond-dusted finish that catches the light from every angle. And while the compact may be small, the effect is anything but. A quick sweep across your cheekbones or collarbones is all you need to make an entrance.

Prefer something a little more understated? NARS Light Reflecting Luminizing Blush combines the color payoff of a blush with the soft sheen of a highlighter, giving cheeks a pretty wash of color with just enough radiance to catch the light. One product, two jobs, and one less thing to squeeze into your bag.

When holiday plans take you from the office to dinner or straight to a party, having a few easy-to-use beauty essentials on hand can make all the difference. Look for products that simplify application, make touch-ups effortless, and help you refresh your look without starting from scratch—or packing a full kit.

Ulta Beauty Collection Eyeshadow Singles let you bring along only the shade(s) you'll actually use—because when was the last time you touched every color in an 18-pan palette? With these silky powders, a quick swipe of your fingertip is enough to refresh your eye makeup, no brushes required.

Ideal for when you need a complexion pick-me-up, L'Oréal Paris Infallible Cushion Foundation puts liquid foundation in a purse-friendly case, so you can touch up coverage around your nose, even out any patchiness, or conceal redness that suddenly make an appearance halfway through the evening. The built-in cushion applicator also means one less tool to pack.

Brows have a habit of doing their own thing after a few hours. Luckily, Benefit Cosmetics’ The Brow Booth Full-Size & Mini Brow Trio includes a full-size brow pencil and wax for perfecting your arches before heading out. #6646. 28 Black-Tie Wedding Guest Dresses That Are Perfectly Formal

So you’ve been invited to a black-tie wedding. Before descending into a formalwear-induced anxiety spiral, consider the benefits—this is your chance to go all out with a statement evening look you’d never otherwise get the chance to wear. (Plus, the people-watching is guaranteed to be incredible.)

The main thing to keep in mind is the definition of the dress code. Put simply, “black tie” means floor-length hemlines, so leave the midi dress at home in favor of something ankle-sweeping. From there, you’ll find there’s a lot of variation within the black-tie wedding guest dress options.

If you’re stuck on where to start, begin by considering the setting. A black-tie event in an upscale city venue requires a different sort of formal dress than a black-tie event in a bucolic setting. Think about fabrics and the season, as well as silhouette: Do you go light and dreamy, with layers of tulle and pleated chiffon? Or moody and sophisticated with luxe silk and embroidered jacquard? When in doubt, a classic A-line or halterneck style offers just enough formality. And for winter weddings, anything in rich tones, from golden saffron to oxblood to inky navy, is a safe bet.

From simple black dresses to beaded sequins, shop our edit of the best black-tie wedding guest dresses, ahead.

You can’t go wrong with a satin dress. Elegant and polished, these slinky gowns feel like the ideal canvas for all sorts of accessorizing. SIR’s short-sleeve dark plum dress calls for minimalism with sculptural gold jewelry; something sleeker, such as Amsale’s liquid gold gown, is an opportunity to play with semi-precious gemstone jewelry (like amethysts, citrines, tourmalines, and aquamarines) to enhance the richness of the hue.

Come winter, velvet is hard to beat. Its plush texture and light-catching sheen add instant depth to a simple silhouette, as seen with Bernadette’s embellished column dress and Liberowe’s halter maxi. Just be sure to pair your look with minimal jewelry to let the fabric take the lead.

It’s in the name: If you’re not sure what to wear for this dress code, black is generally a safe bet. Experiment with the shape to bring interest to a restrained palette. Norma Kamali’s gown, which has a plunging cowl back, and Staud’s blouson bodice dress, which has a cinched waist tie, are both good options; then, use your accessories to bring personality to your look.

Take inspiration from the champagne toast with your black-tie gown. Solace London provides a relaxed fit with lots of shine, while Ralph Lauren’s silver style is great for those who prefer something a little less flashy. If you’re searching for after-hours glamour, look no further than Aje’s feather-trimmed sequined gown or Taller Marmo’s radiant gold mockneck.

There’s something especially sculptural about a draped dress. Whether it’s expressed throughout the silhouette, as on Tory Burch’s design, or shows up in the one-shoulder asymmetry of Simkhai’s dark spruce gown, the fluid finish feels undeniably artistic.

No one said long-sleeve formal dresses had to be frumpy. Try a sleeker silhouette, like Victoria Beckham’s black twist-waist gown or Kallmeyer’s minimalist burgundy maxi. For a looser fit, Proenza Schouler’s cold-shoulder piece with an open back is just what you need.

Need proof that floral dresses aren’t just for garden weddings? Consider, if you will, the following: burgundy versions from Rodarte and A.L.C., a moody but romantic ruffled option from Rixo, and an elegant floral-cloqué gown courtesy of Emilia Wickstead.

Can I wear colors other than black to a black-tie wedding?

Yes! This dress code has more to do with length and style than color—and while wearing a black gown is certainly a shortcut to looking put-together, sometimes your host will actually prefer color. A summer destination wedding is the perfect occasion for bright hues, for instance, while a fall event calls for a moody, autumnal palette.

Can I wear a jumpsuit instead of a dress?

It all depends on the jumpsuit. Something in a luxe fabric, like silk or taffeta, with sharp tailoring is probably alright (though to be safe, you can always double-check with the couple). And if you’re unsure, the staunchly anti-gown guest can opt for a polished suit in similarly upscale materials for a sophisticated twist on the dress code.

Should I choose my black-tie dress depending on the venue or season?

When in doubt, take context clues from the invite. The season, venue, and even time of ceremony are all helpful indicators of what kind of dress to pick—you wouldn’t wear a velvet floor-length gown to a morning ceremony in July, just as a strapless style in floral crepe might be a poor choice for a snowy winter fête.

What are the key guidelines for black-tie wedding guest dresses?

Can a wedding guest wear a midi dress to a black-tie wedding?

Absolutely not. Black tie equals floor-length hemlines, and a midi will look out of place in a room full of gowns.

What are the differences between a black-tie and a black-tie optional wedding guest dress?

Black-tie optional gives you more flexibility with your eveningwear, whereas black tie is stricter about what you can wear. In other words, a sophisticated midi is acceptable at a black-tie optional wedding, though a gown is still your best choice. (Minis, on the other hand, are always off-limits.)

Early this morning, Princess Kate and Prince William landed in Mumbai, India, for their first overseas royal tour in four years. The 2026 Earthshot ceremony is set to take place tomorrow night, but Kate and William are spending a total of three days in India. They began with a trip to the Ballard Estate, the business and shopping district of Mumbai. There, the Prince and Princess of Wales played a bit of gully cricket, took a ride on the metro, and visited local vendors and performers.

For the rest of their time abroad, the royals will be “celebrating innovation, sustainability, youth leadership, and the enduring connections between the United Kingdom and India,” per their office at Kensington Palace.

#6643. How Astronaut Reid Wiseman Keeps His Cool in Outer Space

Welcome to Routine Excellence, a GQ column where high-achievers share the key rituals that help them perform at their best.

During the three years that Reid Wiseman prepped for April’s Artemis II mission—for which he led a crew of three other astronauts nearly 700,000 miles, around the far side of the moon—he memorized everything from lunar geography to the Orion capsule’s elaborate controls. But, understandably, part of his training focused on not dying. Much of the mission “had no playbook at all,” says the recently retired astronaut. Still, he did have a few mantras to guide him. Here are two.

The first: Do uncomfortable things. “If I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral-buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, my world starts to shrink down,” says Wiseman. Meaning he gets better at managing stress by…seeking out stress. “The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things,” he explains. “You can even find it in a difficult conversation with a coworker—anything that gets that anxiety going.”

But embracing challenges doesn’t always guarantee success. After Wiseman and his team failed to survive a couple of flight simulators, they adopted an old aviation saying: No fast hands. “If you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick,” Wiseman says. But to counter any rash decisions, you should first “just watch the second hand on the clock moving around.” The point is to pause before making a high-stakes judgment call. “If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds,” he says. “Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed.”

Wiseman put the mantra to use during the mission when the Orion sprang a propellant leak. “Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away,” he says. He recalls how a crewmember began executing an emergency response, only for Wiseman to hit pause. Surveying the instruments, they realized the leak was minor and not worthy of a red alert reaction. “That was a good example of ‘Let’s be patient here for a minute.’ ” Take a beat and you’re more likely to think clearly—and come out alive.

We chatted with Wiseman—who will begin a new deputy role at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory on Nov. 30—about his method for memorizing the Orion’s intricate control panels, the Artemis II crew’s pre-launch heart-to-hearts, and how writing poetry about the moon helped him do his job that much better.

Reid Wiseman: Actually, I mean, we’re still subject to the laws of gravity. We’re not feeling the effects of gravity.

First and foremost is just, I don’t want to use the CrossFit model of “Be comfortable being uncomfortable,” but you do have to do things that are uncomfortable, and you have to continually do that. I have noticed if I don’t fly in a jet for a few weeks, or if I’m not diving in the neutral buoyancy lab, underwater, in a space suit, that my world starts to shrink down. This is probably a side tangent, but my younger daughter suffered from anxiety pretty bad, and I remember the therapist saying: “You got to keep her moving. She’s got to get outside, she’s got to ride a bike, she’s got to go on a walk.” And I was watching her world shrink down, and I think it’s a corollary to what we do as astronauts. We’re flying planes, a lot of us are skydivers—I am not—and you just stay uncomfortable, stay in confined environments, and then stay really engaged in team skills, keep your mind going. The best thing is continually pushing yourself in an operational environment to do scary things.

Yeah, for instance, I was just over in Switzerland. I do not like heights, I really do not like heights. And my girlfriend was pushing me to go on this rock climbing thing up the side of the Alps called Via Ferrata. You’re clipped into metal. You’re safe, but if you fall, you’re going to hurt yourself at least a little bit. And the whole time I was thinking: I do not want to do this, I have to do this. I went and did it. It was exhilarating, absolutely exhilarating. I was proud of myself at the end of it.

I do still look for those challenges. I definitely look for, if I haven’t done something before, that is usually motivation to try it, to lean into those sorts of things. You can even find it in just a difficult conversation with a coworker or with another human, anything that gets that anxiety going, gets the adrenaline up, something that you don’t want to do, but then you confront it and do it, there is a reward trigger at the end of that that is powerful.

I’m a huge conflict avoider, so it’s a struggle for me to meet those head on.

Into courage of confronting people. I don’t know. People in my office, there’s some people that thrive on it, and they do it great, doesn’t even bother them. And then, I don’t like confronting people, I figure everybody’s trying their best and if they’re getting on my nerves, it’s probably something wrong with me.

About five years ago, I just started reading books around the topics that I’m dealing with at work, and now that is my thing. I’m probably a book a week, usually audiobook, as I’m driving to and from work, but it’s on the stuff like small-team dynamics, it’s on learning environments, a lot of Carol Dweck stuff, on learning organizations, learning environments, and it’s been shocking to me how much that ties into confidence at work.

Somebody, somewhere will say, “Hey, you should read a book about this.” I’ll take a recommendation from a friend. [NASA’s] Anne McClain is a fellow astronaut, and she’s really cerebral, so she’s had a few good ones. [Retired Canadian Astronaut Corps astronaut] Jeremy Hansen, who I flew in space with, [NASA astronaut] Victor Glover’s had a few good ones. [NASA astronaut] Christina Koch has given me a few. So we all kind of trade book recommendations. And then as a crew, there were a few books that we all read as a crew, and it gave us a common language, a way to talk about things together, which was pretty powerful.

Christina had us read [retired NASA astronaut] Eileen Collins’s book, which is a very basic simple book, but it’s Through the Glass Ceiling Into the Stars, about her journey and some of the struggles that she had, and it really gave us a common language there. Then I recommended Growth Mindset by Carol Dweck. I quoted that book so many times, I think my crew all pretty much read it.

It was more in training. When we got onto the mission, we were glued together. We worked with operational psychologists before the mission, we’ve talked about a lot of this stuff and how powerful it was. We worked with a poet, we’ve worked with spiritual researchers, and cultural researchers about the moon. All that stuff just built a shared knowledge, shared understanding. But back to your original question, what do I do? I really do like to read books, I really do get a lot out of them, or at least listen to books.

It’s almost like meditation, but it’s not. But it would really soothe me. And I think in some ways, probably listening to a book or reading a book, it is an ultimate distraction from the thousands of things going on in my mind at all times. I think most astronauts are probably ADHD to some degree, but it’s a way to just put all that stuff aside and let my brain relax in a different direction for a little while.

We had a lot of parts that had no playbook at all on this mission. I think the first answer to your question is, you have to work at it, and memorization tools. For lunar geography features, I made note cards. I have to make the study tools. If somebody hands me study tools, it doesn’t work. I need that function from eyes to brain, to hand, back to eyes to brain. That’s very important for me.

For controls and displays for the Orion spacecraft, I would sit there on Saturdays, on my couch, with a blank sheet of paper, and in my head I would envision every display, and I would start writing every note of every column of every element of data on the display, and then I would check the manual and say, “All right, I’m wrong here, or I missed this….” And over time, that is just setting in stone in my brain where that is.

For emergency procedures, we developed a lot of different techniques as a crew, but two things that are germane to this. First, Victor Glover came up with the mantra of, What is the first right step? So, you’ve got a fire on the spacecraft, there’s a lot of things that matter right now, but what’s the first right step that we all need to act on right now to start combating this fire? It is pretty cool in your brain, if you just really solidify the first right step, all the other steps will come. I was just at a Brandi Carlile concert, and she was saying when she sits down at the piano, if she thinks about what she’s about to play, she can’t do it. But if she sits down and just watches her hands, they will start playing the song. I find that with emergency procedures, if you know the first step to take, usually you can follow on with the rest of the right steps.

Then we also had a really strong mantra that was forged in a couple simulators that did not go well, where we did not survive the simulator, and that is: No fast hands. That’s an aviation motto, where if you have something horribly wrong with your aircraft, you want to do stuff quick, and they train you, the first thing you should do is just watch the secondhand on the clock moving around, or just go slow.

And so, we had a suspense, what is the criticality of our next action? If we can take 30 seconds before we’re dead, let’s take 30 seconds. Some actions require a split second, they require less than a second. So, those are the ones that we really need to hone in the simulator. But even in space, we had a few malfunctions, and we very deliberately executed, no fast hands. Let’s think about what the spacecraft is telling us. Let’s methodically go through where we think we are and where we’re headed. And only when we absolutely must make a decision, let’s make that decision.

The fire alarm, that was a great example of the first right step. When the fire alarm went off, we heard the emergency tone, and immediately Victor and I went to the displays. That is what we were trained to do. And I said, “We have a fire alarm,” and immediately Jeremy and Christina started looking for smoke, or smelling around the far side of the spacecraft to see if they could determine any location for fire, because we didn’t see any. We didn’t smell any. And that was incredible to watch us all act on the first right step principle.

On the no fast hands, it was the middle of the night, and a warning came up. It’s called a runbox failure. That doesn’t matter, but it basically means propellant is being used, but it’s being used outside the parameters of where it should be. So we have a leak somewhere. Either in propellant or pressurization.

Very serious when you’re 100,000 miles away. Jeremy started executing the memorized response because it’s a very critical thing. I said, “Let’s just stop for a second. Let’s see what the vehicle is telling us.”

And Jeremy stopped, and we looked at all of our instrumentation. Pressures were stable, fuel was stable. So, if we did have a leak, it was a very small leak. Turns out we did have a leak, and it was a very small leak. That was a good example of “Let’s be patient here for a minute.” We know what we need to do, but let’s hang on and not do it quite yet.

Those times of lost communication do not bother us. We do train for those, those don’t bother us. I do want to talk for just a second about risk. Look, that mission was risky. We were pretty sure we were going to make it, but it was risky. So, before that, before we launched, we did talk as a crew very openly. We talked to our families very openly about risk—what happens if I don’t come back. I’ve been very public about that. I had a will, I told my kids what the life insurance plans were, where are you going to go if I don’t come back? Who’s going to take care of you? To me, those are conversations that are very powerful. And I think if you get to the launchpad with all of that stuff organized in your brain, you’re very at peace. And all four of us a few days before launch, we all shared the common feeling of peace.

It was very weird. It was not nerves, tension, anxiety. It was peace. Two days before we launched, Jeremy Hansen, at dinner, asked all of us, the crew together, “Hey, let’s talk for a second about how are we going to handle it if we know we’re going to die, but we’ve got a couple days before it’s going to happen.” Almost Apollo 13. We have a failure. We know we’re not going to survive, and we have several days. And it was a pretty quick conversation. We were like, “Let’s just do it with dignity and give each other as much grace as we can because we don’t know how we’re going to react, but dignity. Let’s come back to just doing it with dignity.” Who ever has a conversation like that?

And the four of us had that conversation, and very quickly, we all aligned behind dignity, that is how we’re going to approach this, but we’re also going to have grace because we’re not in that situation right now. We do not know how people are going to handle it. I mean, I could have a total terror attack, a panic attack, you don’t know. But the fact that we were in a place where we could talk about that stuff was very powerful, probably because we’re all around 50, we felt very accomplished in our lives, and very satisfied with where we were. We launched overwhelmingly at peace.

Not quite that aggressive, but exhausting, yes.

It’s a number of things. First, the four of us were all very committed to excellence and to being there for each other. Even if we didn’t always show it, we always committed to it. We talked a lot about wanting to launch as friends and land as friends. That’s a bit of lip service, but it was a motto that we tried to uphold. We’re just never going to give up on each other. We’re going to work on this for the rest of our lives. And then, in training, we often joke that we were like the basketball Olympic dream team, where you took all the best players from basketball, put them together, and they were a terrible team.

For quite a while, we were just not a great team, but we were working on it. I bore a lot of responsibility of that as a commander. Like, why can’t I get these people in line? But also with this crew of experienced and senior astronauts, I couldn’t just say, “You’re getting in line.” It just wasn’t going to work. And I didn’t want that, I wanted us all to be ourselves. Each one of us brings an individual richness into this tapestry of this crew, and I wanted that to show through.

I was willing to deal with some pain and agony over crew dynamics if it meant everyone showing up at the end together. I think that did pay off very well. So, we noticed pretty early on that we had these crew dynamics issues, and we set up a couple extra meetings with our...at NASA, we have these people called BHP, behavioral health and performance folks. They’re all psychologists, operational psychologists.

We set up some meetings with them. They had all these guided points. The first question they asked us, I don’t think they ever asked us another question, we tore ourselves apart. I think every member of the crew cried at some point. We exhausted ourselves, and they were like, Wow, you guys really have some issues we need to work through. So, we did more meetings with them, and we did work through a lot of that stuff. We didn’t work through all of it. But what that process showed with those behavioral health folks is our willingness, our commitment to each other. I didn’t need us to launch perfect, I just needed us to be committed to each other.

Then, I will throw in this one thing a few months before launch, because I also think this was important: We spent a lot of time giving each other feedback. But before launch, I wanted to make sure we also shifted to meeting each other where we are. I mean, you can tell me how to change for the next 10 years. At some point though, I have a personality that is just who I am. I’m going to work every day to be better, but at some point, I think you need to meet me where I am, and I need to meet you where you are. And we did that, and that was very powerful as well. By the time we came off the launchpad in that vehicle, we were really, really, really together. We didn’t have to be. I know there’s been a lot of crews that haven’t been, but we were.

That’s very well said. Because our crew conversations were harder than any technical matter that we had to solve in this training at least.

Yes, but I won’t read it, although some of them were actually very good. We talked to a professor of English, Chris Cokinos, at the University of Arizona. But he held quite a few workshops with us, and he gave us drills. I wrote him an email a couple days ago just thanking him for allowing us to express creativity in the ways that we saw the world and the moon. And his stuff was all focused on the moon. How do you relay the moon in the five senses? And how do you do it in a way that captures imagination?

In the end, we’re all kind of philosophers, and it just helped us be a little bit more creative in the way we saw things, and it reinforced to us that you can find beauty if you’re looking for it. I love the way Chris Cokinos framed for us the beauty of the moon. Because an engineer or a geologist could have framed it as a barren, stark, celestial body, but Chris framed it as a magnificent, beautiful, celestial neighbor. And just having that sense and that feeling really showed through when we were out there.

I kept a journal on my computer on the mission, just putting, remember, every day, just think about sight, smell, touch, taste, feel, and go through those every day in this vehicle. Sadly, the computers were so hard to use in space, I did not journal on that even a singular time. But basically every day we would do a five senses kind of thing, and you could be in the middle of a simulator, and I would pull out my notebook and just jot. All right, I just did this docking maneuver. And that docking maneuver, that’s the most technical thing you can do. What was the sight, smell, sound? And wow, all of a sudden you start pulling out tons of data that you otherwise would’ve neglected.

It is starting to abate a little bit. But we were doing an outdoor podcast, getting interviewed in this beautiful setting in California, and a little breeze came from left to right across my face, and I was like, “Man, that feels incredible.” And I never would’ve noticed that even. I was walking around New York City, and I saw some tulips coming up out of the ground, and I was stopped dead in my tracks for a few seconds just looking at them, thinking about how impossible it is that, in this brown dirt, these beautiful green sprouts are coming up, and it’s like the birth of spring, and summer’s here. It was like, why am I focusing on all this? But I was focusing on all of that.

I say this all the time when we’re out talking to the general public, but in Apollo, those guys talked about peace and joy and hope, and then we went out there and we talked about peace and joy and hope. I just think if you’re a quarter million miles away looking back at this impossibly unique planet, it’s the only words that we have in the English language that can convey even a small portion of what that felt like.

We saw sights on the far side of the moon, and especially when the sun eclipsed behind the moon that I can’t even describe the beauty, especially of that eclipse. It was otherworldly. And when I look at the moon now, I still think about that. I know when the right side of the moon is lit up at night, but not the left side of the moon, I almost don’t even look at it because we didn’t see that. But when the left side of the moon is lit up, that is very relatable to me, and I know what’s on that other side now.

We only saw 18% of the far side on the left side, but I know what that looks like back there, and I think about it all the time. The moon became more of a friend when we were around it, I just felt comradeship with the moon. It was revealing its secrets to us. We were seeing parts of it that it doesn’t reveal to people on Earth, but we were seeing them, and it was very powerful.

Yeah. I think about all my family, all my friends, and now that I’ve talked to you on this, I’ll think about you next time I look at the moon.

It’s the old TV. It’s the thing that we can look at from anywhere on Earth and we know we’re all seeing the exact same picture. I used to look at that and think about my brother when he went away to college, and I’ve always loved that. I was in the Navy; I love being at sea and watching the moon rise over the ocean when it’s just reflecting off the ocean. The moon’s a very powerful, very beautiful thing to get to look at. To me, it’s more a peace and togetherness than anything. ✦

Surviving space is a group effort, and Wiseman has often sought expert wisdom on issues “he’s dealing with at work.” Before retiring in September, he averaged a book a week, which he usually listened to while commuting to and from the Johnson Space Center in Houston. If a book really hit, the rest of his crew might read it too—effectively forming the world’s most high-functioning book club.

A version of this story originally appeared in the December 2026 issue of GQ with the title “Routine Excellence with Real Live Astronaut Reid Wiseman.”

#6641. In Trans Communities Across the Country, Clothing Swaps Are Promoting Style—and Safety

Every time Isaiah Kirk leaves the Uncommon Closet’s clothing swap, he steps out onto the streets of Chicago in a new look. Most recently, his haul included a pair of jeans matched with a Pokémon graphic tee and a button-up shirt. The total cost of this outfit? $0.00.

"It’s a lot of fun," says Kirk, who identifies as nonbinary and transmasculine, of sourcing new wardrobe items at clothing swaps like the one held by the Uncommon Closet. “The environment, the camaraderie, it’s safe and inclusive.”

For Kirk and other trans and queer people, clothing isn’t just about style; it’s about expressing themselves in a way that aligns with their gender identity and feeling as comfortable as possible in their own skin, even as anti-trans legislation continues to threaten or limit trans existence in public life across the United States.

A clothing swap setup at Chicago’s Uncommon Closet.

“I primarily work with people who have body dysmorphia or dysphoria,” says AJ Mix, who runs community outreach at the Uncommon Closet. Many of their clients are trans or queer people who have faced discrimination for expressing a different gender identity than their sex assigned at birth. “A lot of people have trauma going to stores,” Mix says. Their job is often to function as a sort of therapeutic personal stylist, accompanying clients—some of whom are trans women early in their transition—on trips to gendered shopping aisles they might be afraid to navigate alone.

According to Mix, the Uncommon Closet’s clothing swap was meant to be a one-time event in 2024, during the queer sewing and alteration business’s grand reopening. But then they noticed the huge demand for this free service. Mix now hosts three swaps a year—in spring, summer, and winter—to help people prepare for the seasonal shifts in Chicago’s weather. “We have a lot of new people coming in from the South to Chicago due to the political climate,” Mix says. “A lot of people use their entire savings to haul their entire lives up here, and so they just don’t have any money.”

Elsewhere, on the East Coast, Alex Carroll, the 20-year-old founder of NYC Youth for Trans Rights, organizes clothing swaps for young people who struggle to afford gender-affirming accessories. A binder, which flattens the chest to give wearers a more masculine silhouette, can run upwards of $50 and be difficult to source in person. Carroll loves to see people walk away from their clothing swaps, visibly thrilled to have scored a binder for free.

But even more than that, Carroll loves seeing people make new friends and find their community at these meetups. “There’s constantly stuff being thrown at trans people,” Carroll says. “You have to find people who are similar to you to help support each other.”

In Austin, Christabell Nunez wanted to create a safe space for marginalized people of all different body sizes to explore fashion. “It is still so hard to shop for plus-sized people. You really have to scavenge,” Nunez says. “A lot of our trans people, they are getting stared at. They’re getting looked at in retail spaces.”

In 2024, Nunez hosted a plus-sized clothing swap in her backyard that was attended by 20 friends. Now that work has expanded into the nonprofit I Slay, which hosts swaps for well over 150 people every month. Everyone is welcome to take as much as they want, Nunez says; the only limitation is that people are asked not to resell the clothes for profit.

“Our mind gets blown every month,” Nunez says. “There’s somebody who flew in from Canada one time to come to our swap.”

Melissa Grzybowski, head librarian of youth services at the Pflugerville Public Library in central Texas, says the trans clothing-swap program held by the library doesn’t just help the trans community: “It helps everyone.” At one of the library’s first swaps, Grzybowski saw a refugee mother find new clothes for her children after fleeing their country with only two suitcases of belongings.

In 2021, Texas proposed the highest number of anti-trans laws in the United States. Still, Grzybowski tries to make her programming and literature inclusive. “Public libraries are supposed to be welcoming to all people,” she says. “We have lots of books that represent the LGBTQ+ experience.”

A clothing swap attendee browses at Tennessee’s Trans Empowerment Project.

One state over, in Tennessee, Jack Knoxville saw very little representation for trans people when he started a clothing swap back in 2016. At the time, he felt there were only negative representations and ideas of what it meant to be trans in his home state.

“I’ve been on my own and dealt with being unhoused from the age of 14 on, and had to deal with surviving so many things,” Knoxville says. “I know what it’s like to be trying so hard to get a job and getting the door shut in your face because your name on paper doesn’t match the perception of your gender with that interviewer.”

Knoxville says they’ve seen people walk out of their clothing swaps feeling more confident for job interviews and equipped for the cold winter while couch surfing. “It’s the same kind of euphoria that you feel when you have a good haircut… You can feel like you’re on top of the world,” Knoxville says. “Clothing has a huge impact on people and their ability to interact with each other, but then on top of it is that layer of safety and how other people perceive you.”

Now, with the nonprofit Trans Empowerment Project, Knoxville has helped to show people from across the country how to host clothing swaps in their own cities.

“Queer people especially have to be resilient, and they have to tap into creativity and create something from nothing,” Knoxville says. “We find ways to take what’s left, the crumbs that are given to us, and turn them into celebrations.”

#6640. Rashida Jones and Will McCormack on Telling Sex Jokes and Building The Invite Around Its “Prodigiously Gifted” Cast

The two screenwriters adapted Cesc Gay’s The People Upstairs (2020) for a modern American audience

This summer, The Invite dropped audiences into a turbulent middle-aged marriage where only bitterness simmers beneath a thin, leftover layer of love and any sexual desire vanished long ago. The couple at the center of the story, Joe (Seth Rogen) and Angela (Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film), live at each other’s throats, feigning a relationship for their daughter’s sake. This brittle romance is put to the test when a neighboring couple (Ed Norton and Penélope Cruz) come over for dinner and propose, well, group sex. Bottled-up emotions and memories fill the night as four dinner guests banter and battle, delivering the best sex comedy in years, elevated by witty, cathartic dialogue from screenwriters Rashida Jones and Will McCormack.

A great sex comedy relies on a great premise, whether it’s designed to shock or move its audience. Jones and McCormack reworked Spanish filmmaker Cesc Gay’s The People Upstairs (also known as Sentimental), crafting a script that balances both, exploring how romantic turmoil emerges from a culture of emotional suppression and what happens when this lifestyle rubs up against a more radically open approach to feelings and sex. Much of the realism in The Invite comes from Jones and McCormack closely studying their own relationships with love and loss.

“We had all these big dreams when we were young,” Jones says. “It’s a real embarrassment of riches. It’s when you get to 50, and you’ve had a lot of your dreams come true, and you have all the things that you dreamed about when you were 20, 30, and even 40. Here we are, and what now? The ‘what now’ is infused in the movie.”

Decades of friendship have informed Jones and McCormack’s writing. They first met on a blind date in 1999, but the romantic relationship did not stick; in its place, a creative partnership blossomed. In 2012, they released their first full-length feature, Celeste and Jesse Forever, a bittersweet examination of divorce and friendship starring Jones and Andy Samberg.

“When we were young, we were writing about the heartbreak of love, and now we’re writing about the heartbreak of life,” McCormack says. “Marriage is not this triumphant experience. It’s a broken hallelujah; it’s one day at a time. That’s the beauty of it: the endurance of it and the longevity of it.”

Bazaar sat down and spoke with the pair about tailoring their script around a quartet of legendary actors, the “accordion effect” of Olivia Wilde’s direction, and how the two screenwriters have bounced ideas (and sex jokes) off each other for three decades.

Rashida Jones: In 2022, we were approached by David Permit, one of our wonderful producers, and we were hired to write a script for a whole different version of this movie for different directors. It was probably the most fun I’ve ever had, writing that first draft with Will. We just had a great time because we saw the movie and it totally works and it’s culturally specific. We watched it at first, and we thought, “Wow, it’s perfectly executed. What can we contribute?” Then you watch it again and again and again, and you start having conversations about your own life and your own relationships and people that are on your mind. We started to feel like we might have something to say in this world and that could add value and be more culturally specific to being American. How we would have this conversation—this evening, in our country. It felt like the perfect combination of source material and then a place to grow.

RJ: I’ll take the easy part. We’re just immature, and we like to make sex jokes to each other because we’ve been best friends for 30 years, so that was easy.

Will McCormack: There’s no DP. We brought all the DP.

WM: We were having fun with that stuff. Cesc Gay’s movie is so brilliant. When we watched it, you think, “Oh my God, this is so beautiful.” But then, as Rashida said, you start to think about it more, and you say, “Wouldn’t it be fun to do this?” And then you get the job, and you actually get to do that. It’s so rare. When we watched the original one, I remember halfway through, we said to each other, he’s going to go in the other room at the end and play the piano, and it’s going to wreck us. And he didn’t. I liked their ending, but we thought, this is going to be so fun to dive into: [Seth Rogen’s character] pulling up the piano lid, sitting at the keys, and there’s this Graduate-style ending where she’s going to walk in and the camera is going to end on her face, and [we’re left thinking], is she in or is she out? That was our entry point to this version. It’s how we got the job, because we opened the conversation with the ending.

RJ: Rhythm is so important to us. The truth is, when you infuse a role with an actor, rhythms change because there are things that make sense coming out of people’s mouths and things that don’t. For us, this period before shooting was our rewrite period, which was insane because we were doing eight-hour days with the actors and getting a download of their ideas and concerns, then rewriting simultaneously. That period was really when the movie was the version of the movie on the screen. It was designed for these particular actors on the screen. Their cadences entered our heads, so we needed to rewrite with them in mind. We were trying our best Penélope Cruz and Seth Rogen impressions.

WC: These actors are all prodigiously gifted and giants. They all brought their own pathos and idiosyncrasies. Penélope brought this incredible mystery and mystique and aura. Edward brought this radical honesty. Olivia brought a woman on the verge of a nervous breakdown at all times. Seth brought this profound simplicity. So it was such a gift to work with them and help tailor these parts to their voices.

RJ: Penélope had a really strong instinct. She’s one of our best. What can I possibly say about her? She really wanted to talk about perimenopause, which I too have that cross to bear at the moment. She wanted to get into it and was very conscious that her character has depth. She didn’t want her to have this wise, objective point of view. She wanted to have her own life and flaws. All that stuff comes out at the end, where she bites back at Hawk and tells him to shut the fuck up and then apologizes quickly. You get a window into their relationship. That really came out of conversations of “How can we show how imperfect their very new relationship is? How can we show that everybody’s struggling with their version of an issue?” It’s not all perfect over there just because they have figured out a way to live in an open relationship.

WC: The magic of movie-making is that there are a million different versions of The Invite. This version could’ve only happened at this moment in time, in this city, with this director, with these four people. It’s magic. I was most surprised by Penélope, who was so smart and didn’t want to feel like this wise woman on the hilltop delivering sage advice to these people in the room. Because life is not like that. It’s messy and complicated, and she has her own problems. When actors are that good, they just surprise you over and over again. We’ve said it before, but the best element of storytelling and screenwriting is surprise—when you don’t know what’s going to happen next and you’re on the edge of your seat.

WC: Edward is one of the best actors we have as well. He is so smart. Right from the very beginning of the rehearsal process, he wanted. He was adamant that we talk a lot about Hawk’s backstory and that his sexual expansiveness came from a place of real pain and trauma. We talked a lot about Hawk’s backstory. We talked about how he had massive regret and pain and that he had a moment in his life where he was going to fold or turn over a new leaf and live without regret. It was incredible to talk to him about it. We never heard the final version [of the speech until the day we filmed].

RJ: He wanted to surprise the actors. We wrote him a template, a blueprint, so he had that. Then he could do whatever he wanted because he had something in mind. The sentiment was there, and it was something we had talked about because we wanted to make sure whatever, wherever it ended up, had to be tender and raw. Coming out of that, it gave Joe another opportunity to be uncomfortable with feelings. He could just make a joke, and that would set off the next part of the interaction, so everybody could be mad at him for being immature.

WC: We have Joe’s line slotted there, “I’m sorry that your dead wife couldn’t peg you,” which then detonates the entire thing again. Olivia did such a great job of orchestrating this accordion effect of quiet to blow up to quiet.

RJ: We have our go-tos. Nora Ephron. We’re always watching James L. Brooks for rhythm, pacing, and dialogue. Of course, Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf? was a reference for us because it’s a movie we grew up both loving and a play we love. It has this chamber-piece tension that you need to keep. There are literal steals and direct references to that movie in our version, [such as including a character who works as] an associate professor. Movies like Bob & Carol & Ted & Alice and, in general, Paul Mazursky for the reality of being in a messy relationship.

WC: [Ruben Östlund’s] Force Majeure and always Joachim Trier for the honesty of people being really vulnerable with each other. It’s never corny, and it’s really heartbreaking and true and admirable. The end of The Invite gets very real when she says, “We were best friends, and we had sex all the time, and it was incredible.” There is a moment where it really lands.

RJ: Everybody’s so different. We talk a lot because, for us, theme is king. We want to make sure we know what we want to say. We identify how we want to feel and how we want other people to feel, and we write toward that. We’re not going to leave feeling like there’s a bad guy; we want to leave feeling like we root for them as people, separately and together. Whatever happens after this night, this was a necessary step in excavating the deepest emotions and truth that were never revealed, and they are left vulnerable with tenderness and gratitude for the relationship they did have. We talk in those terms, and then we get into structure, and then we can talk about which scenes are which and how we get there.

WC: Luckily, we’ve known each other for so long, and we’re so comfortable with each other. That’s so important to a partnership. I’m not afraid to pitch any idea to Rashida and vice versa. I’m not afraid to write poorly. I feel total freedom of expression, which is an important thing in collaboration. Our lives have orbited each other in an interesting way as friends, but also creatively. We’re both really into loss, and life is a series of losses. There’s so much heartbreak and loss, but there’s so much hope and humor. The hardest moments of our lives have been the funniest, and it’s been a gift to write it all down with her. Hopefully, we can do it again!

#6639. The Greatest Grand Theft Auto Missions, Definitively Ranked

Grand Theft Auto VI drops on November 19th, and there are many ways to prepare. I’ve been replaying every game going back to the original, with a particular soft spot for the 3D era: III, Vice City, and Rockstar's greatest achievement, San Andreas—yes, yes, I'm coming in hot. After some 13 years of GTA Online, with its perpetual content stream and microtransactions, it’s easy to forget how it all began. The franchise has consistently brought freewheeling chaos and mayhem, sure. But it has also always delivered memorable story missions, which evolved from basic lures and assassinations into something like GTA V's “Friend Request or “Reuniting the Family,” culturally scathing mini-movies which have to be played to be believed. “My least favorite mission involves Michael using a tattoo gun on me,” former Rockstar director, writer, and producer Lazlow Jones told me of the latter mission. “I still give Dan [Houser] shit about that one to this day.”

What follows is a ranking of the greatest missions in the series’ history, with one caveat: I only allowed myself four missions per game, maximum. To help sort through the clear classics and happy accidents, I talked to some of the people who made these games come alive, including Jones, former Rockstar North technical director Obbe Vermeij, and West Coast rapper Young Maylay, the beloved voice of Carl Johnson. Shockingly, Maylay says he’s still fond of the infamous “Wrong Side of the Tracks.” “All we had to do was follow the damn train, CJ!” Maylay said, imitating his exasperated sensei Big Smoke. I’m not including that mission on here, though, partly because I’d like to make it out of this piece alive.

Bum. Budupup-budum. For a lot of us, that theme was the beginning of our Grand Theft Auto journey. What follows is barely prologue. There's an ambush on the Callahan Bridge, an escape with 8-Ball, and a drive to a safe house in Portland, Liberty City's Brooklyn-by-way-of-Queens industrial borough. You do not fire a single shot. And yet each playthrough already looked different. Did you open the short manual and splay the map across your bedroom floor, or drive blind to the edge of the Red Light District?

"The most memorable mission for me was the first one I ever played, 'Give Me Liberty,'" Lazlow told GQ. Once the host of Technofile, a syndicated show about technology and video games, Lazlow showed up at Rockstar’s Manhattan offices in 2001 to report a radio piece. Not long after, he was spoofing American radio himself as the iconic voice of Chatterbox FM.

"[Former Rockstar CEO] Terry Donovan brought over a copy of the game the day it came out. Dan [Houser] had given me a PlayStation 2,” Lazlow continued. “I'd worked on the radio for the game all summer with Dan but I hadn't actually seen it. After the cinematic ended, I got into the car and Head Radio came on and I'm driving through town. It blew my mind."

Crazy what a difference three years can make. The Donald Love of GTA III is a composed real-estate scion with a media empire. Liberty City Stories, set in 1998, shows you the man before the polish, who’s way more overt about his hunger for power — and human flesh.

The mayoral race is his project, and Toni Cipriani is his instrument. Toni guns down the incumbent mayor R.C. Hole, somehow engendering only one star. "Steering the Vote" then puts him behind the wheel of a campaign van, zooming across Staunton while the loudspeaker blares: “O'Donovan is a communist!” “O’Donovan hates America!” or “A vote for Love is a vote for happiness!” The van has to reach specific stops before the messaging triggers, which means the game is literally grading you on how much of the world you can seduce. GTA may have predicted everything from Ozempic culture to billionaire doomsday prep, but there was no forecast sharper than this one.

For most of Rockstar’s history, the studio—technically a U.S. company, but with a British development team—has made its bread and butter satirizing America, and nothing has been off the table. But in London 1969, the first of two expansion packs for the original Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar transplants its crime sandbox to London in the late ‘60s, where the Brits take center stage. (“Who gave Paul McCartney a shotgun?” one YouTube commenter asks.) Broken up into chapters, the seminal “Dead Certainty” draws on the high-flying exploits of the real-life Kray twins, the foremost perpetrators of organized crime in London’s East End at the time, who rubbed elbows with politicians and entertainers before ultimately being locked away for life.

Grand Theft Auto is a game about many things, but one of the first things it was—and still is—is a game about cars. If San Fierro’s underrated main story missions aren’t enough (yes, I know, Cesar. The yay is leaving San Fierro again), head on over to Easter Basin for the best edition of “Exports and Imports.” The concept dates back to the original GTA, where it was called “Crane Bonuses,” but it’s a classic here because of its sheer scale. What starts at the docks turns into a mad hunt across the entire map of San Andreas, finding and then delivering 30 specific vehicles.

San Andreas has 212 defined vehicles, more than twice as many as Vice City. You start learning the taxonomy—how to tell a Remington from a Sabre and an Infernus from a Cheetah—and figuring out where certain vehicles turn up. The Camper can be found on top of Mount Chiliad, meaning the hard part isn’t finding it so much as getting the lumbering thing back down in one piece. When I was younger, I never really appreciated these side missions. Now, I love how they slow the game down and make you observe all the GTA sandbox goodness you might otherwise race past.

Rockstar has a long, cruel history of giving you a remote control and trolling. But unlike “Supply Lines” or “Demolition Man,” there’s a certain genius to this one. Vic Vance pulls up outside the Mendez compound and, instead of going in like a cowboy, climbs into a van to command a newfangled robot servant, Domestobot. At this point the game becomes a butlering simulator: Fetch a drink, light a cigar, and clean the floor, all the while trying to crack a drug kingpin’s basement safe. Rockstar didn’t forget about our charming robot after this, either. In GTA V, Radio Los Santos host Big Boy laments the Domestobot future that never arrived: "We have internet glasses, but not our own robot butler!”

In 1995, at age 17, Blair Renaud joined what became Rockstar Canada (now Rockstar Toronto), and stuck around long past his original contract, eventually becoming a technical director. “I basically walked into the boss's office and was like, ‘I'm not leaving. I'll do whatever you want,'” Renaud told me. After designing the London ‘69 map without ever having set foot in England (“I just winged it”), he and his entire Toronto office were put on QA duty for Grand Theft Auto 2, with its grim retro-futurist Anywhere City and sharper graphics.

GTA has always played with consumption (Donald Love likely ate his real estate mentor, Avery Carrington) but “Hot Dog Homicide!” is GTA2 at its most dastardly. In the original PC/Dreamcast version, you steal a bus, load it with civilian passengers, and deliver them to a Russian mob boss's meat grinder to satiate his army. “I think [GTA] was actually more controversial [in the beginning] about the crime, rather than just the violence,” Renaud said. “It was like ‘Oh, I'm like stealing people's cars and running them over.' It was a little bit more real.” For all the creative choices the series has been pilloried for in the ensuing years, a mission like “Hot Dog Homicide!” wasn't nearly as explosive then as it would be today.

I always get excited about missions that let you revisit a location you've already seen, especially when the game gives you a reason to see it differently. “Bury the Hatchet” sends Michael and Trevor back to North Yankton, the snowy Midwestern state where GTA V began, where the two men start digging into the events of the botched bank heist that set their lives on their current course.

It’s San Andreas’s “St. Mark’s Bistro” done better. Instead of briefly dropping you into a familiar location for a quick hit of nostalgia, GTA V actually lets you spend some time knee-deep in the snow. Michael and Trevor each retrace the events of the heist; Trevor unearths a coffin marked with Michael’s name, only to find Brad’s decomposing body inside. Ultimately, the two men aim guns at each other. Michael has spent much of the game on his high horse insisting that he’s changed, while Trevor, always the firecracker, is at least honest about exactly who he is.

Another great LCS mission that adds to Liberty City lore. Donald Love sends Toni to explosives expert 8-Ball (who still has functioning hands at this point) to raze an entire neighborhood, Fort Staunton, and pave the way for his Panlantic deal. With the Forellis giving chase, Toni has to get a van loaded with explosives to the site, then race through tunnels planting charges beneath the neighborhood. No way those tunnels aren’t at least a little inspired by Die Hard with a Vengeance. After the biggest explosion in GTA history (not bad for a PSP game), the National Guard can be found roaming the neighborhood. And by GTA III, Fort Staunton is teeming with scaffolding, construction pits and Cartel members, a neighborhood still reshaping itself after Toni’s seismic contribution.

There are few things more San Andreas than being handed a shoddy military plane by a mysterious government agent and being told to fly it across the state without being detected by radar. “N.O.E.” is the greatest test of your skills acquired in the Pilotwings-esque gauntlet, “Learning to Fly.” Fly too high and the military shoots you down; fly too low and the terrain dings you first. The mission captures just how far Mike Toreno has pulled CJ from the streets and into the shadowy world of government conspiracies.

Greg Johnson, a hip-hop journalist who became Rockstar's senior researcher from 2003 to 2020, traces those wild Toreno missions to the 1992 film Deep Cover. Most people know it through its title song, Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg's first record together. But the film itself touched on government corruption and drug trafficking in Southern California.

“Loved that Dan [Houser] put some Deep Cover-inspired missions in GTA SA with Mike Toreno basically playing Agent Carver and CJ as John Hull,” Johnson said. “I definitely talked to [Houser] a lot about Deep Cover, but he was also having conversations with [West Coast hip-hop producer and Rockstar writer] DJ Pooh, who personally knows [drug lord] Freeway Rick [Ross] about that era, and reading up on books and reports…as they wrote the game.”

Heavy metal band Love Fist is in a pickle. Think Speed, only with a limo, and even thicker Scottish accents than Groundskeeper Willie. The mission is straightforward, but not easy: drive the limousine across the city while keeping the momentum steady enough to hold off detonation. It’s also a testament to how Vice City could turn even its tertiary characters into stars. Love Fist barely occupies a sliver of the game, yet they've stuck around as memorable rockstars for more than two decades. Obbe Vermeij, longtime Rockstar North technical director, also has a soft spot for the mission. “Particularly funny,” he notes, “because the Love Fist voices are just guys from the office.”

There isn't a single on-rails shooting sequence in Grand Theft Auto that I've ever passed easily. Doesn't matter how many times I've played. I’m no deadeye. Luckily, in “Reuniting the Families,” there’s plenty packed in before we get to that. This is back when CJ, Sweet, Ryder and Big Smoke are all still homies, and when the vast map of San Andreas is still centered on the few-mile radius around Grove Street. You head to a motel with the intention of saving the hood, only to find it crawling with SWAT. After battling your way through the rooms and taking down a helicopter on the roof, you escape by car with the cops still in pursuit. Smoke is behind the wheel while an AK with unlimited ammo is placed in your hands. The cops can even climb onto the car and try to wrestle the gun away from you. It’s a wild, arcade-style sequence, but also one of the last hurrahs for the homies before betrayal and more nonsense from that bastard Frank Tenpenny. Fittingly, the getaway car flies straight through a Sprunk soda billboard reading “A Taste of Things to Come.”

“Cop Land” is peak bromance between Tommy and Lance, before the latter decides to ruin the movie. It’s also a snapshot of just how much more active and assertive Vice City’s main character is than man-of-no-words Claude, made all the more credible by the late Ray Liotta’s swagger in the role. Tommy isn't merely taking orders and working his way up someone else's criminal ladder. By this point, he's building the Vercetti Estate into his own empire and making his own destiny.

In “Cop Land,” the entire northern portion of the first island experiences a demographic shake up and now consists of exactly two assets: cops on foot in tan and brown and cops in green police cruisers. First, Tommy and Lance have to steal cop uniforms, a step that can get clunkier than it should when the garage door won't shut with the right number of cops inside. From there, you head to North Point Mall in disguise, plant a bomb and hightail it out of there with a five-star wanted level. Vice City’s officers were particularly bloodthirsty, and getting to a Pay 'n' Spray with Lance still intact—my man is drawn to dumb deaths—was one of my greatest teenage achievements.

Dubai-born real estate heir Yusuf Amir can buy anything. So naturally, the thing he wants most is an experimental attack helicopter parked on an arms dealer’s yacht. Rockstar was mining Gulf excess for laughs more than a decade before Dubai Bling and Love Is Blind: Habibi. Yusuf’s gaudy apartment tells you everything you need to know about him. There’s a miniature model of Algonquin laid out in his penthouse, as if the entire city were already one of his properties, and a giant dollar sign mounted on the wall. He dances to “Arab Money,” peppers his speech with hip-hop slang, and adopts the mannerisms of a culture he knows nothing about. Luis, unsurprisingly, is not particularly moved.

That makes “Sexy Time” the perfect introduction to him. Boat out from the marina, slip past the patrol and steal the Buzzard. Only, mid-flight, Yusuf calls and asks you to turn around, blow the yacht apart and run down what’s left of the arms dealers. For those who felt GTA IV took itself way too seriously, The Ballad of Gay Tony was a breath of fresh air. “Yusuf Amir is one of my all time favorite characters Dan [Houser] created,” Lazlow said. “The dialogue in this mission is hysterical, and he's constantly trying to sound street while going on about building luxury condos.”

The final chapter in the InterGlobal Studios asset arc turns Vice City into a formidable platformer. Tune in to Flash FM (Talk Talk’s “Life’s What You Make It”) or Fever 105 (Kool & The Gang’s “Summer Madness”) as Tommy leaps across rooftops on his trusted PCJ-600 bike in a single bound—though it’s far more likely that you’ll tumble to the streets at least once. There’s a delicate balance required for each stunt jump, but also a sense of reward once you master timing and speed.

This mission is, as the kids say, vibes. Something about scaling the ‘80s skyline by night while the rest of the city sleeps is unforgettable, along with the hilarious payoff, when Tommy triggers a spotlight that projects a massive X-rated image promoting adult performer Candy Suxxx (née Candice Shand) onto the side of a building. The most memorable GTA characters have a way of appearing in multiple forms: voices on the radio, bodies in cutscenes and, here, as advertising beamed across the world itself.

Small-town America gets the GTA treatment in “The Paleto Score.” Michael, Franklin and Trevor roll into sleepy Paleto Bay to rob the Blaine County Savings Bank, but the getaway quickly becomes less Ocean’s Eleven and more like Terminator or even MechCommander. Even before the heist, Lester, the master of elaborate setups, proves to be an unlikely master of conflict resolution too. His dry little “Hello, Franklin” to break up another Michael and Trevor spat still has me in stitches.

What starts as a relatively conventional bank job becomes a slow, lumbering march through an entire town, with our antiheroes mowing down cops, SWAT and eventually the military along the way. There’s even a reward for going overboard. One of the gold-medal requirements is to fire more than 4,000 bullets — because apparently, just robbing a bank wasn’t impressive enough.

Every time we see our hippie friend The Truth, his missions get better. In the apex of his mission tree, “Black Project,” CJ infiltrates Area 69, Rockstar’s twist on Area 51. There’s a stealth way of entering the maximum security facility, but that’s not nearly as fun as going in guns blazing. The level abounds with hilarious one-liners (“Get the General Mills on the line!”) and lab announcements (“Tonight’s menu is posted in the canteen. Barf bags can be ordered from Human Resources.”).

After GTA III’s and Vice City’s limited interiors, San Andreas gives you lively environments like Area 69, where you can disappear down corridors, into laboratories and through underground tunnels. And once CJ steals the coveted jet pack prototype, it becomes a way to fast travel across the state of San Andreas, bringing a whole new perspective to the final hours of the game. “The Truth. He stayed high as a motherfucker talking about conspiracy theory shit,” Young Maylay said. “But he would hit it on the head.”

Niko spends much of GTA IV doing other people’s dirty work. By “Late Checkout,” the diamond deal has gone so badly that Ray Boccino has lost his money, his diamonds and what remained of his patience. Isaac Roth, the diamond dealer who helped blow up the deal, is hiding in the Majestic Hotel. Ray wants him dead.

This mission is a choose-your-own-adventure affair. You can take the elevator and fight your way up through the guards, floor by floor, or use the window-cleaning platform outside to reach the penthouse from above and then fight your way back down. Either way, Niko eventually has to work his way through the hotel, killing Roth and his associates before making his escape.

It’s Rockstar’s take on the Plaza Hotel, minus Tim Curry, turned into a bonafide shooting gallery. Bonus points if you shove the front desk manager, who may respond by hopping over the desk to fight his own bellman.

Phil? Phil Collins? That's right. The former Genesis drummer and self-styled “Little Elvis” made gaming history by becoming the first real-life celebrity to lend his name and likeness as well as his voice to GTA. Like Vice City, VCS is inspired by the ‘80s TV drama Miami Vice; Philip Michael Thomas, who played Ricardo Tubbs on the show, voices Lance Vance in both VC and VCS, and Collins, as it happens, guest-starred on the series in 1985, as con man Phil Mayhew.

In this mission the Mob is after the Brit, and Vic has to ward them off. It all comes to a head during “In the Air Tonight” at Hyman Memorial Stadium. You're up top clearing Forelli saboteurs looming in the rafters while Phil is down below working the crowd.

For the man voicing Vic, this history wasn't lost on anyone. "Miami Vice was literally my favorite show as a little boy," said voice actor Dorian Missick. "I still have pictures of me in what I call my Miami Vice suit. One year, my mom let me get a little suit that they used to wear, but the collar’s turned up. I wore something like that for Easter. So to me, it was my opportunity to kind of be on the Miami Vice episode that I never got a chance to do. So all of these things, the Phil Collins of it all, and just that energy of it — it was exciting to be a part of that."

“Caida Libre,” Spanish for “free fall,” is one of those missions that finally makes the sprawling expanse of GTA V’s San Andreas feel like one cohesive playground. Michael and Trevor are hired by Martin Madrazo to take down a plane carrying his cousin Javier. Michael starts things off by shooting at the aircraft from Galileo Observatory with a sniper rifle.

The best part is the handoff, a seminal showcase of GTAV’s character-switch mechanic. First, Michael is coolly shooting down a plane from a mountaintop, and moments later you’re controlling Trevor, flying down country roads on a Sanchez motorcycle, chasing the falling debris like a man following his destiny. Eventually, Trevor finds Javier, kills him and climbs into the wrecked plane to retrieve the package. And, because this is Trevor, the mission ends with Trevor pining after Martin’s wife, Patricia, and kidnapping her. So much for the moral of Obsession.

When GTAIII first dropped, I spent the first few hours of the game gazing longingly across the river to Staunton Island, imagining what came next. Back in those days, Grand Theft Auto’s world opened up in stages and phases, trusting players to forgo instant gratification. That little stretch of water felt like the portal to another world entirely.

After Claude is victim of a double-cross, Maria helps him flee from Portland to Staunton where he meets his next boss, Asuka. But here’s the rub: Claude first has to prove he’s no longer the Mafia’s strongman, which means gunning down the beloved don Salvatore Leone in the heart of his turf. Once the deed is done, the Leones turn on you for the rest of the game, transforming the St. Marks neighborhood into a veritable “shotgun hell,” as YouTuber The Professional dubbed it in a video rant a few years ago. “Sayonara Salvatore” is thrilling enough. But its lasting impact on the open world is what players still can’t stop talking about.

If “Three Leaf Clover” feels familiar, that’s because it is. The mission is Rockstar’s loving homage to Michael Mann’s Heat. Niko joins Packie McReary and his brothers to rob the Bank of Liberty, complete with suits, masks, enormous bags of cash, and a getaway that quickly turns into a war through the streets of Liberty City.

There’s a little Point Break in there too: A civilian tries to play hero inside the bank, killing Michael Keane before being killed himself, echoing a similar moment in the 1991 film. Then comes the seemingly endless firefight through Algonquin’s neighborhoods, followed by an escape into the subway tunnels — the best transit system, by the way, in GTA history.

Vermeij says that in GTAIV, missions were often centered more around story than gameplay, but both are top-notch here. “These scripts could get quite big,” he said. “Thousands of lines in some cases…With every fix the script got a little more complicated.” This is GTA IV at its most cinematic, channeling the American crime movies and cop thrillers that have long shaped the series, all the while paving the way for GTAV’s slew of heists. “Four Leaf Clover,” though, remains the gold standard.

#6638. Robert Pattinson Is the Next James Bond! Here’s Who He Beat Out for the Job

It’s official: Robert Pattinson is the next James Bond. After months of speculation, it has finally been confirmed that the 40-year-old Brit will slip into 007’s tux.

Probably the most high-profile name on the list of likely contenders, Pattinson may seem, to many, a more logical choice for a Bond villain than 007 himself, but I’d already argued he’d make an excellent franchise lead: The Batman shows that he can be a convincing action hero, and with his weird and wonderful array of projects of late (Dune: Part Three, Primetime, The Odyssey, The Drama, et al), he’s the perfect person to breathe new life into this dated cinematic universe.

Last year, Bond fans received seismic news about the future of the classic British spy franchise: Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson—the children of Albert R “Cubby” Broccoli, the legendary producer of the original James Bond films—who have overseen the series since the ’90s, ceded creative control to Amazon Studios. (The streamer bought MGM, the studio which produces the Bond movies, back in 2022, but has now reportedly shelled out an additional $1 billion for the right to freely develop this particular cinematic universe on its own terms.)

Then, a few months later, it emerged that Denis Villeneuve, the Oscar-nominated helmer of the Dune franchise, would be in the director’s chair. After that, we got some more intel, thanks to a report in Deadline. Villeneuve was said to have embarked on his search after completing production on Dune: Part Three.” At the time, fans learned he was apparently after “a fresh face”, ideally “an unknown,” possibly “in his late 20s or early 30s.”

According to reports in Deadline, The Hollywood Reporter and Variety, as well as Pattinson, the final screen tests featured Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor, and Nicholas Hoult. Harry Styles allegedly “had discussions about the part,” and Theo James was in the mix at one point, too.

As Pattinson emerges victorious, revisit his major competition below.

At 36, the Emmy-winning, Southampton-born actor was about the right age, and a beloved star of stage and screen—from Challengers and Disclosure Day to indie hits including God’s Own Country, La Chimera, and The Mastermind, and his latest stint on stage at the Almeida in Golden Boy. Given his impressive acting chops and penchant for working with internationally lauded auteurs, he would have been a high-brow choice in the Daniel Craig mould (lest we forget the latter was a critics’ favorite before he slipped on the tux).

Callum Turner as the next Bond? In many ways it made perfect sense. Dua Lipa’s husband is easy on the eyes and incredibly talented—just see his performances in Emma, Masters of the Air, and The Capture, the latter of which earned the Londoner a BAFTA TV nomination. Though not an unknown, he just about qualified as a fresh face.

His turn as a floppy-haired young intelligence officer in Apple TV+’s Slow Horses saw the gruff Scotsman enter the race, though when asked by British Vogue if he’d consider swapping River Cartwright’s low-key sweatshirts for a tuxedo and martini, he was coy. Of Daniel Craig, whom he grew up watching as 007, the actor said: “It’s going to take a long time to get him out of my head. Or anybody else’s.”

Brilliant in Nosferatu, The Great, and The Favourite, as well as more contemporary projects like The Menu, the 36-year-old from Berkshire had the action credentials (he’s Lex Luthor, after all) and the charisma for the top job.

Since his stint on The White Lotus, the dashing 41-year-old Oxford native had been considered a potential 007 (and The Gentlemen no doubt helped, too).

If you thought the musical superstar’s acting days were already behind him, post Dunkirk, Don’t Worry Darling, and My Policeman, then think again—apparently the opportunity to shrug on 007’s suit might have persuaded him back onto set.

#6637. Hot Honey Brussels Sprouts

These honey-glazed brussels sprouts are saucy, tangy-sweet, and have a bit of kick. Caramelizing the honey gives it a deeper, toastier sweetness. Vinegar, red pepper flakes, and a good dose of butter transform it into a sticky sauce that seeps into the nooks of each and every sprout. The recipe makes a generous amount: Use it all, or save some for drizzling on pizza a few days later.

The trick to perfectly charred brussels sprouts? Preheat the sheet pan, then arrange the halved sprouts cut side down on the hot metal. It might feel a little fussy flipping each sprout onto its flat side, but the deeply browned results are worth it.

Make the glaze while the sprouts roast or up to five days ahead, then toss everything together just before serving to preserve those crispy edges.

Glossy and pourable, about the consistency of warm maple syrup—not thick like caramel. The honey will foam as it cooks, and the mixture will bubble aggressively when you add the vinegar. Both are normal. The glaze will thicken a bit as it cools, so don’t worry if it seems slightly thin while still bubbling.

They have a noticeable kick, but they’re more tangy-sweet than fiery. The honey and butter temper the chile flakes. If you’re sensitive to spice, use less than the suggested ¾ tsp. or leave the flakes out entirely.

Place a rimmed baking sheet on bottom rack of oven; preheat to 450°. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, and ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil in a large bowl; sprinkle with ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and season with freshly ground black pepper.

Carefully remove baking sheet from oven. Using tongs, arrange brussels sprouts cut-side down on hot baking sheet. Roast brussels on bottom rack until softened and deeply browned, 15–25 minutes.

Meanwhile, bring ¼ cup honey to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat. Reduce heat to medium-low and cook, stirring often, until honey is a deep amber color but not burnt (it will be foamy, that’s okay), 3–4 minutes.

Remove from heat and add ⅓ cup sherry vinegar or red wine vinegar (it will bubble up quite aggressively) and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes; whisk until sauce is smooth. Return saucepan to medium heat and add 3 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, whisking constantly, until glaze is glossy, bubbling, and slightly thickened, 3–4 minutes.

Transfer roasted brussels sprouts to a large bowl. Add half the hot honey glaze and scallions and toss to combine. Taste and add more glaze if desired. Transfer to a platter and top with lemon zest. Serve remaining glaze alongside.

Do ahead: Glaze can be made 5 days ahead; refrigerate after cooling.

Editor’s note: This recipe was first published in September 2018 as “Charred Brussels Sprouts With Warm Honey Glaze”; it has been updated for style and clarity. Head this way for more of our best Thanksgiving side dishes →
