#6625. David Duchovny on Books, Band and ‘The X-Files’

David Duchovny has been famous for as long as I have been alive. From 1993 to 2002, The X-Files made government conspiracies a staple of primetime television. Duchovny’s FBI special agent Fox Mulder, with his skeptical counterpart, Gillian Anderson’s agent Dana Scully, personified the imminent breakdown of consensus reality in the coming century, delivering the paranoid fringe into 20 million American living rooms. The show belongs to a world of monoculture that no longer exists, and it launched Duchovny into a realm of visibility that’s hard to imagine now, when famous people are produced and consumed at an industrial rate. A few weeks ago, as my boyfriend shopped for a suit jacket at Crowley Vintage in Brooklyn and I edited this story on my phone, I watched a college-age boy put on a long, gray trench coat and announce to his girlfriend: “Mulder mode.”

Duchovny went on to star in Californication, a raunchy dramedy about a divorced novelist navigating the sexually and professionally parasitic Hollywood studio system of the 2000s. Many viewers interpreted Californication as a kind of autofiction, although Duchovny did not write for the show. The actor has written a number of novels, but it’s apparent to anyone who has spent 30 seconds with him that this soft-spoken, reluctant celebrity has nothing to do with the character Hank Moody. Still, Californication did anticipate something about art, celebrity, and self-commodification: Anybody who writes today must contend with marketing an artistic persona for a public that does not, as a rule, read.

In addition to his six books, Duchovny has released four records, and written and directed a number of feature films. He greets the degraded state of American arts with a charming blend of rigor and self-deprecation. “I’m not Jonathan Franzen,” he says of his fiction-writing process. “But if I work on something every day, it deepens. And eventually, hopefully, I can achieve one tenth of what Jonathan Franzen achieves.” But he has an aversion to the sort of publicity that might make his various artistic ventures more lucrative. He tells me he finds it “spiritually impoverishing.”

I meet Duchovny with his band—millennial slackers half his age—at their practice space in Carroll Gardens, where they’re preparing to tour their fourth LP, Prince of Pieces. He wears a white Hanes T-shirt, tight underneath his athletic arms, and he has a tattoo on his ankle—a compass pointing west, something he got when his daughter, West, was hospitalized as an infant. (She’s 27 now, an accomplished actor. “She wanted to be a doctor,” he says. “I was so happy when she told me she was going to pursue acting. Thank God.”)

The albums are composed of subdued, easy-to-listen-to folk-rock tracks, not dissimilar from early Kurt Vile. It’s the band’s first rehearsal in ages, and one of their only chances to prepare in advance of a European tour. In person, they play the songs harder and heavier, sprinkling in crowd-pleasing covers: “Godzilla” by Blue Öyster Cult, “The One I Love” by REM, and—“sadly only one time,” Duchovny says—“Hotline Bling.” The energy in the room is high. These men like one another. Duchovny’s manager offers me a beer from the cooler I’m perched on. I gesture to the tallboy in my purse. He looks disappointed. “You didn’t trust us,” he says. Duchovny steps aside to take a sip of water and picks up the microphone.

“You can sing along,” his keyboardist, Colin Lee, says.

At 66, David Duchovny remains a sex symbol. He’s in better shape than he was on The X-Files. He’s in better shape than the boys in the band. The night after practice, during a Q&A for a screening of his 2023 film Reverse the Curse, he mentions that the wardrobe department had to fashion a “BDSM harness” for him to wear under his clothes to remind him to hunch like an old man. He plays a Red Sox fan who bonds with his estranged son over baseball, marijuana, and their shared lust for a beautiful, young death doula. Duchovny’s character has terminal cancer. “I’m in my dying era,” he tells the crowd. “I die in every film. ”

For the most part, the audience at Westchester County’s Irvington Theater is old enough to have watched The X-Files as it aired. At least two esoteric-looking old men carry David’s poetry collection like a prayer book. There are a handful of young people. A college-aged girl in a KN95 mask raises her hand to ask about Bucking Fucking Dent, the novel adaptation of the Reverse the Curse screenplay, which Duchovny wrote while the movie was in production purgatory. “In the book, Ted and Marty’s last name is Fullilove. In the movie you change it to Fullaker. Why did you do that?”

“Good question,” Duchovny says, stalling. “Full of love. Full of shit. It’s all the same.”

Inevitably, someone asks about the new X-Files. Ryan Coogler is rebooting the show for Hulu. Duchovny will later suggest to me that Chris Carter, the show’s original writer, has designs on a reboot of his own—“He has plans, and wants to end with the original show.” As for Coogler’s version, he says, “I know he said he wants me to come do something, but we haven’t figured out what yet.” During the audience Q&A, Duchovny seems to have misheard the question, and spoils the ending for The Exiles, his forthcoming Taiwanese crime film: “I die in that one too.”

Duchovny’s latest book, About Time, a collection of poems published last year by Akashic, is also largely about dying: the death of his father, the death of his first marriage, the ambient death that hung in the air at the beginning of the decade. He started writing the poems when his therapist encouraged him to talk to dead people. “He was talking about Rudolph Steiner’s belief that you can talk to the dead. And he said: You can talk to your father and you should. My dad and I didn’t connect like we might have,” Duchovny says. “When you’re younger, you think you have all the time in the world to get the relationship you want. But the relationship doesn’t end.” In conversation, he is cerebral without being annoying. “There’s a power struggle when you read a really good novel,” he says. “Somebody’s mind is taking over your mind. I think about language a lot and how we take it for granted as being an accurate signifier. When I was younger I thought communication was possible. I’m not so sure now. But it’s fun to try.”

Duchovny’s humility complicates the sexual charisma that still lives at the center of his public persona. His introduction to About Time begins, “I know what you’re thinking: Just what the world needs now—a bunch of poems from an actor.” There’s a sense that he wants to get ahead of the reader’s skepticism. But there’s also plenty of perceptive lines in the poems themselves: “You dreamt you wrote something so good, / so ambivalent and destructive, so creative, / so lacking in morals, decency, or instruction, / so sad and so funny, / so useless and old, / so familiar and new, / so full of theft and power / that they had to name a god after it.” I ask him if good writing is necessarily amoral. He says, “Probably. Which is why any politically correct work of art is usually super successful and really bad. Usually artists are difficult people, and I have no problem separating the art from the artist. But people do now.”

In college, Duchovny wanted to be a poet. “I thought it was an actual occupation you could have,” he says. When an underclassman turned up in his workshop who was better than him, he quit writing poems on the spot. “It was actually Walter Kirn,” he says. “He showed up at 16-years-old. He was a genius. I was like okay—I’m not a poet.”

The two men have become close in the last decade. Kirn, who wrote Up in the Air and founded the newspaper County Highway, tells me what Duchovny was like at Princeton: “He was golden. He had an aura. I was a little starstruck by him.” Duchovny has agreed to play paranormal radio host Art Bell in American Nights, a biopic that Kirn is developing alongside director Alex Lee Moyer. Bell’s Coast to Coast, a cult AM show during the ’80s and ’90s, was beloved by long-haul truckers and compound preppers alike, who called in to report UFO sightings, cattle mutilations, and crop circles. “I, like the rest of my generation, grew up on The X-Files,” Moyer tells me. “It made a massive impression on me, and I’ve been a fan of David ever since. The synchronicity of him being a part of this is not lost on me.”

I ask Duchovny if he always needed to be the best. “I at least needed to be the best in my class,” he says.

In LA, I meet Duchovny in a quiet restaurant to talk about his books. He describes his first novel as “an act of cowardice.” Holy Cow is narrated by an anthropomorphized barnyard animal who uncovers the conspiracy theory that is factory farming. “I thought: Well, they’re not gonna cut me off at the knees on this. Because I’m clearly not that serious. It was calculated. I didn’t want to try for the great American novel the first time as an actor.” The books that followed are more ambitious, each one better than the last. By the time he was promoting his fourth book, 2021’s Truly Like Lightning, he made his ambition plain. “I want to be taken seriously,” he said on Marc Maron’s podcast. “That’s my weakness. I want that book to be taken seriously.”

“You don’t want people to be like the guy from The X-Files wrote a book,” Maron said.

“That’s what they’re gonna say,” Duchovny said, “but I hope and I believe that eventually people will see that I mean business.”

Truly Like Lightning centers on a Mormon polygamist family forced to enter the godless world of Los Angeles when their homestead is upended. “When I started to read about Mormonism, it struck me as super optimistic. Everyone’s gonna get their own planet and everyone’s gonna be able to propagate souls. As opposed to a European perspective, which was always about the end of something, being 2,000 years removed from this thing. The Mormons said no, this is still happening.” The novel takes cues from the literary critic Harold Bloom, who wrote that Mormonism was an “American original” and called its founder a “religious genius.” Duchovny studied under Bloom at Yale, where he earned some of an English PhD. “Everything goes back to Bloom,” he says. “And you never really leave grad school. I’m not sure I’ve left grad school. They might still be waiting for my dissertation.”

But Duchovny did leave grad school. He signed with a talent agent one summer to try to earn some money acting in commercials. His agent told him that if he wanted to go out for theater or film roles, he’d have to get into an acting class. “I said: I’m not doing anything. When I stepped into acting class, something happened. I wasn’t a demonstrative person—I was an intellectual person. So it was like: Yeah, be unreasonable. Be irrational. It opened up a different world, a world of fiction, a world without consequences. I’m doing a scene, and I’m yelling at this person and I’m going to murder them, but I don’t have to go to jail.”

For someone with half a dozen good books and an enormous public profile, it’s surprising there haven’t been more reviews. Johnny Temple, who published Duchovny’s two most recent books on Akashic, tells me, “It’s certainly frustrating that there hasn't been more review coverage of David’s books. For any well-known actor, musician, or other type of public figure, there’s always going to be obstacles to being taken seriously in a different medium.” Kirn tells me, “That makes writing fiction a much purer achievement in my mind. You’re doing this because you love it, and you know that two thirds of your fans will only remember you as a TV character. It’s a brilliant, Sisyphean task. Also, he’s a superb writer.”

I ask Duchovny whether he still thinks about being the best. “I think now I can acknowledge that it’s a hollow designation,” he says. “Especially in the arts. Even though we give awards, which is silly. Holy Cow made the Times bestseller list. Ever since, everything I write sells less and less.”

“It’s hard for someone to champion it,” he adds. “If I wrote a memoir, I’m sure it would get reviewed in the Times.”

Talking to Duchovny, one is reminded that wanting to be taken seriously and being in on the joke aren’t mutually exclusive. As band practice winds down in Brooklyn, the guys are excited to cover Lou Reed’s “Perfect Day.” Duchovny crosses his arms in front of his lap like a schoolboy as he sings. To my ear it sounds just fine, but Lee, the keyboardist, asks the mixer to lower the reverb on David’s voice.

“Maybe lower David’s mic in general?” the bassist, Mitchell Stewart asks.

“Lower than zero,” Duchovny says. “Less than zero.”

A few days later, he texts me. He just screened an early cut of Soapbox, a Hollywood satire he wrote and stars in opposite Laverne Cox. At first, he’s bummed that the test audience has decided that his character shouldn’t get killed in the final moments of the movie. But a couple hours later, he writes me again: “People don’t want me to die. I guess I should be flattered.”

#6624. All the Celebrity Couples at the 2026 Governors Awards

Last night, awards season kicked off with the 2026 Governors Awards, an annual gala hosted by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, which acts as a precursor to the Oscars and includes the presentation of three lifetime achievement awards: the Academy Honorary Award, the Jean Hersholt Humanitarian Award, and the Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award.

To celebrate these special honors, many of Hollywood’s biggest stars united at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles. The guest list included A-listers like Julianne Moore, Charlize Theron, Timothée Chalamet, A$AP Rocky, Penélope Cruz, and Florence Pugh.

And a few of the attendees chose to turn the evening into a date night. While Kylie Jenner joined Timothée Chalmet inside the ceremony rather than walk the carpet with him, The Gilded Age’s Carrie Coon did walk the carpet alongside her husband, actor and playwright Tracy Letts, while Matt Damon brought along his wife, Luciana Barroso. Emma Stone also made a rare public outing with her husband, Dave McCary.

But, perhaps one of the most high-profile couples present on the carpet was Zendaya and Tom Holland, who chose to walk the carpet separately. Throughout the years, these two have made very few public appearances together, usually only tied to their joint work in the Spider-Man franchise. In the past, Holland has even noted that he tends to avoid walking carpets for Zendaya’s movies, because “it’s not my moment, it’s her moment, and if we go together, it’s about us.”

Ahead, see all the celebrity couples at the 2026 Governors Awards.

Zendaya in archival Giles Deacon and Holland in custom Louis Vuitton with Christian Louboutin shoes and a Cartier watch.

#6622. Sauer Celebrates 85 Years With a New Assouline Book

Gabriel Sauer and Stephanie Wenk on how jewelry connects us to the real world.

For 85 years, Brazilian jewelry house Sauer has built a world of its own, one where vibrant gemstones, unexpected materials, and an adventurous spirit come together. Founded by Jules Sauer, a pioneering gem hunter whose fascination with Brazil’s natural treasures helped shape the country’s gemstone industry, the house has always approached jewelry a little differently. Today, that same curiosity remains at its core, even as a new generation takes over.

To celebrate its 85th anniversary, Sauer is looking both backward and forward with the release of a new Assouline book highlighting its remarkable history, out December 5, alongside an anniversary collection that reimagines some of the house’s most recognizable designs. For creative director Stephanie Wenk and third-generation family member Gabriel Sauer, the milestone is about more than honoring the past. It’s an opportunity to reflect on how a family business rooted in tradition can continue to evolve without losing what makes it special.

Stephanie Wenk, creative director of Sauer.

The anniversary collection is a testament to that philosophy. Drawing on an extraordinary archive of gemstones, some of which have been tucked away for decades, Wenk brings new life to Brazilian imperial topaz, aquamarines, and other precious stones through unexpected combinations. It’s an approach that feels true to the house’s history while pushing its creative boundaries. But beyond the jewelry itself, Sauer’s story is one of family, discovery, and a deep connection to Brazil. From Jules’s early adventures to the house’s growing international presence, each chapter has been shaped by a love of experimentation and embracing the unexpected. As the brand celebrates this milestone, Wenk and Sauer share how they’re staying true to the house’s original spirit.

The cover of Sauer: Dialogues Between Worlds from Assouline.

Gabriel Sauer: We’ve been with the company for almost 14 years now. The anniversary is an important milestone for the company, but it also marks more than 10 years of our generation of the Sauer family leading the business. I think we now have the material and the maturity to showcase our vision for the future of the company. It’s important that, in a book like this, we can tell a little bit about the past but also share our vision for the future. If we had done this book five years ago, it wouldn’t have had the same substance that it has now. We had the idea in previous years, but I feel that the timing came naturally.

Stephanie Wenk: I think it was the adventurous spirit of Sauer. Jules was always very nonconformist in everything he did, from his discoveries to his travels. He did things differently and in his own way. I think that’s what continues to inspire us today. While making the book, we were also talking about the history with Gabriel’s dad and the rest of the family. It’s very inspiring. Jules’s spirit is still very much alive.

GS: It was interesting to have these conversations with the second generation of the family while putting the book together. The story of how Jules came to Brazil and founded the company still shapes how we approach business and challenges today. He was an optimist with a deep passion for craftsmanship and gemstones, something we continue to carry forward. Every time we revisit his story, we’re reminded of our values and purpose.

I also learned more about the historical context of some of his discoveries. During the war, American companies were coming to Brazil to mine minerals for the war effort, and some of that activity was connected to his earlier explorations. I hadn’t fully understood how his discoveries fit into that period of history, so it was fascinating to learn about that connection.

GS: Working in a family business is a great responsibility. It’s also a challenge because we’re the third generation, and most family businesses don’t survive beyond the third generation. One of the biggest lessons I’ve learned is the importance of giving each generation creative freedom. Every family has its own formula, and there’s no single formula that works for everyone. In our family, we’ve always welcomed new generations and allowed them to express their vision for the future without having someone hovering over their heads. I think this philosophy came from Jules and [his wife] Zilda together, and it’s been an invaluable lesson in how to run a family business.

I remember that, when I was a kid, my grandfather used to carry gemstones in his pocket and give them to people with whom he felt a good connection or energy. He would say that gemstones take billions of years to form in nature and that they carry the heart of our world inside them. I would see the impact that these gifts had on people. He was passionate about honoring gemstones and bringing out their best qualities. That’s something we continue to express through our designs. A lot of our creations begin with the stone itself, sometimes even with one specific gemstone.

SW: We’re very lucky because we have this amazing inventory of stones, and I’m always discovering new ones. I think about 80 percent of the stones we used in this collection came from our archives. We used a lot of Brazilian stones, like imperial topaz and aquamarine, which are also very important to our history. Our signature elements are really important to our vocabulary, our DNA, and the foundations of our designs, but the stones play a very big role. There are a lot of one-of-a-kind pieces in this collection, including more high jewelry than we usually do, as well as some brooches. Some of the stones have been in our archives for 40 years, so it’s really special.

SW: Researching, introducing, and combining different materials is very important to our work, and it’s something I’m really drawn to. I love exploring the dialogue between different materials, how one enhances the other, and how combining them can give a new perspective to a material you might not normally imagine alongside a precious stone. We’ve been doing it since the beginning. We manufacture everything ourselves, so we also have the opportunity to test materials and develop ideas. Sometimes that process takes a long time, and you have to be able to experiment. It’s really valuable that we’re able to do that.

GS: Since we started as a stone-cutting workshop, we’ve always explored different types of stones and how we can cut and use them in different ways. This exploration of different forms and creative applications is something that’s ingrained in our DNA.

SW: We revisited a few pieces, but it’s also a collection that looks very much toward the future. We reinterpreted the Constellation ring, one of our most iconic designs, which won the De Beers prize. We also combined elements of Constellation with Illusion, another design from about 10 years ago. It was an opportunity to experiment with both designs and bring them together in a new way. We also revisited signature elements, like the use of onyx and lapis lazuli, as well as our distinctive framing techniques, and developed those ideas further.

GS: We also created a new version of an archival necklace incorporating pearls, revisiting a design language that’s been part of the house for years.

SW: I think all of our collections revolve around art, nature, and spirituality, so it felt very natural. Collaborating with artists, bringing in a contemporary vision, working across different disciplines, and interpreting different worlds are all part of that. I have a lot of different interests, including music, texture, design, art, and cinema. I don’t like to look at other jewelry. I prefer to look at things that inspire me, and I think that shows in what we do. Bringing that perspective into the house felt like a very natural evolution.

GS: I think it’s definitely something we inherited from previous generations and have carried forward. Jules was always passionate about art. He was a collector himself, and previous generations had already explored partnerships and collaborations with artists. When Stephanie started exploring this as well, it came very naturally because she’s so passionate about art. We’ve been fortunate to collaborate with some incredible artists. It wasn’t something that was particularly planned. It happened naturally, and eventually we realized that art had become one of the main pillars of the brand. We then started collaborating with art fairs as well, and we felt that establishing the art prize was a way to give back.

GS: We wanted to tell the story of how Jules first came to Brazil, which is very inspiring, but also highlight the different explorations and discoveries he participated in. For example, there was the discovery of emeralds in Brazil and how he worked with the GIA [Gemological Institute of America] to establish that the stones were actually emeralds. It was a very important milestone for Brazil as a gemstone producer.

He was also an advocate for gemstones and traveled around the world, giving speeches about removing the label of “semiprecious” from certain stones. He used to say that gemstones are a one-time harvest and that every gemstone is precious. He had an amethyst with an amazing color that he considered incredibly valuable, and he wouldn’t sell it at any price. Today, we can see that many different gemstones are recognized in the market and have very high values. He was really ahead of his time.

SW: I hope they understand the history of the brand, Jules’s story, and all the wonders of Brazil, especially because we have so many stones that are unique to the country. I also hope they see the creativity, the craftsmanship, and the different perspectives that define Sauer. It’s about understanding how you can take a heritage brand into the future while still respecting its past. Heritage shouldn’t be something that limits you but something that gives you more to build upon.

GS: I think we’ll always preserve it because whenever someone discovers Sauer, one of the first things they want to understand is how the company came to be and what makes us different. It’s inspiring to see how excited our team at the Madison Avenue store is to share that story. As we expand internationally, our Brazilian heritage will always remain an important part of our identity. I also feel that the pillars of the brand are timeless. Everyone can relate to nature, art, and spirituality, and people often find their own meaning in our jewelry. We’re also a multigenerational company, with people from the first and second generations alongside Gen Z. That range of perspectives keeps us fresh and allows us to continue evolving while staying true to our roots.

SW: We have a growing community of younger clients, and it’s interesting to see how different generations influence one another. Sometimes it’s the sons and daughters who influence their mothers. There’s a lot of meaning and symbolism in the jewelry. It helps people build connections and create their own personal interpretations. It’s all about connecting.

GS: I hope we still have the same energy and free spirit that we have today. I don’t necessarily think in terms of becoming a huge company with lots of stores. That’s not our approach. Of course, we may open new stores in new places, but I think it’s more about being in the right places and achieving greater global recognition. I feel that jewelry connects you to the real world. We live in a very digital world, and I think jewelry offers an opportunity to give clients real experiences and enhance human connection.

SW: I hope we continue to inspire people, connect stories, and create new stories through jewelry. I want more and more people to discover Sauer. Jewelry is very intimate. It’s something you wear on your body forever. You might wear an engagement ring for 40 years without ever taking it off. There’s almost nothing else in the world that you could wear every single day for your entire life. That intimacy and the fact that something can hold so much meaning are really unique to jewelry. Even before language existed, humans were adorning themselves.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

#6621. Ciara and Russell Wilson Help Macy’s Usher in the Holiday Season

Last week, Macy’s welcomed guests to the eighth floor of its Herald Square flagship for an exclusive preview of Santaland and the reimagined holiday experience. Upon entering, a crowd of all ages was greeted by a sprawling red carpet surrounded by Christmas trees, setting the festive mood for the evening.

Co-hosted by Ciara and Russell Wilson, the celebration took place across two main spaces. In one room, holiday-inspired cocktails flowed as attendees, including Nicky Hilton Rothschild, Candace Bushnell, Tiler Peck and Roman Mejia, and Alec and Hilaria Baldwin, enjoyed light bites and a DJ set by Brendan Fallis. In the other, families stepped into the magic of Santaland, boarding the new North Star Express before visiting St. Nick himself.

Macy’s Santaland opens to the public on November 27. Ahead of the holiday season, the couple shared more with Vogue about festive dressing, gift-giving, family traditions, and what’s next.

What are you most excited for this holiday season?

Ciara: This time of year has always been so special to me. Our schedules are so busy, and I really cherish the opportunity to slow down, spend quality time with our family, decorate the house together, and see the excitement on our kids’ faces throughout the season. This year, we are especially looking forward to soaking up those special moments together and getting ready to welcome Baby Cinco.”

You’re wearing a head-to-toe Macy’s for tonight’s celebration. How would you describe your personal style during the holiday season?

Ciara: Tonight I wanted something that felt elevated, but still comfortable for running around with the kiddos. I knew Macy’s would have exactly what I was looking for. I’m wearing a Lauren by Ralph Lauren look, with a cozy cableknit tank, satin skirt, and sweater that felt perfect for this time of year.

Russell: I’m wearing Alfani. The style I always feel my best in is classic, timeless, polished, and comfortable. I love a great tailored look that also has a fun spin to it, especially during the holidays. Macy’s is the perfect shopping destination because it has such a great range of styles, I love putting together different pieces and making them feel unique to me.

With a busy career and a full house, are you someone who has all your holiday shopping done by November, or are you more of a last-minute, Christmas Eve kind of shopper?

Ciara: I’m definitely a planner and take holiday shopping very seriously! With a big family, you need the time to find something special and thoughtful for everyone. Especially with my kids, their interests are always changing, so I’m always paying attention to what they’re into and thinking about what would make them happy. I just love finding those special things that I know they’ll be excited to open on Christmas morning.

When it comes to gift-giving, what’s your signature style?

Ciara: For me, the best gifts are the ones that show how well you know someone. I’m a sentimental person, so I always think it’s more about the thought and intention behind the gift than how much you’re giving.

Russell: When it comes to giving gifts to my family, I get so excited. I love to go all out—go big or go home! I also love surprising Ci and the kids with something they aren’t expecting: Their reactions are always the best. At the same time, I always make sure gifts are thoughtful and personalized. I love giving them things that remind us of a special moment in our lives, an inside joke, or something they can cherish for years to come. So for me, it’s really a mix of everything.

When you’re hosting for the holidays, what’s your secret to throwing a memorable celebration?

Ciara: I like to plan ahead, and I actually have a lot of fun with that part of hosting. There’s always a lot that goes into putting a party together, but a good playlist is a must. You can usually count on a few of my songs making the list, especially “Level Up” or “Yes.” I also love having games and activities for everyone to enjoy. We’re big UNO fans in our family, so that’s always a fun one to bring out. Lastly, it’s not a party unless the host is having fun, so I make sure to relax and spend time with my guests.

As the year winds down, what are you most looking forward to in 2027?

Ciara: 2026 was such a special year for me with so many personal and professional achievements, so I’m really excited to continue creating and growing in 2027. This year, I released “Yes” and its remixes alongside some incredible artists I admire, so I’m excited for what’s next musically. I’m also looking forward to continuing the work we’re doing through the Why Not You Foundation and finding more ways to support communities and make a meaningful impact. And beyond all of that, just spending quality time with my family, making memories, and enjoying all the little moments. That’s always what matters most to me.

Russell: There is so much to look forward to in 2027. I’m excited to continue working with my amazing CBS Sports team while also exploring some exciting personal projects, continuing to grow the Why Not You Foundation, expanding 3BRAND, growing our family, and prioritizing our health and wellness with the help of QALO. We have some incredible projects in the works that we'll be announcing soon, so stay tuned. It’s going to be a special year!

#6620. Robert Pattinson Might Be the Most Fashion-Forward Bond Yet

From Sean Connery’s immaculately tailored suits in Dr. No to Daniel Craig’s thigh-bearing trunks in Casino Royale, each man who has played James Bond has brought a new aesthetic sensibility to the role. For Connery, this meant soft-shouldered Savile Row tailoring, polo shirts, and knit ties to suit the era of Ivy Style, while Roger Moore’s wardrobe of safari jackets and nylon ski suits embodied the sporty hedonism of the 1970s. In the 21st century, Daniel Craig’s Bond was built around a timely blend of Brioni, Tom Ford, and stalwart British brands that complemented the contemporary #menswear scene. Today’s news that Robert Pattinson—a longtime Dior ambassador and one of the most consistently thrilling dressers in Hollywood—has been cast as 007 suggests Bond’s most fashionable era may be yet to come.

Daniel Craig is no slouch in the clothing department, but before donning the tux for Casino Royale, he was primarily known as a stage actor with a penchant for distressed jeans and Chuck Taylor high-tops. Pattinson, meanwhile, has been the face of Dior’s menswear for a decade, during which he’s established his impeccable taste and a willingness to take big swings with his outfits—not to mention a reputation for wearing the absolute heck out of a gray suit. Now, with fellow Brit Jonathan Anderson (who cast Craig in Loewe’s quirked-up fall 2024 campaign and posted this heartwarming pic today) running the show at Dior, the stage is set for a Bond with a taste for capital-F fashion.

Tradition dictates a vibe shift whenever a new Bond is chosen, but whatever James Bond wears has an outsized impact on menswear. Pierce Brosnan’s era had structured Brioni suits and made the Omega Seamaster a star, while Daniel Craig helped cement Tom Ford’s tailoring as a red-carpet staple and juiced sales of N.Peal ribbed Army sweaters and Drake’s suede chukkas. As GQ’s Cam Wolf noted in a 2018 article about Skyfall, Daniel Craig’s Barbour jacket, sweater, jeans, and brogue boots from that film—a classic but fairly unremarkable outfit—became the aspirational template for untold numbers of men on r/malefashionadvice. A few years later, when Craig wore a Rag & Bone slim-fit henley in No Time to Die, the brand sold out of the unassuming undershirt in a matter of days.

It’s been five years since No Time to Die’s release, and it will likely be at least a couple more before Pattinson’s first outing as 007 hits screens. That’s a long wait to see how the next Bond era aesthetic comes together, but given Pattinson’s distinctive approach to fashion, it should be well worth it for the clothes alone.

#6617. 10 Best Sunscreens for Face That You’ll Actually Enjoy Wearing

When people talk about the “good old days,” I stay quiet—I’m pretty certain I was born in the right generation. I love waiting in line for $10 artisanal matcha, and I love having access to hundreds of sunscreens that don’t pill, feel greasy, or leave behind a ghoulish white cast. Considering that sunscreen is arguably the most important step in your beauty routine (every dermatologist and aesthetician worth their license would agree), having so many options feels particularly worth celebrating, especially given how much the global sunscreen market has evolved.

If you need a refresher on why we talk about sunscreen so much at Vogue, board-certified dermatologist Marnie Nussbaum points out that while our skin-care routines may include plenty of salmon sperm and copper peptides, the most effective step is also the least exciting: sunscreen. Used diligently and consistently, it can help prevent much of the damage we might otherwise try to address later, including collagen and elastin loss, skin laxity, hyperpigmentation, fine lines, and, most importantly, skin cancer.

As for the market itself, board-certified dermatologist Lindsey Zubritsky, MD, FAAD, attributes much of the category’s growth to increased consumer education. “In the past few years, there has been so much incredible education about the importance of wearing sunscreen every day,” she says. “With more people looking to incorporate SPF into their daily routines, the market has drastically expanded.” Today, that means everything from invisible formulas and tinted sunscreens to SPF lip balms and on-the-go sticks.

Another perk of being alive in 2026? Having easier access to formulas that were once largely limited to their home countries. Whether you’re discovering Korean, Japanese, and Australian sunscreen innovations on TikTok or asking a friend to bring back a French pharmacy favorite, it’s never been easier to explore what the rest of the world has to offer. The US has historically been slower to approve newer sunscreen filters than other markets, although that’s beginning to change. In June 2026, the FDA approved bemotrizinol, a UV filter already widely used abroad and the first new sunscreen ingredient permitted in the US in more than 25 years. Still, international markets offer formulators a broader range of UV filters, helping explain the variety of textures, finishes, and formulations available overseas.

Sunscreen has come a long way from formulas that focused primarily on UVB protection. Broad-spectrum options added UVA protection, and newer formulas have made daily SPF easier to wear. Board-certified dermatologist Dara Spearman, MD, FAAD, adds that newer formulas are not only more wearable but also easier to incorporate into everyday routines. “They’re more lightweight and suitable for everyday use across skin types,” she explains. Many newer tinted formulas are designed to blend more seamlessly into a wider range of skin tones. Several also contain iron oxides, which help protect against visible light, making them especially beneficial for those with melasma or hyperpigmentation.

But knowing how important sunscreen is and actually wearing it every day are two different things. According to board-certified dermatologist Sandra Oska, MD, daily use remains inconsistent. “There has been a genuine shift in how consumers think about sunscreen, but the majority of people still aren’t wearing it every day,” she says. Men, in particular, tend to underuse SPF, while women and Gen Z are generally more consistent. Even among regular users, common mistakes like underapplying can limit protection.

Ultimately, usability is what drives consistency. As Oska notes: “What are consumers actually going to use first thing in the morning, and what’s going to make it into their bag for reapplication?” Formulas that layer well with skin care tend to win out for daily use, while sticks, powders, and SPF lip balms have become essentials for touch-ups throughout the day.

After testing dozens of sunscreens—from the classics to each new bottle that hits our desk—and speaking with esteemed dermatologists and estheticians, we evaluated them all to bring you this edit of the best of the best. (Each of them has been tested and worn IRL!) Below is a look at all the best facial sunscreens of 2026 so far.

British Vogue’s Ellie Davis tests the Beauty of Joseon Relief Sun sunscreen.

According to Dr. Nussbaum, sunscreen helps protect against both UVA and UVB rays, which cause different types of damage. UVB rays primarily cause sunburn and can damage DNA, increasing the risk of skin cancer. UVA rays penetrate deeper into the skin, contributing to collagen and elastin breakdown, fine lines, and premature aging. They can even penetrate windows, making daily protection important when you’re indoors, too.

When it comes to sunscreen formulas, there are two main types of UV filters: mineral and chemical. Mineral sunscreens use zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, or both to protect the skin, primarily by absorbing UV radiation, with some reflection and scattering. Chemical sunscreens also absorb UV rays and convert that energy into less harmful forms, primarily heat. Both can provide effective sun protection, although their textures and how they feel on the skin can vary. Mineral formulas are often recommended for sensitive skin, while chemical formulas tend to be lighter and less likely to leave a white cast.

SPF Level: “Picking a sunscreen does not have to be complicated!” Los Angeles dermatologist Chris Tomassian says. “Look for a sunscreen that is SPF 30 or higher and broad-spectrum, meaning it blocks both UVA and UVB rays. You want to use at least two finger lengths of sunscreen for the full face, and when you are out in the sun, reapply every two hours to maintain adequate sun protection.” Apply sunscreen at least 15 minutes before going outside.

Type: Mineral sunscreens use zinc oxide, titanium dioxide, or both to protect against UV radiation, primarily through absorption, with some reflection and scattering. Chemical sunscreens also absorb UV rays, converting their energy into less harmful forms. “Although both can be incredibly effective, chemical sunscreens can be somewhat more irritating to sensitive skin,” explains Dr. Nazarian. “Physical sunscreens are a bit more stable, but are also a little more occlusive and can trap heat, so it may feel a little heavier than the chemical sunscreens.” Zinc oxide and titanium dioxide are mineral sunscreen ingredients to look for.

Texture: How the sunscreen sits on the skin can make all the difference in how it wears. Those looking for something under makeup might appreciate a lightweight formula or something with a primer-like texture. Conversely, someone with dry skin might consider a richer, emollient formula similar to a face cream. That being said, keep your routine (and skin type) in mind when selecting your SPF this year.

White Cast: A white cast is a whitish, almost purplish hue left behind after applying some sunscreens. This often happens with mineral formulas that utilize zinc oxide to provide a physical barrier between the skin and sun rays. Fortunately, most sunscreens these days—even mineral options—do not leave a white cast.

Broad-Spectrum: Broad-spectrum means your sunscreen protects against both UVA and UVB rays. If a sunscreen is not labeled “broad-spectrum,” it may not provide adequate UVA protection, leaving your skin more vulnerable to sun damage and premature aging.

Editors’ Review: Our editorial team has tested each sunscreen on this list (and more that weren’t featured!), so we can speak to everything from texture and finish to how well they layer under makeup. Where our editors feel particularly strongly about a formula, you’ll find their firsthand experiences alongside insights from our dermatologist experts.

“Broad-spectrum describes the quality of providing sun protection against a wide range of ultraviolet wavelengths,” Dr. Murphy-Rose explains. “Broad-spectrum sunscreens protect against both UVA and UVB rays.”

Dr. Murphy-Rose recommends applying two finger lengths of product to the face each application. “One of the most common mistakes in sunscreen application is not applying enough product,” she continues. “Always remember to apply to your whole face, including over the brows, ears, and around the lips. These are areas where I very often see pre-cancerous skin growths, and I believe that’s partly due to less sunscreen use on these areas.” She also recommends using an SPF lip balm.

There’s an ongoing debate about mineral versus chemical sunscreen. In fact, you might be wondering what those terms even mean, and which you should use in your routine. Here’s what you need to know:

What Sunscreen Is Recommended by Dermatologists?

In our reporting, dermatologists often recommended broad-spectrum sunscreens with SPF 30 or higher from EltaMD, SkinCeuticals, La Roche-Posay, and Supergoop!. For more insight into their picks, see the expert recommendations featured throughout our product reviews.

Should You Wear Sunscreen Every Day—Even Indoors?

Wearing sunscreen every day helps protect against cumulative sun damage, which can contribute to skin cancer and premature aging. And while you might think you’re safe from UV rays indoors, UVA radiation can penetrate ordinary window glass, making sunscreen particularly worthwhile if you spend time near sunny windows. Visible light from the sun can also contribute to hyperpigmentation, especially in people with darker skin tones or melasma. However, there’s little evidence that the blue light emitted by phones, computers, and other electronic devices has a meaningful effect on the skin.

How to Apply (and Reapply) Sunscreen Properly

Now that you know what to look for in a sunscreen, it’s important to apply it with care. “It is a common issue that consumers are not applying it correctly, whether applying a product that is substandard, applying an insufficient amount, or neglecting to reapply appropriately,” Dr. Murphy-Rose explains. “A good guideline for sufficient coverage is about a shot glass’s worth of product for one application for the whole body or the equivalent of two finger lengths for the face.”

If you’re in direct sunlight, you should reapply sunscreen at least every two hours, as well as after swimming, sweating, or towel drying. This means applying the same amount you did initially (read: the two-finger rule!). Sunscreen sprays and powders can be convenient for touch-ups, especially over makeup, but it can be difficult to apply enough to achieve the SPF protection stated on the label. For the most reliable coverage, stick with a lotion or cream when reapplying. According to Dr. Tomassian, another misconception is that makeup with SPF is sufficient for your daily sunscreen: your SPF-laced makeup must be layered on top of a layer of sunscreen. “Always remember the sunscreen that you will use is the one that is going to be most effective!” Dr. Karen adds.

Sunscreen should generally be reapplied at least every two hours when you’re outdoors, and more frequently after swimming, sweating, or towel drying, according to the product’s water-resistance instructions. Over time, sunscreen can wear off or become less effective, so regular reapplication is essential to maintain protection.

You might be wondering: Does SPF matter? It’s a common question we beauty editors get, especially with so many different sunscreens on the market. Not to mention, you might receive different advice based on who you’re talking to.

“SPF (Sun Protection Factor) measures the amount of UV radiation needed to produce sunburn on protected skin (with sunscreen) compared to the amount of UV radiation required to produce sunburn on unprotected skin (without sunscreen),” Dr. Green explains. “The higher the SPF, the more UV radiation exposure your skin can handle before getting sunburned.” Generally speaking, most experts recommend an SPF of 30 or higher, but Dr. Green advises a minimum of SPF 50.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—for professional insight into the industry’s standout products that specialists use themselves or recommend to clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

For sunscreens, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, texture, finish, SPF level, and the skin-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our own tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine which we would recommend.

#6616. Is Jeremy Allen White Playing Wolverine? His Mutton Chops Say Yes

Marvel has filled most of the seats for its new X-Men film. Sadie Sink is Jean Grey, Kit Connor is Cyclops, Christopher Abbott is Professor X, Samara Weaving is Emma Frost, Inde Navarrette is Rogue, and Maya Boyd is Storm. But there’s still one grizzly gap in the line-up: Wolverine.

Earlier this month, Jeremy Allen White was linked with the role after insider Jeff Sneider reported that he had met with Marvel about a small part that could become much bigger later on. Nobody has confirmed that the part is Wolverine (and Sneider has since stressed that White isn’t officially in talks) but the internet did the math pretty quickly. And now there’s a smoking gun: facial hair.

While walking around the Studio City Farmers Market over the weekend (because, of course), The Social Reckoning star was spotted carrying a bouquet of flowers bigger than his torso and wearing some extremely Wolverine-y mutton chops. Normally, growing out your sideburns wouldn’t count as casting news. But when you’ve just been linked with Logan and suddenly look ready to join the X-Men, people are going to ask questions.

White would make a lot of sense. He’s 5’7”, which puts him much closer to the comic book Wolverine’s famously stocky 5’3” frame than Hugh Jackman ever was. He also spent months getting absolutely massive for The Iron Claw, so the muscle is already there. And after years of watching him play Carmy in The Bear, we know he can do angry and exhausted and permanently one minor inconvenience away from losing it. That’s basically three quarters of the Wolverine job description.

Jackman has owned the role since the first X-Men film landed in 2000. He’s played Wolverine across 10 movies, most recently returning for 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine. His version became so definitive that it’s difficult to picture anyone else with the claws (other than the time Troye Sivan briefly had them in 2009’s X-Men Origins: Wolverine), even though the 6’2" actor looked very different from the shorter character drawn in the OG comics.

Maybe White just fancied some giant sideburns. Maybe the flowers are covering three adamantium claws. Either way, Marvel should probably give him a call—assuming it hasn’t already.

#6614. In Being Heumann, Ruth Madeley Brings to Life One of America’s Most Important Disability Activists

The film, based on the Judy Heumann memoir of the same name, is now streaming on AppleTV

Being Heumann, the new film about disability activist Judy Heumann, played by Ruth Madeley, opens with one of those classic New York City street montages: the morning rush hour commute, a close-up of feet pounding the sidewalk, yellow cabs buzzing by. Then, a wheelchair speeding down a bumpy road, splashing in puddles. Judy, a woman riding a motorized wheelchair in the middle of the road, weaves between traffic and over steaming manholes. She crosses the street, but there are no ramps on the sidewalk, so she gets back on the road, zig-zagging between drivers yelling at her to get out of the way. When a giant city bus gets behind her and threateningly honks its horn, Judy simply raises her right hand, gives the driver the middle finger, and continues on her way unfazed. We are barely three minutes into the film.

Written and directed by Sián Heder, whose previous film Coda, won Best Picture and Best Adapted Screenplay at the 2022 Academy Awards, Being Heumann chronicles the 504 Sit-In, which is the longest non-violent occupation of a federal building in US history which led to the passing of Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act which, among other things, made it illegal to discriminate on the basis of disability, and also called for making public buildings and transportation accessible, and would set the basis for the American with Disabilities act, 1990’s landmark civil rights legislation.

“So often, disabled characters in particular—and especially women—are very softly introduced,” says Madeley a few days before the movie debuts on AppleTV+. “[But] This is who Judy is. She was doing this every day. You’re completely captivated by, ‘Oh my god, where is this woman going?’ I remember her brother said there were so many times she nearly got hit by a car.” Judy’s unapologetic attitude is the driving force behind her activist group—even if it sometimes puts her at odds with others.

There is a popular saying on social media, “Well-behaved women rarely make history,” and yet so often women—even activists, or especially activists—need to fit into neat preconceived notions of how to respectfully ask instead of demand for change. “[Judy] wasn’t always likable. She was an asshole sometimes, she was stubborn and she could railroad people sometimes… but I think that’s what makes her so compelling,” says Madeley. “The audience understands where she’s coming from because she had years of being told ‘No, you can’t go to school,’ ‘No, you can’t be a teacher,’ ‘You can’t come in here, you’re a fire hazard’... just years of injustice. And she was done with it. She was tired of it.” Madeley adds, “I was so excited that Sián and Rebekah [Tausig, who co-wrote the script], didn’t round off Judy’s edges because she was a complex person. She was messy, and I love playing a messy, complicated woman.”

Being Heumann tells the story of one of the most important leaders of disability rights in American history, and has already broken ground for its diverse cast of actors who are disabled for its main roles. Still, Madeley rejects its purpose as a mere “history lesson.” “This is what people want to go to the movies to see. They want to laugh, they want to cry, they want to go on a ride with a bunch of people storming a building when they have absolutely no idea what they’re doing,” she explains. The movie does in fact have the ebullience of the classic “us against the world” trope (my mind goes to Empire Records, a personal favorite, except with higher stakes)—as the activists hunker down inside the Federal Building in San Francisco, they turn the space into a temporary utopia: the Black Panthers bring them food and weed and they host classes and panels on topics like sexuality. (In one of the best scenes in the movie, as Judy is getting intimate with Jim Pechin, her fellow activist who’s been flirting with her since the beginning of the movie, she says, “I’m going to tell you what I want and you’re going to do as I say.” What other movie has ever displayed this level of control and empowerment in a sex scene? “The complexity and the different nuances of that scene really interested me, and I’d never seen anything like that on screen before,” Madeley explains.)

Another scene that broke ground on how we’ve seen disability on film came early on, when Judy is in bed waiting for her home attendant, who is running late, and Judy really has to go to the bathroom. “Movement fascinates me on screen, it always has,” Madeley reveals. “What really interested me was how Judy was so quick and forever moving and busy when she was in her chair, like she is free in her chair and then the stark contrast to how vulnerable and dependent on other people when she’s out of her chair. That scene is really poignant because Sián didn’t make it choppy, she wanted it to be in real time, and she wanted the audience to feel the rigamarole. Judy has no core strength, so she has to be balanced, she has to move the plates on her wheelchair, then she’s transferred, then she has to move the plates back, take the locks off… There are all these different stages just to be able to use the bathroom.” She adds, “Honoring Judy’s physicality was just as important to me as honoring all the different layers of her personality.”

Madeley, who also portrayed British disability rights advocate Barbara Lisicki (in the BBC film Then Barbara Met Alan), wants people to have fun while watching Being Heumann. That said, she also hopes they come away with “a better understanding of the physical world around them.” She continues, “Every time I go down a curb cut, I’m like, ‘Thanks, Judy.’ That curb cut wasn’t just there, it didn’t just appear. It was fought for.”

#6612. 40 More Million-Dollar Watches Just Sold at Auction

This is an edition of the newsletter Box + Papers, Cam Wolf’s weekly deep dive into the world of watches. Sign up here.

Back in June, I reported on the bonanza of watches crossing the million-dollar-plus mark at auction. What once felt like a unicorn price for watchmakers, auction houses, and the industry as a whole no longer feels so magical. “I joke with people that $1 million is like the new $250,000 of five years ago,” Paul Boutros of Phillips auction house said over the summer.

In just the first half of 2026, the number of million-dollar watches sold nearly eclipsed the total from all of 2025. Now, after a raft of high-profile auctions in Geneva a couple of weeks ago, the industry has set yet another record. In just the last month alone (including Monaco Legend Group, which kicked things off in late October), 40 million-dollar watches hammered, according to numbers provided by EveryWatch. That’s more sold than in any entire year before 2020.

If you’re keeping score at home, we’ve seen 133 watches sell at or above seven figures this year. And we’ve still got plenty of year left.

The question is: How much steam does the auction world have left? And what’s driving this radical spike in big-ticket timepieces?

A $10 million Patek Philippe Perpetual Calendar Chronograph ref. 2499

Mike Nouveau, WatchTok King and dealer, has told me that if more kids knew how much growth potential there is in the vintage market, they’d put down the creator-style tiny microphones and start studying reference numbers. The vintage market spiked in the middle of the pandemic, when prices on sport watch grails like the Patek Philippe Nautilus and Rolex Daytona went crypto-mode as a new wave of speculators flooded the high-end collecting scene.

But while the steel sport watch craze has cooled—or at least leveled off—the market has continued riding a remarkably durable wave, helped in part by the arrival of a previously quiet category: the insiders-only independent brands. “For many years at auction, we always said, ‘You have Patek Philippe and Rolex. What’s the third brand that can compete?’” Alexandre Ghotbi, a deputy chairman at Phillips auction house, told me in 2024 for a story on the beloved watchmaker Rexhep Rexhepi. “Today’s third brand is not a brand—it’s a genre: independent artisanal watchmakers.”

Think F.P. Journe, Berneron, Phillipe Dufour, Rexhepi’s Atelier Akrivia—companies helmed by watchmaking auteurs turning out hyper-limited runs, most of which sell out long before a perfectly-lit product photo ever hits the web. Oftentimes, the only way to get your hands on one of their wares—if you haven’t yet achieved friend-of-the-brand status—is by raising a paddle at auction.

When I asked dealer Eric Wind if he thought the indie insanity would remain strong, he was unequivocal: “At the top end, yes.” The dealer Zoe Abelson, of Graal Watches, actually believes we haven’t reached the peak yet. “I do think there's still room for the pieces that are actually rare to continue to grow in value with a continuance in new interest in collecting watches and the yearning to build the most impressive collection,” she said.

Two weekends ago, a new independent brand joined the list of million-dollar watchmakers. Sylvain Pinaud cut his teeth restoring antique watches and established his eponymous brand in 2018. He’s known for showing his work—the instrumental components of his watches are often highlighted on the dial. A unique version of his Origine, a model that only launched in 2022, sold for 1,011,200 Swiss francs (roughly $1,211,500).

Pinaud’s success is indicative of what happens to the elite independent brands that hit the big time. Compared to many of the heavyweight Swiss makers working at scale, independent watchmakers are seen as artisans who hand-produce their designs in extremely limited quantities. It’s why a watchmaker like Kari Voutilainen, considered a master of his craft, has sold more million-dollar pieces this year than many of the big fellas getting rap lyric shoutouts. “There's a growing appreciation for what these watchmakers are producing,” said Ben Horesh, EveryWatch’s CEO. “It’s great to see more independents challenging the old guard."

Look at that list above. Voutilainen ranks just after Rolex and Patek Philippe but ahead of Cartier for the most million-dollar watches sold at auction in 2026. The list is heavy on independents, including Rexhepi’s Akrivia, George Daniels, Philippe Dufour, and Vianney Halter. The real headline, though, is seeing F.P. Journe—the godfather of the indie scene—at the very top. If one area of the market doesn’t feel entirely sustainable, it’s the inferno around FPJ’s pieces. For deep-pocketed newcomers to the “hobby” of catching big-ticket whales, the Geneva-based maker has come to represent the grailiest of grails. Nearly every Journe piece that comes to auction sells for multiples of its estimate. And I mean everything: an empty watch box made for a set of FPJs sold for $230,000 at Christie’s! “The less rare—or in Journe's case, current production—pieces that get swept up in the overall market growth will slow down soon,” Abelson said. “I don't think it's sustainable; at a certain point the values will price out enough people that there should be a correction.”

A $13 million F.P. Journe Chronomètre à Résonance "Régence”

If six-figure watches were once rare, 10-million-plus pieces were true spectacles. Between 2020 and 2023, not a single watch crossed that threshold. In the last decade, from 2015 to 2025, there were just seven 10-million watches total. But with some time still on the clock, seven watches have already topped that threshold in 2026. A solid chunk of that is thanks to the wild one-of-one Daytonas that Rolex made for a charity auction—three out of the four sold for seven figures—but it’s still an astounding feat. The rest of the list is filled out by:

These days, it’s hard to find a category of watches that isn’t doing well at auction. Cartier hasn’t fallen off—in fact, the brand keeps setting records: a very cool clock known as Portico No. 4 hammered for approximately $5,768,400 at Phillips the weekend before last, becoming the most expensive Cartier ever sold in the process. Breguet is, rightfully and finally, on the rise. And after relaunching just last summer, Urban Jürgensen’s vintage pieces are hotter than ever. A super sexy pink-gold version of the brand’s Reference 2 went for 358,400 Swiss francs (about $430,000) at Sotheby’s.

To put a fine point on all this, just look at how overall sales are soaring. Last year, Phillips set the record with $83,018,538 worth of timepieces sold in a single auction. It only took 12 months to shatter that number. This month saw Phillips reset the record with a $112.3 million auction. I would say 2026 is an inflection point for the industry…if I didn’t anticipate that we’ll be back here talking about even more record-setting sales every year for the foreseeable future.

#6611. Skyler Gisondo Is Using His First Awards Show Circuit to Experiment With Style

Last night, ahead of the 2026 Governors Awards, Primetime actor Skyler Gisondo put the finishing touches on his Louis Vuitton look in a rather unusual location: the projection room at the Aero Theater in Santa Monica.

The theater hosted a Gisondo-themed double feature: Primetime and Licorice Pizza (you may also know him from his scene-stealing performance in Booksmart). Still, this is all new to him. Though Gisondo has been a working actor since childhood, Primetime marks his first-ever awards season campaign. “It’s not even a dream come true because it’s almost like something I never even allowed myself to dream of,” Gisondo tells Vogue.

With an awards blitz comes extra attention to fashion. “I’m 30, and I feel like I just recently started to figure out what I like,” says Gisondo, who loves a vintage workman jacket and admits, “I seem unable to eat anything without spilling on myself, so that is kind of prohibitive for me wanting to get nicer shirts and stuff.”

Enter menswear maestro Jason Bolden, who is helping Gisondo achieve a look inspired by his favorite actors: Redford and Newman. “I think there’s a certain timelessness to it—it’s cool in any era at any time. That’s certainly the stuff that I find myself responding to,” he says.

While he’s kicking off awards season with a classic black suit (though the Vuitton tuxedo blouson adds a cool, unfussy touch), Bolden is nudging the actor toward bolder pieces. “I’m pretty tame in my fashion decisions,” Gisondo says. “I’m probably Jason’s most boring client, but to me, the stuff he has me in, I’m like, oh my God, this is crazy.” What is crazy, you may ask? “He’ll put me in a leather jacket or something, and I’ll look at him and say, ‘Jason, I don't know if I’m this guy, man.’ And he’ll say, ‘Oh, you’re this guy.’”

Bolden isn’t the only one encouraging Gisondo to broaden his fashion horizons. “My girlfriend is also lovingly pushing me to dress cooler,” he says. He recalls an instance when she suggested he buy a pair of baggy pants. “I was like, ‘I just can’t do it. They’re too big. This just isn’t me.’ Now they’re not even the biggest pants I own.”

Up next on Bolden’s agenda? To get Gisondo into a pair of leather pants.

“If I learned anything from Primetime, it’s that you just got to try things. You can’t be afraid to fail,” he says. “You can’t be afraid to fail at work, in your fashion choices. You only live once. Let’s try some things. Put on the leather pants. Let’s see how it goes.”

Here, Skyler Gisondo brings Vogue to the projection room ahead of the 2026 Governors Awards.

In the room where the magic happens—the projection room.

Big thank you to Louis Vuitton for tonight’s look

#6609. 31 Pumpkin Purée Recipes From Cake to Pie

As soon as fall arrives, canned pumpkin purée earns a permanent spot in the pantry. After all, it’s shelf-stable and can be turned into a trillion recipes, sweet and savory alike. Just be sure you’re using plain canned pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which already contains sugar and spices.

Some recipes, like our Pumpkin Spice Crumb Cake, call for just half a can, while others, like Weeknight Pumpkin Chili, use the whole thing. But if you have leftover pumpkin purée hanging out in the fridge, consider it a good thing—it just means another pumpkin recipe is on the horizon. And if you’ve gone the extra mile to make pumpkin purée from fresh pumpkins, you overachiever, check the recipe before swapping it in: Homemade purée can be wetter than canned. So grab a scarf and let’s take a stroll, shall we?

These pumpkin pancakes are tall, light, and warmly spiced with tangy buttermilk and fresh ginger in the batter. Top with maple-syrup-spiked butter and crunchy pecans for a breakfast worth getting out of bed for.

As if pumpkin muffins with a crunchy pepita streusel weren’t enough, these have a hidden surprise: a pocket of sweetened cream cheese. They’re part breakfast, part cheesecake, and entirely worth getting out of bed for.

Tart cranberries punctuate these tender pumpkin scones, while a sprinkle of raw sugar adds a crisp finish. Serve them warm with the accompanying cinnamon-maple butter, which you can make up to four days ahead.

Part pancake, part custard, this Dutch baby comes with a bonus pumpkin purée recipe: ¼ cup goes into the batter, and the rest of the can becomes a silky, spiced pumpkin butter to spread on top. Leftover butter is excellent on toast.

Fresh ginger gives this super-moist pumpkin bread a little kick, while pumpkin seeds add crunch. The secret to its tender crumb? Extra-virgin olive oil. And don’t skip the salted maple butter for slathering on every slice.

Read more: What Kind of Olive Oil Should You Use in Olive Oil Cake?

Sweet, mellow pumpkin and sharp, salty cheddar are a perfect match in this hearty strata. Assemble it the day before to let the bread soak up the savory custard, then bake until golden and crisp on top.

A pumpkin spice latte you don’t need to leave the house for. Unlike many café versions, this one actually contains pumpkin purée. Don’t have an espresso machine? Swap in strong coffee instead.

This tender, deeply spiced pumpkin cake comes together without a stand mixer and gets a generous swoop of tangy cream cheese frosting. A drizzle of maple syrup is optional but highly encouraged.

This plush chocolate-pumpkin cake draws inspiration from Mexican chocolate, with cinnamon and a pinch of cayenne for warmth. The pumpkin glaze doubles down on the seasonal flavor.

With nearly as much brown sugar streusel as plush pumpkin cake, this New York–style crumb cake takes its topping seriously. If there is a more comforting afternoon snack, we need not know it.

Cinnamon-spiced pumpkin cake wraps around walnut-studded cream cheese frosting in a pretty spiral. The batter comes together in one bowl, but be sure to roll the cake while it’s still warm to prevent cracks.

Pumpkin and chocolate cake batters combine for a dramatic marbled effect in this striking Bundt cake. A glossy chocolate ganache finishes the job. It looks like a project, but you don’t even need a mixer.

Classic crumb cake meets chewy, bouncy mochi in this pumpkin-spiced mash-up. Sweet rice flour gives the cake its distinctive texture, while a buttery pecan streusel adds crunch. It’s particularly good for sharing at Friendsgiving.

Silky filling, flaky crust, a whisper of spice: This is pumpkin pie done right. And there’s no need to roast and purée a fresh pumpkin—our favorite canned variety delivers the consistency we’re after.

With its deeply browned top and creamy, pumpkin-spiced center, this Basque cheesecake looks impressive but skips the fussy water bath. No crust required, either. A full can of pumpkin purée goes into the filling.

The caramelized notes of bourbon and tang of sour cream balance this classic Gourmet dessert. Chopped pecans give the graham cracker crust a little extra crunch.

Can’t choose between pumpkin pie and cheesecake? These maple-sweetened bars make a pretty convincing argument for having both. Swirls of creamy cheesecake and spiced pumpkin filling make them especially handsome on a dessert platter.

Imagine a pumpkin pie with pecan pie’s best feature—obviously, the candied nut topping. A splash of rye whiskey adds a little malty complexity to this two-for-one Thanksgiving dessert.

This positively fluffy pumpkin pie gets a little nutty depth from tahini, whose toasty, slightly bitter flavor balances the sweet pumpkin filling. Whipped cream keeps things light and airy.

This autumnal riff on Puerto Rican flan de queso gets its exceptionally velvety texture from cream cheese. Pumpkin purée and warm spices bring the seasonal flavor, while a glossy caramel topping makes it hard to resist.

What’s more satisfying than cracking through that caramelized sugar topping? Finding a luscious, pumpkin-spiced custard underneath. This recipe uses an entire can of purée, and you can finish the sugar under the broiler if you don’t own a kitchen torch.

Everything you love about classic tiramisu, with the warming spices of a pumpkin spice latte. Ladyfingers dipped in bourbon-spiked espresso alternate with creamy pumpkin mascarpone filling. Make it ahead and dust with cinnamon and cocoa just before serving.

This streamlined recipe turns three hardworking ingredients—curry paste, coconut milk, and pumpkin purée—into a cozy, flavorful soup in just 30 minutes. Proof that a pantry dinner doesn’t have to feel like a compromise.

A whole can of pumpkin purée becomes a silky pasta sauce with garlic, Parmesan, and a kick of chile. Just the thing for a weeknight when you want something comforting without committing to an afternoon of cooking.

A full can of pumpkin purée becomes the sauce—no simmering required—for these cheesy black bean enchiladas. A quick turn under the broiler melts and browns the cheese; lime and crunchy pepitas finish the job.

A full can of pumpkin purée adds richness, body, and an autumnal hue to this speedy chili without making it taste like pumpkin pie. Ground beef, beans, and savory spices keep the flavors firmly in chili territory.

Adding pumpkin purée to Bolognese might not seem obvious, but it gives the sauce rich body without hours of simmering. Cooking it with tomato paste brings out its nutty, caramelized flavor.

Rolling the filled noodles into spirals adds a whimsical touch and ensures every bite has the perfect balance of spinach-ricotta, tender pasta, and creamy pumpkin sauce.

Canned pumpkin purée gives no-knead focaccia a golden hue, subtle sweetness, and plush crumb. Finish with rosemary and flaky salt (both optional, both recommended), and serve with a dish of olive oil for dipping.
