#6594. Exclusive: The World’s Top Players Look Back on a Wild Year in Men’s Tennis

It was Friday the 13th, and Turin, Italy, the site of the Nitto ATP Finals, glowed with cobalt light as a fingernail moon hung in the air. It looked almost like a Tintoretto painting.

At the Piazza San Carlo, a blue carpet had been laid out lengthwise for the world’s eight best (and currently active) men’s tennis players as fans called out for autographs and selfies. Carlos Alcaraz in Louis Vuitton and Ben Shelton in Ralph Lauren walked among them; missing was the home favorite, Jannik Sinner, who qualified for the field but is sidelined with a knee injury. The scene delivered a surreal, Hollywood-esque half-hour of public stagecraft—paparazzi flashbulbs, police escorts—with all of it designed to celebrate the end of a very notable, and sometimes odd, year in men’s pro tennis.

Speaking of the dreamlike: the evening included an ATP-commissioned portrait session with the photographer Szilveszter Makó, a man who has skyrocketed to industry prominence for having shot multiple covers this year—including for the American, British and Italian editions of Vogue. Makó’s aesthetic itself is rather painterly; photographs as aged frescoes, both cerebral and unusual. Within Turin’s Inalpi Arena, he forged two vignettes with his signature box sets. We stepped in to take a look as Arthur Fils, wearing Balenciaga, was instructed to stand tall and lift his right foot, balancing it on the heel. (“It’s kind of weird, no?” Fils asked, before leaning in.) Makó lensed seven of the eight athletes; due to extenuating circumstances, Alcaraz was unable to stop by the makeshift studio.

But, no matter. In a mad dash between the Principi di Piemonte Hotel, the Piazza San Carlo, a jam-packed van ride across gridlocked roads, and, finally, the Arena, we caught up with all eight players, who together offer an apt representation of the deep and diverse present state of the world’s elite-most men’s tennis. What was discussed: everything from self-reflections to coaching change-ups to cellys to the popularity of the Maldives.

2026 was the biggest year of Zverev’s career: he won his maiden Slam at Roland-Garros, then followed it up with a victory at the US Open. The German also reached the world number 1 spot for the first time (it’s worth noting here that Zverev also holds a super-rare tennis title: an Olympic gold medal, from Tokyo). At 29, he is a half-generation older than the sport’s current dominant duopoly of Sinner and Alcaraz, but if he keeps his current level of play up, he’ll make a strong case for another “Big Three”(the nickname assigned to Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal and Novak Djokovic during their long run of supremacy). Despite the settlement of a domestic abuse lawsuit involving his ex-partner Brenda Patea, a new case was brought to light just a few days ago: the tennis writer Ben Rothenberg reported that Patea has sued Zverev for public misrepresentations. It’s been a career year, but it has to be said that Zverev remains a polarizing figure.

The finest Canadian tuxedo I’ve ever seen.

When you wear head-to-toe denim, yes. You’ve had an incredible year. What worked—and is working—best for you mentally, looking back on it now?

I made a decision with my team last year to change my game style—changing the way we play. I think it was quite a bold move at the age of 29. But we said: it had been working, I’ve had a great career, but it wasn’t working at the final stage of Grand Slams. It hadn’t worked to achieve the dreams and the goals we had. So, sticking to the new game plan, I think that was the biggest thing. Sticking to it and being brave enough to accept it. I think, in the end, it paid off.

Definitely. Two Slams this year, the number one ranking. Are you happy with your game right now, or is there anything you want to improve in 2027?

No, I don’t think I’m complete at all. There are always things you have to improve—and at the end of the day, everybody else is improving, too, so you have to keep with it to stay relevant.

You had some frustration a few weeks ago in Paris in having to defend your number one ranking. Are you still reckoning with that?

I think in Paris it was all just quite new, and I was mentally a little bit tired. There were a lot of new things. And of course, it’s a different kind of pressure. But, I think it’s all settled down, and I’m very happy to be here among the best in the world. It’s an honor.

What’s your vacation plan once the season ends?

Alcaraz—men’s tennis’s brightest star—nicely bookended an otherwise turbulent 2026. The Spaniard, 23, won his first Australian Open all the way back in January, and has enjoyed a surge of recent title wins (in Vienna, Tokyo, and Paris) after returning to the tour from a bout with wrist tenosynovitis that kept him offline for nearly five months. His return at the US Open—where he reached the quarterfinals—brought with it a much-hyped collaboration with Nike’s Cactus Jack line and a tousled new hairstyle. One interesting note going into Turin: Alcaraz has not yet won an ATP Finals, and will be hungry to add that to his resume.

What’s your best 2026 memory off of the court?

Oh, well, I have a couple, to be honest. One of the highlights I had this year was attending the World Cup final. Seeing Spain win the World Cup was unbelievable. So yeah, I’m going to say that! Ferran Torres’s goal, that was the turning point of his career. From that, I would say his stock is really high.

You’ve come back from injury, and you’ve had a strong tail-end of the year, winning Tokyo and Paris. After being hurt, did your mentality change at all? Any hesitation?

I knew that, coming back, I needed matches. I needed competition. I need to feel I was back in the rhythm of competing, and I’m still [building that back]. I need to go out there and feel those nerves of competition. I’m still working on being strong for these difficulties.

With the season ending, what will you try to do in the offseason?

Well, I am not allowed to play golf yet, because my team [won’t let me]. Probably the first thing I’m going to do after the season is over is play golf.

Shelton, 24, had two standout moments on the court in 2026: he defended his Canadian Open title and reached his first Major final at the US Open. Though he lost to Zverev there, it was still a considerable level-up for the Florida-born phenom. Shelton made recent industry news by tapping Juan Carlos Ferrero—Alcaraz’s former coach—to join his team in 2027 (Shelton’s father, Bryan, will remain his coach as well).

You’re bringing on Juan Carlos Ferrero as a coach. Talk us through that decision.

Yeah. Even in the early stages, I think we’ve done a good job of putting together a schedule where I will have two coaches. I don’t want either of them to have to travel 40 weeks a year. So I think we’re putting together a really good formula where they’re both traveling about half the weeks. That’s the ideal scenario for us.

What’s the strongest, most resonant moment you’re taking with you from 2026?

Defending my title in Canada is one. I thought that was the best tennis I’ve played in my career. I didn’t drop a set all week. I was clinical. It was fun for me to see that I can play at that level. But, I have to say, walking out on court for a US Open final and feeling the energy of that stadium on that day, even though I took an L, was pretty special.

I’m just going to play it by ear. I might go on vacation with Arthur Fils, but we’ll see.

The tennis world is happy to see Medvedev, 30, back in elite form. After a less-than-stellar 2025, the lanky Russian has been playing significantly better in 2026, having won four titles and returned to the top 10. Yes, he still has outbursts, and yes, crowds will either go with him on them or boo relentlessly. But that’s just part of the Medvedev Experience. What’s helped on a deeper level: coaching change-ups, and a newfound self-assurance. Don’t forget: Medvedev is a Slam winner (US Open, 2021), a former world number one, and an ATP Finals winner (2020).

Looking back at 2026, what’s the most significant thing you fixed?

What I was looking for was probably finding confidence in myself. Sometimes that requires changing things, and I wanted to take a bit more responsibility. That was probably the biggest fix I managed to make, closer to the end of the year.

Was that rediscovering your old confidence, or was it something new?

Rediscovering in terms of tennis, yes. But more in terms of… I want to say, it’s more like confidence in a tennis life path. I was listening to my old coaches a lot rather than trusting myself fully. So there was always a bit of back-and-forth. Where do I trust them? Where do I trust myself? And now it’s more about trusting myself fully, and then discussing that trust with the team, if that makes sense.

You’re known for your heated interactions with crowds. At this stage in your career, how much of that is just a reaction versus a choice?

It’s never a choice. It’s always a natural reaction.

Any indulgences you’re looking forward to after the season ends?

I have a photo shoot with Lacoste, and then I’m in the Maldives the next day. I would love to go to Hawaii, I don’t know, or wherever. But it’s way too far from where I live.

Cobolli, 24, had the best year of his young career in 2026. His breakthrough: reaching the final of the French Open, where he lost to Zverev in five sets. In Turin, the Italian naturally received the loudest cheers on the blue carpet. With Sinner absent, he’s the home favorite. Cobolli is well-liked on social media, too; the ATP sometimes jokingly calls him their “admin.” He’s had some struggles with fatigue as the season nears its conclusion, but here’s hoping the Florentine can turn on the jets in Piedmont.

At Wimbledon this year, you made some headlines for doing Matheus Cunha’s “surfing” celebration. Should tennis have more cellys?

No, you know why? Two weeks ago, Cunha beat AS Roma. He beat my team, so I’m really pissed with him. [Laughs] But no… I think [for celebrations] if I have something on my mind, I just do it.

You’re the home favorite in Turin. What does that feel like?

It means a lot to me to play here and to win in front of the Italian crowd. Of course, we miss Jannik a lot. He deserves to be here. So I play for him, for the country, for my team, for myself, and for my family. I just want to play for everybody!

Fils, the 22-year-old Frenchman, struggled in the beginning of the year with a back injury that forced him out of the Australian and French Opens. But he had a strong enough summer to qualify for the year-end tournament, winning his first Masters 1000-level title at the Cincinnati Open. In tennis circles, many believe Fils has the natural talent to eventually challenge the Tour’s stalwart top three Sinner, Alcaraz and Zverev. But he’s already matched them if not exceeded them in aura: in Turin, Fils stepped out on the blue carpet in a full Balenciaga look—he has a deal with the brand—and space-like sunglasses. Audiences went wild.

What are you most happy with regarding your play this year?

I’m serving better, moving better. I mean, I knew I was a great competitor. But I didn’t know I could be that good in competitive moments.

When the season is said and done, what’s going to be your first indulgence?

I’m going on holiday in the States, so I think I’m going to go with… having some ribs.

Tell us a little about working with Balenciaga.

They’re changing [internally] now, I know. But I love the brand. It was kind of a dream when I was a kid to sign one day with a huge fashion label. I feel very comfortable wearing them. It’s a new world for me, but I enjoy it.

Tiafoe, 28, has reached the ATP Finals for the first time. It’s testament to his grit and commitment—what he calls a re-established sense of “showing up” day in and day out. “Big Foe,” as he’s endearingly called, has had a productive year; he won his first 500-level tournament in Halle, reached the semis at the US Open, and recorded the fourth-most match wins of any man on Tour. He was all smiles in an expertly tailored Giorgio Armani double-breasted suit on the blue carpet, too.

You’re having a great season. What are you most happy with, not necessarily numbers wise, but in terms of your play?

I think I just found a flow state. I found this peace, and I’m showing up every day. I think sometimes you try to figure out this whole thing of how to get to X to Y to Z, or how to do X, Y and Z together. And it’s kind of just: you show up, man.

Every day looks different, but you just go out there and give your best and be okay with the result. Every time I’ve been able to lay it out there and lost, I was cool with it, rather than having regret that I could have done a little more. I was also focused on my preparation, and once preparation meets opportunity, you get the results.

During the long season, what was a favorite memory away from the court?

I saw the Chris Brown and Usher concert in D.C. and it was out of control. One of the biggest things was getting to meet Matthew McConaughey at the US Open. He’s a special individual.

What are you looking forward to during the break?

Jodar, the youngest man in the Turin field, has been lightning in a bottle this year. He broke men’s tennis’s record for the quickness of his ascent: from his tour debut to hitting the top 10, Jodar needed only 296 days. With that in mind, the Spaniard can be forgiven for speed bumps along the way: a highly publicized outburst at a ball kid during the Shanghai Masters, and a gamesmanship debate around equipment changes. He’s among the youngest of tennis’s new guard—a quarter-generation behind Alcaraz and Sinner, even—and his future feels bright.

So much has been said about the speed of your year, and how quickly you’ve risen. Is there anything you wish would slow down?

Well, I think how it works is that if you do well on Tour, you’re going to have more expectations. That’s something you just have to deal with when you’re doing well. Not every day you’re going to be in a happy mood. But at the end of the day, you just have to handle the situation in the best way possible, and keep focusing on and trying to get better at the game.

What do you do with your limited free time?

I think I’d say spending some time at home and doing some activities in Madrid. Probably, the thing I want to do most is go to the Bernabéu to watch Real Madrid. That’s when I disconnect completely from tennis, and focus on the football game.

#6593. Discover the Best Dresses for Every November Occasion

All products featured on Vogue are independently selected by our editors. However, we may earn affiliate revenue on this article and commission when you buy something.

No matter the occasion or season, there are always plenty of opportunities to wear a dress and, of course, an overwhelming number of options from which to pick. We’ve put together an edit of the best dresses of the month; check back every two weeks for a new selection of styles, handpicked by Vogue.

There’s no better time than mid-November to embrace a little holiday cheer. Based on this month’s standout dress finds, the key elements are texture, color, and fabric. Art Deco influences were plenty on the fall runways, and drop-waist styles like Tory Burch’s deep red midi make for excellent party attire. ‘Tis also the season for autumnal textures in wool, velvet, jacquard—try a brocade number for an evening occasion, or pick up a sweater dress from either Me+Em or Proenza Schouler to wear throughout the winter. And for all fall weddings and holiday festivities on the horizon, there are simply too many good options—from Toteme to Staud—that will make you the best-dressed guest.

Whether you’re shopping for new essentials, vacation, or a destination wedding, these are November’s best dresses.

Cos reimagines the LBD with swishy godet panels, for a flattering, effortless silhouette. Pair it with flats for the office or kitten heels after dark. Did I mention this makes for a perfect cocktail dress?

The classic slip dress gets a romantic update in satin and Chantilly lace. An elegant choice for holiday soirées or the bride-to-be.

Toteme puts a fresh spin on the reverse collar trend with this pale pink silk dress. The draped silhouette makes for effortless office dressing.

A gala, a wedding, or an evening at the ballet? With its decadent embellishments and Art Deco allure, this dress is the epitome of 1920s glamour, fit for right now.

A favorite from Kallmeyer’s holiday capsule, this beaded mini is made for after parties. Style it with sheer tights and strappy sandals.

Fresh off Tory Burch’s fall 2026 runway, this drop-waist dress is ready for the holiday circuit. Pair with embellished heels for extra festive flair.

Two looks in one. Me+Em’s versatile set pairs a sleeveless turtleneck dress with a coordinating long-sleeve sweater. Drape the merino wool knit over your shoulders or tie it around your waist.

As temperatures dip, this textured bouclé dress offers a chic alternative to traditional winter knits. Finish the look with a ’90s-inspired tailored coat for understated elegance.

RSVP, yes! This dazzling purple dress makes a compelling case for bold color at upcoming weddings.

Decadent velvet without the decadent price tag? Zara delivers with this sumptuous crushed velvet gown. A true steal!

Taller Marmo’s red mini is a statement in itself. Pair it with sheer tights, strappy sandals, and a pouch for holiday events, or go bare-legged for a glamorous beach event.

Cooler temperatures are no reason to retire color. Consider this your invitation to embrace it. Fforme’s elegant take on the evening dress features a dropped waist, mock neckline, and sleeveless silhouette—all in a rich berry hue.

What’s a fall wardrobe without a knit dress? This under-$300 find from Banana Republic makes for a go-to in any wardrobe. Style it with knee-high boots for effortless cold-weather dressing.

Tory Burch sent this printed dress—in a trompe l’oeil pattern resembling tiger stripes—down the runway in two iterations: a delicate pastel jacquard and a rich purple version. With a fitted bodice that cascades into a handkerchief hemline, it’s a romantic silhouette that needs little extra to feel styled. A close-cut jacket and patent pumps should do the trick.

A knit dress is always a good idea. Simkhai’s ribbed iteration, accented with a delicate white trim, makes a subtle yet striking statement. Add a knee-high boot, a sweeping opera coat, and a chic clutch.

A dress that’ll get you multiple double-takes. This red maxi with a built-in cummerbund reimagines traditional black tie dress codes for a feminine-meets-masculine twist.

ICYMI: Jacquard is having a moment. This black V-neck dress, accented with a cummerbund sash, brings a polished edge to evening dressing. Even better? It’s under $300.

Conner Ives can do no wrong. Spaghetti straps, delicate pleats, and a vibrant color story—the dress is composed of four different printed vintage scarves—make this a vacation must-have, whether you’re spending Thanksgiving in Nayarita or St. Barths.

The shift is a forever classic and Posse’s silk-satin take is minimalist in the best way. Bring that less is more ethos to accessorizing with a simple pouch and drop earrings.

Emily Dawn Long—a CFDA 2026 runner-up—has a knack for intuiting what we want to wear before we do. This bright color-blocked midi is just one recent example.

Consider this sleeveless, funnel-neck knit dress a blank canvas for styling. Layer it over or under a long-sleeve knit (for extra warmth), throw on a sweeping shearling coat, then finish with flat boots. The possibilities are endless for cold-weather dressing.

You know the LBD, you (we hope) love the LBD. Play with proportions to give it a fresh look: a long duster coat, statement brooch, and polished loafers toughen up its feminine spirit.

Why yes, it’s Kallmeyer’s fall collection opening look: a creamy drop-waist style made from a silk charmeuse with caped armholes and a high funnel-neck. Follow the fall show’s styling notes and pair it with patent leather knee-highs–a pulled-back bun and minimal jewelry give the dress its well-deserved moment.

Maria McManus first introduced this dress in an off-white shade; this rich eggplant hue makes for a wonderful autumnal option.

Khaite’s chiffon maxi strikes the perfect balance between delicate and wearable. Give it heft by styling with a leather coat, tights, and strappy sandals.

Weddings or galas on the horizon? This strapless satin gown—as seen on supermodel Karlie Kloss, who wore it earlier this year for Taylor Swift’s wedding—works for either occasion.

Minimal, elegant, and endlessly versatile, this long-sleeve satin number is the kind of wardrobe staple that moves easily from desk job to after-hours plans. Dress it up with pumps or keep things understated with a flat—it looks sophisticated however your style it.

Kallmeyer’s Ivette dress is easily one of the season’s most talked-about dresses. With Art Deco influences leading the trend conversation, its embellished design feels especially on-trend.

Feathers, feathers, and more feathers! Whether you’re dressing for a special occasion or are a bride-to-be, this Loulou de Saison dress is designed to make an entrance. The drop-waist silhouette, adorned with feather embellishments around the hips, delivers just the right amount of drama. More is more!

Print enthusiasts, look no further than this floral maxidress from Banana Republic. Rendered in a rich persimmon print, the silhouette skims the body before flaring into a sweeping skirt. A romantic take on fall florals.

J.Crew’s cult-favorite rollneck sweater has officially entered its dress era. Just in time for sweater weather, its simple silhouette makes a strong case for becoming your new go-to. Style it with hosiery and loafers, then tie a colorful knit around your for an extra layer.

ICYMI: Purple is the color to own this season, and this violet maxi from Zara features an alluring open-back silhouette. Not quite ready to bare it all? Layer a lightweight top underneath, either in a neutral hue or a contrasting pop of color.

Caftans can be worn year-round—you just have to pick one in a more fall-friendly fabric. Taller Marmo’s long-sleeve is cut from double satin, with adjustable buttons that allows you to wear it in more ways than one—off-the-shoulder, single-shoulder, or or with a boat neckline.

Velvet chartreuse has never looked better, courtesy of Reformation x Alexa Chung, whose recent collaboration delivered one of the finest evening dresses of the month. Pair it with a satin bag and kitten heels.

This Staud dress creates the illusion of separates: A fitted black silhouette contrasts with a white draped skirt. A study that proves that opposites really do attract.

Meryll Rogge’s debut collection for Marni has officially dropped. The color-block mini is cut from one of the collection’s most memorable prints: a playful floral print that captures the house’s signature eccentricity. Pair with loafers and a long necklace.

For a quiet statement, consider this tea-length dress from Merlette, crafted from a rich butter yellow satin with ruched sleeves. On chillier days, add a faux-fur coat on top.

Altuzarra’s flutter-sleeve dress balances romance and structure, with delicate draping that creates soft movement. Save this for a special occasion.

Straight from the runway, this sleeveless knit turtleneck is a master class in sculptural dressing, crafted from a stretch rib that contours the body and falls to a handkerchief hem.

Who needs a necklace when the dress is the jewelry? Brandon Maxwell turns a V-neck dress into a work of art, with a beaded neckline that moves like fringe. An elegant, embellished option for an evening affair.

No dress roundup is complete without a little black dress. This off-the-shoulder option from Fforme is cut from a thick scuba fabric for a sculpted look. Complete the idea with strappy sandals and an embellished evening bag.

This Tory Burch runway dress was an editor favorite. Cut from jacquard in a slate blue and cherry-check motif, the color combination creates an optical illusion of a rich purple hue (one of this season’s trending hues). Two versatile details make it especially wearable: Both the necktie and belt are removable. Complete the look with fall boots.

To celebrate Vogue’s book club selection Sense and Sensibility, Vogue collaborated on a limited-edition nightgown inspired by Jane Austen's heroines. A nightgown that isn't exclusive to home can be styled with a trench and equestrian-inspired boots for an effortlessly romantic look.

Simon Miller's take on the slip dress is both elegant and flattering. This dress works season after season; it's the kind of piece that always makes an entrance, whether paired with boots or sleek mules.

CJR is known for its bold use of color, and this dress is no exception. Inspired by the work of Ettore Sottsass, the graphic polo maxi makes for a statement for any occasion. Dress it up with pumps or style it with flat boots for the weekend.

For upcoming weddings or formal events, look to this artful Tove dress. Playful yet sophisticated, the halter-neck silhouette is elevated by sculptural detailing. Finish off with strappy sandals for a polished finish.

For a minidress to wear this fall, opt for Khaite's Scarla dress. The modern skater silhouette, cut from delicate silk chiffon, feels romantic yet contemporary, making it an especially chic option for a bride-to-be.

Call it the ultimate party dress. The holiday season may still be a little off, but it’s never too early to plan your party wardrobe. This embellished Posse mini will make you the best-dressed guest.

Zara has collaborated with filmmaker Luca Guadagnino and production designer Stefano Baisi on a collection spanning from ready-to-wear to homeware. This scarf-draped dress strikes the perfect balance of elegance and ease.

Minimal yet statement-making, this Magda Butrym gray dress has an off-the-shoulder neckline and a fitted silhouette. A tonal floral appliqué adds a feminine, sculptural finish. Pair it with kitten heels and a clutch for an elegant evening look.

When your wardrobe is craving a dose of color, look to yellow. This H&M Studio dress is cut from a lightweight fabric with romantic ruffle detailing, making it an effortless choice for a warm-weather holiday or a destination wedding.

For a fall dress, look to this minidress inspired by the ’60s. Cut from a wool blend, this double-breasted dress is an ideal layering piece. Style it with a colorful turtleneck or button-down and add tights and boots for a milder fall day, or pair it with loafers.

Alaïa's approach to construction is like no other, creating some of the most flattering silhouettes around. Cut from velvet, this tank dress makes for an understated yet impactful evening option—a minimalist statement.

Maygel Coronel’s dress proves that simplicity can still make an impact. The elongated drop waist, fluid draping, and bubble hem give the silhouette a fresh modern feel.

A fall wardrobe essential, this long-sleeve satin dress is a versatile piece that works from nine to nine. Polished enough for the office and elegant enough for an evening, it transitions seamlessly from day to night.

A black dress is a timeless choice, and this Altuzarra option interprets the style for modern wardrobes with draping and an asymmetric knotted waist. A chic choice for fall weddings: Just add a kitten heel and a clutch.

A little lace, or in this case a lot, goes a long way. This runway favorite from Khaite strikes the perfect balance between romantic and edgy. Ground it with sleek black shoes.

Violet! Purple! Amethyst! However you choose to call them, deep shades of purple are having a serious moment. Style with something red—a clutch or heels, or even a bold lip—for contrast.

Toteme makes the kind of dresses you’ll want to wear on repeat—and this draped maxi is one of them. New in for the season (we’ve written about it in cream, red, and butter yellow), this rich olive hue feels just right for fall.

Casual meets sophisticated in this fresh-off-the-runway Prada mini, featuring a drawstring waist and cultural motifs at the hem. Wear it over pants for an unexpected look.

Cut from a thick satin, Róhe’s sculptural one-shoulder dress contours the body just so, and needs little in the way of styling to feel complete; simply finish with a tassel clutch and kitten heels. Also available as a top, it’s equally chic styled as a full ensemble for an important event.

Color is all everyone can talk about this season—and chartreuse is one of the It hues. This Taller Marmo dress with an integrated cape makes for a striking wedding guest option.

A knit dress streamlines getting ready on a cold, rainy day, and this colorful knit intarsia style by Celine–as seen in the Vogue Shopping print guide to fall–is one worth investing in. Wear it with loafers on a crisp fall day, then switch to knee-high boots for the winter.

The kind of dress Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy might have worn. This simple boatneck style from Zara is minimal yet endlessly versatile.

Tory Burch knows her way around a shirtdress, and this style–straight off the fall runway–comes with a removable necktie, allowing you to switch up the look depending on the occasion.

From weddings to galas, look to this Fforme drop waist dress in blue sapphire hue. Pair with strappy sandals and a sleek pouch bag.

&Other Stories’s pleated mock neck dress is an effortless style that can easily be transformed for any occasion. Pair it with blazers and loafers for the office or dress it up with pumps for evening events.

For a lace dress that’s feminine but not overly sweet, look no further than Maria McManus’s black satin midi. Style it with a button-down or cardigan knotted at the waist, then add an unexpected pop of color with either your shoes or your bag.

A rich blue hue and draped silhouette give this dress a modern take on the 1920s drop-waist silhouette. Dress it up with heels for evening or ground it with loafers for an uptown-meets-downtown approach.

The nightie was a summer favorite, and for fall, Dôen gives it a polished update in a maxi silhouette with silk and lace trimmings. The result is a romantic yet refined style that works just as well at the office as it does for cocktails.

The LBD for minimalists comes courtesy of Toteme, who’ve crafted a short sleeve style from a bonded scuba crepe with darted seams for a subtly sculptural silhouette. Pair with tights and patent heels.

Khaite’s new fall collection has arrived, and this layered maxi, crafted from a sheer silk organza, is a standout. An elegant bustle detail at the back adds unexpected drama.

You’re not imaging it: Purple is one of the season’s standout shades and Toteme’s scarf dress is one of our favorite renditions. Finish with contrasting red or lemon hues for a jaunty color story.

Florals aren’t just reserved for spring. Ulla Johnson’s long-sleeve turtleneck dress makes the print feel autumnal. Pair with boots for this transitional period.

Kallmeyer’s Nala dress has Vogue bride written all over it. Keep the finishing touches pared-back with drop earrings and sleek white shoes.

Straight from Proenza Schouler’s fall runway is this artfully printed dress that’s great for any number of September occasions on your calendar. Pair it with kitten heels and a leather jacket for dinner out with friends, or with boots on cooler days.

Alaïa knows how to celebrate the female form, and this maxi from Pieter Mulier’s final collection for the house does just that. Crafted from ultra-soft merino, it’s also available in a zesty chartreuse, and classic black.

Not your typical minimalist ’90s slip. This olive-green version gets a romantic update with intricate lace trimming.

Whether you’re heading somewhere warm this month or simply leaning into fall’s version of artful bohemian dressing, a caftan always delivers. Easy and elegant, all you need is a long pendant and some chunky bangles to style it out.

COS reimagines the gather dress with a twisted detail at the front for asymmetric like draping. A no-brainer 9-5 option that needs minimal styling.

#6592. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6590. Robert Pattinson’s Hair Is Already 007 Material

Whether you like it or not (or placed bets on Kalshi), Robert Pattinson is our next James Bond. During the years-long process in casting 007, we used our best detective skills to narrow down the field to who would join His Majesty’s Secret Service. And if you were going by hair type alone, well, Pattinson makes a rather compelling case.

Let’s review the canon for a moment. In the 1957 novel From Russia, with Love, Bond creator Ian Fleming describes the spy’s mane thusly: “The hair was black, parted on the left, and carelessly brushed so that a thick black comma fell down over the right eyebrow.”

Pattinson’s hair might be naturally light brown, but a darker ‘do is hardly out of the question for the actor’s upcoming transformation. For his turn as Bruce Wayne in The Batman, he dyed his hair to a darker, almost pitch-black hue. The rest of Fleming’s description fits the actor nicely, particularly the bit about being “carelessly brushed.” In real life, the actor’s hair is rarely anything approaching immaculate. Even at more formal engagements, it tends to retain a certain studied dishevelment, with stray strands escaping an otherwise respectable comb-through. Fleming’s famous “comma,” after all, isn’t a carefully sculpted curl. It’s simply a lock of hair allowed to fall where it pleases, which just so happens to be very on trend in 2026.

We got our first glimpse of the 40-year-old actor taking on the role in a video posted by the official James Bond X account where he’s seen stepping out of the shadows pointing a gun at something (or someone) just outside the frame. It’s hard to tell whether the golden lighting is playing tricks on his hair color, but the accompanying promotional image certainly seems to suggest a shade of black. Plus, his hair’s parted on the correct side.

It’s worth noting that Daniel Craig’s casting as Bond was initially met with considerable resistance, much of it centered on one detail: He’s blonde. Fleming’s Bond, after all, was famously dark-haired, and Craig represented a departure from the physical template established by the novels and previous screen incarnations. We know how that turned out. Craig went on to deliver one of the most celebrated interpretations of 007, proving that a little deviation from the source material needn’t be a deal-breaker.

Pattinson will still need to prove himself to be agile in a tuxedo, nimble behind the wheel, and thirsty for a martini or two, but one thing’s sure: He's got the hair down pat.

#6589. Everything You Need to Know About Korean Scalp Scalers

If you’ve ever been to a Korean head spa, you know it’s less a hair wash than a full reset. Before reaching for the shampoo, a technician typically examines your scalp with a magnifying camera, then applies a treatment to loosen the oil, dead skin, and product residue a regular wash leaves behind. It’s the step that makes your hair feel impossibly light afterward, and it’s called scaling.

You don’t need a spa appointment to get the same effect, though. Scalp scalers bring that deep clean home, whether that’s an acid-based treatment you leave on before shampooing or a salt scrub that lathers up in the shower. They’re especially useful if you lean on dry shampoo, work out often, or have fine hair that goes flat a day after washing.

Below, experts explain what a scalp scaler does, who should use one, how to avoid overdoing it, and which formulas are worth trying.

The name actually comes from the dentist’s office. “In Korean, ‘scaling’ is the same word we use for dental cleaning,” says Ellie Byun, a doctor of Korean medicine and licensed acupuncturist. “Plaque builds up on your teeth even when you brush, and in the same way, oil and dead skin build up on your scalp even when you shampoo.” For many Korean women, it’s a familiar routine. “I’ve been using scalp scalers since high school,” says Kristin Lim, founder of Base-K.

Some scalers work differently from regular shampoos because they require additional time on the scalp. “A clarifying shampoo only cleanses during the short time it’s on your scalp,” Dr. Byun says. “A scaler stays on for several minutes and chemically dissolves dead skin and oil with acids and enzymes—the same principle as an exfoliating toner for your face.”

That’s true of some chemical scalers, but others, including several below, use salt granules instead of acids, or a combination of chemical and physical exfoliants. “A scalp scaler focuses on loosening dead skin and buildup, using acids, physical exfoliants, or a combination of both,” Lim says.

If you go the gritty route, keep it gentle. “A scrub physically buffs the surface with grains, and if you use it too often, it can make the scalp barrier sensitive,” Dr. Byun says. “It’s especially good for oily scalps, flaking caused by buildup, fine hair that goes flat quickly, people who use a lot of dry shampoo and styling products, and anyone who sweats a lot.”

Flaking is where it gets tricky, though. “It can also help loosen surface flakes, but persistent flaking and itching deserve a closer look,” Lim says. “Dandruff and other scalp conditions may need targeted treatment rather than more exfoliation.”

The first thing most people notice is how light their hair feels afterward. “Removing that residue can leave the scalp feeling cleaner and the hair feeling lighter,” Lim says. With regular use, it can reduce oil and flaking. Some research suggests that exfoliating ingredients can help address scalp flaking and discomfort. In one small study, a four-week regimen containing salicylic acid and other scalp-care ingredients improved dandruff, itching, redness, and oiliness in people with seborrheic dermatitis. However, the results don’t necessarily apply to every scalp scaler. Improving scalp health may also benefit hair quality over time. “Studies show that when scalp health declines, hair quality declines too, and when the scalp recovers, hair quality recovers with it,” Dr. Byun says.

The biggest risk is doing too much. “Over-exfoliating weakens the scalp barrier and can cause irritation, dryness, and even a rebound increase in oil,” Dr. Byun says. It’s not the right fit for every scalp, either. “Individuals with sensitive or irritated scalps should approach exfoliating treatments cautiously,” says Joe Cho, team lead of media relations at Medicube. Even a product labeled gentle may cause problems. “Even a gentle formula may not suit a scalp that’s actively inflamed,” Lim says. If something feels off, don’t push through it. “If you notice sudden heavy shedding, pain, or lesions, see a professional,” Dr. Byun says.

“Some scalers go onto a dry or damp scalp before shampooing, while others are used on wet hair as part of the wash,” Lim says. Either way, the product needs to reach your scalp, not just your hair. “Part your hair in sections about an inch apart and apply it directly to the scalp along each part,” Dr. Byun says. “Then massage with your fingertips, never your nails, for two to three minutes, pressing slowly on the crown and the base of the skull.” Then rinse it out on time. “Leaving it on longer or scrubbing harder won’t improve the result,” Lim says. Because formulas vary, follow the timing and application instructions on your particular product.

Less is more when it comes to frequency too. “I recommend once a week for oily scalps and once every two weeks for normal or dry scalps,” Dr. Byun says. Your scalp will tell you when you’ve gone too far. “Signs you’re overdoing it include tightness, stinging, redness, or tenderness, more flaking instead of less, new itching, or a scalp that feels oilier than before.” Lim also recommends sticking to one exfoliant at a time and avoiding combining several scalp exfoliants in the same wash.

Afterward, think of your scalp the way you’d think about your face after an exfoliating toner. “Korean care follows a simple idea—clear first, then nourish,” Dr. Byun says. “Use a mild, low-pH shampoo, then a lightweight scalp serum with niacinamide, panthenol, or centella, and apply conditioner only from the midlengths to the ends.”

Not directly. “While scalp health plays an important role in overall hair care, there’s currently limited clinical evidence that scalp exfoliation alone can directly stimulate hair growth or prevent shedding,” Cho says. Dr. Byun sees it as groundwork. “A scaler doesn’t grow hair on its own, but it does have a real, research-backed role,” she says. “So I see scaling as the first step in creating an environment where healthy hair can grow.” Lim is just as clear: “Promising that a scaler alone will regrow hair or stop shedding would be overpromising.”

Many scalp scalers can be used on color-treated hair, but it’s important to check the product’s instructions, since some exfoliating ingredients and cleansing formulas may affect color longevity. “It’s generally fine on color-treated hair as long as you apply it to the scalp, not the hair itself,” Dr. Byun says.

#6588. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6587. Gina Bruno Wants You to Be a Guest at Your Own Party

“Dinner is never just dinner. It is so much about the people, and the food is just the excuse to get those people around the table.”

I’m 60 seconds into my conversation with Gina Bruno and find myself nodding in agreement, something I’ll continue to do for the next 20 minutes. The self-proclaimed “chef, mom, and host” wears a lot of hats. Private chef, event producer, event space owner, and host of the newly-launched food show Salt The Water presented by Brami are just a few of the titles Bruno claims, but central to all of her work is a palpable love of people and of creating a space for gathering, both of which make her a natural-born host.

Bruno cites her Italian roots and the Sunday dinners she had as a child as the sources of her hosting instinct and ethos. “I am a family-style cooker when I’m hosting, and I just want to fill people up. I want to fill their glasses up; I want to fill their plates up. And the best compliment that I could ever get is having to tell someone, ‘Hey man, it’s really time to go home because I am exhausted and I need to go to bed.’”

Not everyone has a natural inclination toward hosting, though, so to help them out I asked Bruno to run me through her tips for throwing a gathering, be it an intimate dinner or a rowdy holiday party.

“On a table, I will always have one kind of grand slam big, big dish, and then there’s all the supporting actors on the table,” Bruno says. While she uses saved folders on Instagram and Pinterest and likes to browse the Bon Appétit app, Bruno primarily looks to the market for inspiration, describing herself as a “very, very in-season cooker.” “I have so many recipes saved, and sometimes some of those get used, but there is something that just happens when you’re walking, and you see all of these fresh ingredients, and you just get to create a dish right in front of you.”

Bruno’s main tip for anxious hosts is to prep as much in advance as possible. “Sauces and dressings you can absolutely do the day before, and that alleviates so much time the day of. You could go as far as literally setting your entire table the way you want it to be set with napkins, plates, silverware,” Bruno says.

“Lighting is a huge thing,” Bruno says. For evening soirees, she kisses the big overhead light goodbye, opting instead for lower light from lamps and candles tucked into corners to make the space feel moody. “The mood needs to be right, and you want to feel sexy when you walk into somebody’s home,” she says.

Bruno worked in restaurants and went to culinary school in Paris, where she learned the importance of maintaining a clean workspace. “If something spills right then and there, you are wiping it right then and there. If you use the spoon and you’re done, it’s going in the dishwasher. Cleaning as you go is a big step,” she says.

When hosting a more intimate event, one of Bruno’s favorite moves takes the form of an interactive game meant to encourage a bit of deep conversation. “Right before I serve dessert, I have everyone lift up their plate, and there is a little note underneath,” she says. The note has a question on it, either handwritten or printed depending on how much time Bruno has, and every question is different. “It adds a layer of, ‘Oh, our conversation maybe wouldn’t have gone here…. I just love getting to more juicy parts of the person, whether it’s a close friend or an absolute stranger, and it keeps people on their toes,” she says.

“It’s so easy to stay in host mode and think that you have to do all of these things to please people. But as soon as people arrive, it’s almost like, your job is done—or at least as soon as you drop the food, your job is done. And now you get to sit back and enjoy what you’ve done and be a part of it, because the worst feeling ever is you had all these people over, whether it’s four people or 10 people, and you were stuck in the kitchen and no one got to see you. So be a guest,” Bruno says.

Bruno recounts a recent conversation with a friend who was afraid, on the one hand, to try making and serving something new, but felt the dishes that were in her repertoire were too simple for company. “You should never apologize for something that you’re cooking. If you are putting yourself out there and you want to cook something out of your realm, and, say it absolutely f*#%ing fails, that’s fine. I feel like your guests are going to be like, ‘Awesome. We will take a bite and not tell you our honest answer, and then we’re going to order a pizza, and it’s going to be amazing.’ The triumph of just trying is so much bigger than the actual meal,” Bruno says. “Food is the second tier. It’s more about the people around your table. You could serve potato chips and dip and people will actually be pretty happy,” she adds.

“Nine out of 10 times, if I am cooking for people, there is going to be a pasta dish on the table,” Bruno says. She’s a big fan of the protein pasta brand Brami, and not just because she just partnered with them on a YouTube show—she says the brand has organically become the only pasta she keeps at home.

As for sauce, Bruno’s go-to is a spicy vodka. “If I’m making it at home, I’m actually leaving out the vodka and I’m swapping in mezcal, and it gives such a sneaky, smoky flavor that everyone will ask [about it]. And I will then go even further and usually pair it with a mezcal cocktail,” she says.

Now that you know all of Bruno’s tips, these are the products she uses to make gatherings more special and less stressful.

Bruno always keeps three types of olive oil on hand: “One that is not so fancy and you could fry or make dressing with it—just one that’s kind of the back burner; a topping oil; and then an amazing peppery oil that you would maybe more so dip bread in or drizzle on top.”

“Flaky salt is always in my house,” Bruno says. She typically opts for either Maldon or a fleur de sel.

“We could consider Brami a staple. I mean, [my husband and I] cook it at least two times a week, whether there’s meat thrown in it or it’s just a sauce or a pesto or it's anything in between,” Bruno says.

For hosting, I love big platters. Whether they’re vintage or new, I kind of love mixing those two together on the table,” Bruno says. She likes having a collection of larger serveware specifically for hosting: “It’s kind of like your special stuff that you take out for friends.”

Jean Couzon Silverplate Serving Tray Fish Handles

1970's Kromex Sculptura Walnut Accent Lazy Susan Serving Tray

“I love silver, so I have a lot of silver trays, a lot of silver bowls. I think it makes a table,” Bruno says. “I have quite the collection. I almost always buy vintage or second-hand when it comes to silver. There’s simply something about the life the piece had,” she adds.

“I recently splurged and got a really lovely cream and red dishware set from Porta. That was a big purchase for me, and it is a purchase that I am excited to bring out sparingly because I don’t want anything to break,” Bruno says.

When it comes to flatware, Bruno is a Sabre person. “I have three different colors in my house. It’s the only cutlery that I have at this point,” she says.

“We are a big wine-drinking family, so I have a wine fridge. There are on average at least 15 bottles of wine in that fridge always, and it is a variety because you never know what somebody likes,” Bruno says.

When hosting, Bruno keeps a candle burning in her bathroom and on the kitchen counter at all times. She’s partial to Keap’s Wood Cabin scent, which she orders in bulk for both her own home and her event space, Frank’s House.

#6585. The Wide-Leg Jeans That Every French Girl (And Kate Moss) Owns

Last month, while taking in the spring/summer 2027 shows at Paris Fashion Week, I was eager to write about the street style trends bubbling up around the showgoers in town. Which proved harder than anticipated. For one thing, the flashiest dressers had been given full looks by the brands whose shows they were being paid to attend, and reporting on those felt like a somewhat dishonest exercise in journalism. For another, the consensus seems to be that we are living in a post-trend world, and fashion people in particular have little interest in dressing like anyone else. And so I turned my attention to real-life Parisians, among whom one item seemed to proliferate: jeans.

No, this isn’t going to be a trend report on something as perennially popular as denim, but on a particular high-waisted, flared style that I spotted so frequently, I was forced to dredge up what little French remains from my GCSEs to ask a woman where hers were from as I caught her climbing onto a Lime bike outside Le Saint-Gervais bar. “Excuse-moi, madame, votre pantalons… le brand?” She paused for a moment, swung her leg over the saddle, and unleashed a torrent of French from which I managed to decipher just two words: “Anna” and “Gérard Darel”, the latter needing no explanation.

Founded in Saint-Germain-des-Prés in the 1970s, the brand has long been a shorthand for what the rest of the world considers the tenets of French-girl style: discreet, easy-to-wear classics with a cultivated air. (So cultivated, in fact, that the brand acquired the original handwritten Proust Questionnaire in 2003, and recently collaborated with the philosopher Alain de Botton on a card-game version.) Which is all very Left Bank, of course, but perhaps the clearest evidence of its credentials is just how commonplace Gérard Darel is in everyday Parisian life. You can scarcely move for its iconic 24H bag—a soft, logo-free shoulder bag that Vogue once named among the bags of the century, alongside the Hermès Birkin – during the school rush on the Métro, where it is generally to be found stuffed with binders and tangled wired headphones.

But back to the jeans–an American invention, admittedly, but then again, this is the land of French fries. What made my startled Parisienne’s look so good? Much of it comes down to the cut–something Kate Moss, a woman who found fame in nothing more than a pair of jeans, understands, having been photographed in the brand’s Anna jeans as early as 2019. Designed by former creative director Valérie Gerbi and named after her daughter Anna – granddaughter of the brand’s founders, Danièle and Gérard Darel–the design braces at just the right point on the hips, fits snugly through the thighs and flares outwards just below the knee, skimming the top of a pair of shoes to create the illusion of longer legs. The double belt loops, meanwhile, criss-cross along the waistband to give the impression of a cinched waist, while the back pockets perform a similarly flattering service for the bum.

And yet the technicalities of a good fit can only explain so much. Perhaps the true appeal was in the way she wore them–with white ballet flats that I’m convinced were from Repetto’s men’s section (the Luciens) and a navy three-quarter-zip jumper with the sleeves pushed up–or the ease with which disappeared into the Marais, hair whipping in the wind.

Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.

Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.

I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.

That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.

Allen was put on life support and had to be intubated for five weeks after getting sick with flu.

Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."

Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.

The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

After getting out of hospital, it took years for Allen to recover, eventually having part of her lung removed that had been badly damaged by the virus.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.

With thanks to Families Fighting Flu, a non-profit organization that promotes flu vaccination and raises awareness of the severity of the infectious disease through families that have been affected.

#6583. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.
