#6548. Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie

The one thing that can make classic apple pie better? Caramel! That it’s laced with a generous dose of bourbon vaults it straight into hall-of-fame territory. Made using a double batch of our never-fail Perfect Pie Crust, this pretty lattice-topped pie is a crowd-pleaser, familiar enough to appeal to the traditionalists with just enough of a surprise from the booze and the smoky burnt sugar to make the thrill-seekers come back for more. Like all good things, apple pie can’t be rushed. It needs time to chill, bake, and rest—so plan ahead, especially if it’s for Thanksgiving.

Welcome to Bon Appétit Bake Club, a community of curious bakers. Each month senior Test Kitchen editors Jesse Szewczyk and Shilpa Uskokovic share a must-make recipe and dive deep on why it works. Come bake and learn with us—ask questions, share pics, listen to our podcast, and lots more here. And don't forget to join the Bake Club Group chat over on Substack.

2 hours 15 minutes (plus 7 hours for chilling and cooling)

Whisk 3⅓ cups (417 g) all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. baking powder in a large bowl to combine. Add 4 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces; rub into dry ingredients with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 1¼ cups (2½ sticks) chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash with your fingers into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea-size).

Make a well in the center of mixture and pour in ½ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute, then knead in bowl a couple of times to bring dough together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn out dough onto a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour; dust top of dough with flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold dough in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Divide dough in half and pat each piece into a ½"-thick disk. Wrap each disk tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap each disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

Place 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar and ½ cup water in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot and cover. Bring to a boil over medium heat (no need to stir); cook until sugar is dissolved, 4–7 minutes total. Uncover and continue to cook, stirring or swirling pot occasionally, until caramel turns a deep golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Add zest of 1 lemon, 3 lb. Honeycrisp apples (about 6 large), peeled, cored, quartered, thinly sliced crosswise, ½ cup bourbon, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. ground cinnamon to caramel (it may become stiff). Cover and cook, stirring occasionally, until caramel dissolves and apples have released a generous amount of liquid and are tender but still retain their shape (they should look mostly translucent), 15–18 minutes.

Stir ⅓ cup heavy cream, 3 Tbsp. cornstarch, and 2 Tbsp. cool water in a small bowl until cornstarch is dissolved. Pour into apple mixture and cook (it should be bubbling), stirring often, until mixture is thick, about 5 minutes. Transfer filling to a large bowl; let cool. Cover and chill until cold, at least 45 minutes.

Meanwhile, let dough sit at room temperature 5 minutes. Unwrap 1 disk and roll out on a surface lightly dusted with rice flour or all-purpose flour to a 12" round, about ¼" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and wrap around rolling pin. Transfer to a 9"-diameter pie pan (such as East Fork Spun Iron Pie Dish). Unfurl into pan, then lift edges and allow dough to slump down into pan. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Chill 15 minutes.

Unwrap remaining disk; roll out on surface lightly dusted with more rice flour to a 18x12" rectangle, about ⅛" thick. Brush excess flour from dough and transfer to a large parchment-lined baking sheet. Brush dough with a thin film of cold water; sprinkle remaining ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar over and press gently with your hands to cover dough completely in an even layer (coating dough before cutting into strips will give you the most even coverage). Chill 15 minutes.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Spoon chilled filling into pie pan and smooth surface to level. Using a ruler, cut dough rectangle into 1"-wide strips. Lay 5–8 strips over filling, spacing evenly across surface to cover. Weave another 5–8 strips over, then under, alternating to create a lattice crust (you may not use all of the strips). Trim overhang to match bottom crust. Press edges of top and bottom crusts firmly together to seal, then trim again, leaving about ¼" overhang. Fold overhang up and over lattice so crust is flush with edges of pan and crimp as desired with lightly floured fingers.

Place pan on a rimmed baking sheet (to catch drips) and bake pie until crust is set and golden, 45–50 minutes. Reduce oven temperature to 350°; continue to bake until crust is deep golden brown and filling is bubbling up through lattice, 40–50 minutes more. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let pie cool in pan at least 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 2 days ahead; keep chilled. Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6546. This Three-Day Wedding Brought Persian Traditions, Dramatic Design, and an Ibiza-Style Rave to Oaxaca

Brian Downs and Sarvenaz Shahbazi had a classic college library meet-cute. One day, while they were both at Columbia Business School, Brian was tutoring their mutual friend—and future wedding officiant—Alex in a study room. Sarvenaz, who goes by Sarvi, walked by and jumped right in, taking the lead in guiding everyone through accounting problems. “I remember immediately thinking how pretty she was, but also how smart and confident she was,” says Brian. The two became friends, and by the time they were back from winter break, Brian asked Sarvi out for drinks at The Commerce Inn on January 7, 2022. Says Sarvi, “I had mentioned to him in passing that I had been wanting to go a month or two earlier since it had just opened, so I was very impressed with his thoughtfulness and planning!” The two were inseparable from that point on.

The couple got engaged two-and-a-half years later, over July 4th weekend on a trip to Puglia. Sarvi’s parents had planned a week-long vacation in the region, and Sarvi and her brother decided to join last minute with their partners. Brian, who was already on an engagement ring search, expedited the process to have it ready for the trip. “At the time, I genuinely did not think an engagement was on the table for at least a few more months,” says Sarvi. “We had only recently started talking about it, and Brian had very strategically staged our first-ever ring shopping trip the week before we left, which I then learned was just a decoy.”

Sarvi’s family, who were in on the plan, told everyone to meet for sunset drinks at the beach club of the masseria where they were staying. When the couple arrived, one of Sarvi’s favorite songs was playing, and a single table was set with flowers and Champagne with views of the water. “I looked at the setup and immediately said to Brian, ‘Oh my God, I think someone is going to get engaged here. We’re going to see it,’” Sarvi says. When they walked towards the deck, Brian pulled out the ring and got down on one knee. “She was in utter shock,” recalls Brian. “I had thought a lot about what I was going to say, but the only thing I actually remember saying is ‘eshgham,’ which means ‘my love’ in Farsi.”

When choosing a destination to tie the knot, Brian and Sarvi found themselves constantly drifting back to Mexico, ultimately deciding to exchange vows in Oaxaca City on November 15, 2025. The couple went on their first trip together to the country and had each visited countless times before and after they started dating.

The bride took charge to bring their dream wedding to life. “I work in hospitality as the director of strategy and development at Catch Hospitality Group, so what I truly find most fulfilling in life is creating experiences for others centered around exceptional food and drink and a carefully curated ambiance,” she says. Alongside planners Gutierrez F Studio, Sarvi helped orchestrate three days of events that blended this ethos with traditions from her Persian culture. The weekend would kick off with a rehearsal dinner full of delicious food and speeches at Criollo, followed by a Persian wedding ceremony and party at the historic Proyecto Murguía, and finally, the big day at Loma Noble. “We had so much fun creating a completely different world, each with a distinct personality, for every part of the wedding day—leading our guests on a journey from a ceremony in a bucolic agave field, to an energetic and dramatic dinnerscape, all the way to an after-party rave in a cactus garden,” says the bride.

While Sarvi had clear ideas of how to bring together all the events, it took some work to come up with her wedding wardrobe. “I wasn’t a bride with a pre-constructed Pinterest board, so when I first started thinking about what I would wear, I was completely overwhelmed by the sheer number of options,” she says. “I never wanted to wear anything that felt stiff, stuffy, or overly traditional.” This drive to find something unique led her to a pale butter-yellow dress with a sheer cape from Harithand for her rehearsal dinner, which she paired with diamond and ruby flower earrings from her aunt. “I felt immediately comfortable in it—it was soft, ethereal and subtly sexy—and felt perfect for our dinner under the stars at Criollo,” she says.

Her ceremony dress search ultimately led her to two iconic bridal designers: Danielle Frankel and Vera Wang. When Sarvi first saw Wang’s Ariel dress, it reminded her of Van Gogh’s Starry Night. “It ultimately felt perfect for our Persian ceremony,” she says. “There is so much artistry, symbolism, and craftsmanship that goes into an ‘aghd’ and the ‘sofreh’—the traditional ceremonial table—with countless individual symbolic items and details coming together to create something incredibly beautiful. There was a similar sense of artistry and romance in the Vera Wang gown that felt especially fitting for that night.” She paired the look with pink sapphire and diamond flower drop earrings from her maternal grandmother, who recently passed.

For the western wedding day, Sarvi wore a strapless gown by Frankel. While she wasn’t planning to try it on before she entered the showroom, the style called to her. “I loved the contrasting shades of white, the different textures, and the subtle lace throughout the skirt, which gave the dress so much dimension and movement,” she says. Once again, the bride wore a jewelry piece from her grandmother: a pearl choker with a gold flower and a tiny ruby. “They were playful, distinctive, and deeply personal, with those unexpected touches of color that I always love,” she says.

After dinner, the bride changed into a custom look she made with Brooklyn-based designer Delfina Balda. The two-piece look featured a mix of textures and fabrics with varying degrees of sheerness. “It felt like the perfect party look—artful and completely unique, but something I could actually dance in,” she says. For the after-party, which was modeled after DC10 in Ibiza with a completely red lighting scheme, Sarvi decided to change out of bridal white and donned a red dress by The Attico. “It has this intricate soutache detailing and a fringe skirt that gives the dress incredible texture and movement, especially on the dance floor,” she says.

The groom wore a mix of vintage and bespoke looks throughout the wedding weekend. For Friday night, Brian donned a relaxed suit found at Ebreo Vintage in Williamsburg that fit him perfectly. “Even the owner basically said, ‘Honestly, you should just buy that.’ I got pretty lucky,” he says. His next two looks were made alongside Tyler Sequeira at P. Johnson. The groom wanted to wear a double-breasted chocolate brown suit for the Persian ceremony to complement the natural tones throughout the celebration. “On my second visit, when I was picking fabrics and locking everything in, Sarvi’s uncle Mohammad, or Momo, insisted on joining me,” says Brian. “It’s a tradition in their family to buy a new suit for the groom joining the family, so he ended up helping me design the suit for the aghd. I loved that the suit became something more meaningful than just something I had picked out for myself.” For the black-tie wedding day, Brian wore a bespoke tuxedo made in midnight blue.

The wedding weekend began at Criollo, for an open-air dinner filled with mezcalitas, tacos, and chickens roaming freely through the space. “It immediately gave everyone a sense of the place we had fallen in love with,” says Sarvi. The night full of speeches ended with a night of dancing at a local vinyl bar. “It was one of the first moments where I looked around and really processed that all of these people we loved had traveled to Oaxaca to be there for us,” says Brian.

On the Persian wedding day, the couple paraded with their guests through the streets to their venue, where the space was filled with florals, Persian food, music, and a sofreh table ready for the ceremony. The bride’s uncle officiated the aghd and her mother and other family members participated throughout. “By the time the ceremony ended, the night very quickly became a full-on Persian dance party,” says Sarvi. “We had hoped Friday would have just as much energy and dancing as Saturday, but even we underestimated it.” Adds Brian, “Seeing my parents and friends dancing to Persian music alongside Sarvi’s family is one of the funniest and most joyous memories I’ll have from the weekend.”

The ceremony the next day was held at sunset among the agave fields of Loma Noble, an agronomic project outside the city of Oaxaca. “We wanted the ceremony to feel as though it belonged within the landscape rather than creating something that completely competed with it,” says the bride. Sarvi walked down the aisle to a string rendition of “Creep” by Radiohead. “Certainly not the most traditional wedding choice, but one of my favorite songs of all time and, to me, one of the most beautiful songs ever written,” she says. The couple’s business school friend Alex officiated, weaving in sentimental passages from Brian’s late grandfather Jack, and the groom’s mother shared a reading. The couple wrote their own vows, including an entire section Brian prepared in Farsi. “I learned afterward that my younger cousin had secretly been tutoring him so he could learn and practice that portion,” says Sarvi. “It was one of the most deeply sentimental gestures I could have imagined.”

The couple share they were both emotional, yet calm and present for the ceremony. The two recessed to “California Dreamin’,” which they sang with joy down the aisle. “It was this perfect release of all the emotion we had been feeling, and immediately shifted the energy from the ceremony into pure excitement for the night ahead,” says the bride. The two spent a moment alone together in the bridal suite before joining guests at cocktail hour along a tree-lined pathway.

When guests moved into the reception tent, they found the space decorated with a nod to an eclipse, complete with a glowing orb above a circular central stage and serpentine tables along the room. Dinner was punctuated with speeches, assigned “table captains” to keep the energy alive, and dances with their parents. The newlyweds shared their own first dance at the end of dinner to “Sunny” by Bobby Hebb. “As soon as it ended, Brian and I grabbed the microphones and essentially announced, ‘Now, it’s time to party.’ At that exact moment, trays of carajillos came out for everyone, giving the room one more jolt of energy before the curtains separating the dinner space from the dance floor opened,” says the bride. Their 300 guests moved to the disco-ball-filled space complete with a martini bar and music by DJ César.

“At one point, Brian and I ended up dancing on top of the bar and apparently were dancing hard enough that the staff became concerned it might come crashing down—so the bartenders were literally holding it up beneath us while we were dancing,” says Sarvi. “That probably sums up the energy of the night better than anything else.” The party didn’t stop as guests next moved through a glowing red tunnel. “Once you emerged into the cactus garden, everything was washed in red light, with an enormous triangular LED structure framing the dance floor,” says the bride. “It felt almost otherworldly and created exactly the kind of late-night atmosphere we wanted.” The couple danced until 6 a.m.

Looking back, the couple describe it as the most magical weekend of their lives. “I constantly find myself wondering what I did to end up married to someone so cool and so loved by her friends and family,” says Brian. “She draws people into her orbit, and getting to stand next to her while all of those people showed up to celebrate us is something I’ll never forget.”

#6545. A Beautiful Cabbage Galette

Cut this festive galette into little squares for a hearty appetizer, or serve sizeable wedges as a vegetarian main or standout side. It’s worth seeking out savoy cabbage, the ruffly sort that looks like lace. Ordinary green cabbage, which has a higher moisture content and flatter texture, doesn’t work here (we tried).

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Whisk 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, ¼ tsp. baking powder, and 1⅔ cups (208 g) all-purpose flour in a large bowl. Add 2 oz. chilled cream cheese, cut into 1" pieces, and rub in with your fingers until incorporated (mixture will look very shaggy). Add 10 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, sliced ½" thick, and toss to coat in flour, then smash into smaller, flatter pieces (about chickpea size). Make a well in the center and pour in ¼ cup ice water. Toss with a fork or your hands to distribute. Knead dough in bowl just to bring together (some dry bits may remain).

Turn dough out onto a lightly dusted surface and sprinkle with all-purpose flour. Roll out to a ½"-thick rectangle. Fold in half, rotate 90°, and fold in half again. Roll out again to a ½"-thick rectangle and repeat folding process, dusting dough with more flour as needed to prevent sticking. Pat into a ½"-thick disk and wrap tightly in plastic. Chill at least 2 hours and, preferably, up to 12 hours.

Do Ahead: Dough can be made 1 month ahead. Wrap disk in 2 layers of plastic and freeze instead of chilling. Thaw in refrigerator 12 hours before using.

When dough is almost done chilling, cut 1 medium head of savoy cabbage (1¾–2¼ lb.) in half and cut out triangular core at bottom; discard. Separate leaves and tear into pieces about the size of your palm. Transfer about half to a large bowl and set aside.

Melt 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium heat. Add 1 medium white or yellow onion, thinly sliced, and season generously with kosher salt. Cook, stirring occasionally, until softened and starting to turn translucent, about 5 minutes. Add remaining 1 Tbsp. unsalted butter and ¾ tsp. cumin seeds (if using) and cook until butter is melted. Add remaining cabbage leaves and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is translucent and lightly browned and cabbage is wilted, 18–22 minutes. Transfer to a large plate or a small baking sheet; chill in fridge or freezer until cool.

Place a rack in bottom third of oven; preheat to 400°. Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ⅓ cup heavy cream, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a measuring glass to combine. Pour cream mixture over reserved raw cabbage leaves and toss with your hands to coat. Add 5 oz. Gruyère or sharp cheddar, coarsely grated, and toss again to combine.

Unwrap dough and roll out on a lightly floured sheet of parchment paper to a 13–14" round (some dough will extend beyond the parchment). Transfer on parchment paper to a baking sheet.

Spread cooked cabbage mixture over dough, leaving about a 1½" border around edges. Fold dough up and over filling, folding and tucking as needed to make a rustic border. Pile raw cabbage mixture on top of cooked cabbage mixture to make a dramatic heap. (It will look ridiculously high at first but will cook down when it bakes.)

Bake galette 25 minutes. Rotate baking sheet front to back, reduce heat to 375°, and bake until cabbage and crust are deep golden brown, 25–35 minutes. (If cabbage seems to be browning too much, reduce heat to 350° toward the end.) Let galette cool on baking sheet at least 1 hour and up to 4 hours before serving.

Do Ahead: Sautéed cabbage can be made 1 day ahead. Transfer to an airtight container and chill. Tightly wrap undressed raw cabbage in plastic and chill.

#6544. Stanley Tucci’s Airplane Snack Is the Messiest Meal Ever

Stanley Tucci isn't settling for pretzels and peanuts on his next flight!

Between busy airport security lines and delays, eating while traveling can be unpredictable. And sure, maybe you ate breakfast before leaving the house. But then suddenly it’s six hours later and you’re struggling to navigate your way to baggage claim with a headache and a growling stomach. Trust me, I’ve been there too many times!

Which is why I have one simple rule when traveling: Eat when you can. Packing plenty of plane snacks is important, but getting a full meal is really ideal. So when I saw the kind of food that Stanley Tucci brings on flights, I felt incredibly validated. However, I don’t know if I could manage something quite this messy in the air.

In a very charming TikTok video, Stanley Tucci’s wife Felicity Blunt records him as he unwraps his plane snack. I watched in shock and awe as he unwrapped aluminum foil to reveal a sandwich. But not just any sandwich—I mean, this is Stanley Tucci we’re talking about. He’s known for whipping up Italian meals for pop stars and cooking cozy comfort meals on a whim. It’s no real surprise then that he brought eggplant Parmesan on a plane!

His wife joked that they should “film a before and after” of his shirt. I mean, this sandwich looks incredible. It’s got tons of creamy marinara sauce and is piled high with thinly sliced eggplant and cheese. The bread is toasted and really looks like it’s doing the best job it can at containing the feast within.

Would I have the confidence to eat an eggplant Parmesan sandwich on a plane? Probably not. I am a notoriously messy eater to begin with, and if bibs were more socially acceptable for adults, I would wear one with every meal. So I can’t imagine diving into this on a plane!

But Stanley loves it. In fact, he’s the one who made the sandwich, or “Stan-wich” as Felicity calls them, for the plane ride. So maybe I need to amend my earlier assertion: I would eat eggplant Parmesan on a plane if Stanley Tucci made it for me.

What’s your go-to airplane snack? Is it as messy as this one? Sound off in the comments below!

During dreams, bizarre scenes you encounter can seem as tangible as reality; you feel as though you're really flying through the sky or being chased through a jungle of bright-purple trees. But in special cases, people realize they're in the midst of a dream as it's unfolding.

Called lucid dreaming, this phenomenon occurs when we suddenly regain our capacity for metacognition, or thinking about our own thoughts, in the middle of a dream. Lucid dreamers can sometimes even control the content or trajectory of their dreams. Now, researchers claim that they've found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they're awake.

In a study involving a few dozen participants, the scientists found that repeating this training twice a week for a month significantly increased how often participants experienced lucid dreaming. They say the approach could have practical applications as an intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder — but those applications are theoretical, for now.

If you could learn how to lucid dream, would you? Let us know in the poll below, and add your thoughts in the comments.

Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

#6542. The National Black Theatre Raised a Glass—and $1 Million—at Its Inaugural Fall Fête

“Ordinary People” might be the title of a Grammy-winning song by John Legend. Yet Legend’s persona and career trajectory have proven to be anything but ordinary—as exemplified by his attendance and performance at The National Black Theatre’s inaugural Fall Fête.

The benefit gala recently welcomed Legend alongside Mickalene Thomas, Lena Waithe, Mike Jackson, Cyndi Lauper, and Donna Murphy to Current—a private event space within Pier 59 at Chelsea Piers. Inside the venue, a crowd gathered for a cocktail reception as the Kotchegna Dance Company helped kick off the evening with their powerful rhythmic processional while Reverend Rhonda Akanaké McLean-Nur poured libations to set the tone.

Television personality Bevy Smith, who was on hosting duty for the evening, fielded well wishes from the crowd, having just celebrated her 60th birthday. “The room is so full—full of hope, love, laughter, and impact. And tonight is a firm reminder that Black enterprise and artistry stem from community,” celebrity hairstylist Vernon Francois told Vogue as they took their seat. Sharing a similar sentiment was Pose star and NBT alum, Ryan Jamal Swain: “Honestly, this is a full-circle moment for me. Walking through the door tonight and seeing a large photo of myself on the wall takes me back to the beginning of my career—I’d just graduated from Howard and moved to New York, and Sade [Lythcott] welcomed me with open arms.”

In the dining room, linen-draped banquet tables topped with roses, mini orchids, and calla lily arrangements provided a colorful setting for warm plates of grilled artichoke, artisan steakhouse beef, steamed halibut, and Caesar salad. “Tonight is a call to action,” Smith said as she headed toward the podium. “This gala is further proof that Black people must continue to show up and show out. At the election booths, at special events, and all across the globe, because the world needs your talent and your energy.”

As the night progressed, event co-chairs Andi Bernstein and Sonja Warfield joined Smith onstage and spoke of the importance of NBT’s legacy. Esteemed industry creatives including Michael F. Lythcott (NBT board chair), Thelma Golden, Charles Randolph Wright, Debra Martin Chase, and Nina Shaw presented special awards to gala honorees Margaret Anadu, Sanford Biggers, Nona Hendryx, and Get Lifted Film Co.’s Mike Jackson, as well as Legend.

Accepting the Excellence in Creative Producing Award with his business partner Jackson, Legend stated: “It’s a blessing to be a Black storyteller, and I’m so grateful that the National Black Theater exists for times such as these.” Shortly after his acceptance speech, Legend serenaded the crowd with a medley of hits, including the soul-stirring “Ordinary People,” along with a new song from his upcoming NBT-backed musical Imitation of Life—a reimagining of the 1959 film.

Additional stage presentations saw Liza Jessie Peterson perform a spoken word poem, while jazz singer Somi Kakoma provided a moving vocal selection. Describing the program, actress Murphy said it was “an honor to witness and experience, because the arts can transform every single human being, and NBT does it so well.”

The fundraising total of almost $1 million was powered by Subyn Novelle’s boisterous paddle-raising expertise. Afterwards, a disco-fueled dessert reception closed out the evening with porcelain trays of raspberry macarons, brownies, and coconut cream bites doing the rounds. DJ Stormin’ Norman spun upbeat R&B tunes from Stevie Wonder and Chaka Khan to Earth, Wind & Fire as guests flooded the dance floor to celebrate.

Holding court next to the espresso café station was NBT’s chief executive officer Sade Lythcott, who reflected on the night’s success: “When Black culture takes center stage, it’s a reminder that anything is possible for all people. And tonight’s fundraising—which partly benefits The Theatre of the Future—is a long-awaited dedication to the extraordinary vision and original building plans of my mother,” she told Vogue.

NBT’s executive artistic director Jonathan McCrory echoed the sentiment. “Tonight, we celebrate 58 years of Black artistic excellence and deep-rooted Harlem legacy founded by Dr. Barbara Ann Teer in 1968. And as we near completion of our new world-class cultural arts complex, we’re reminded of how far we’ve come—but we’re also inspired by how much further we can abundantly support our community.”

#6541. This Simple Storage Trick Can Keep Lettuce Fresh for a Month

The trick to keeping lettuce fresh for a month is already in your kitchen.

There are few things more irritating than throwing away food you had every intention of eating. Fresh produce is especially frustrating because it seems to operate on its own schedule. You buy a beautiful head of lettuce, imagining all the fresh salads and sandwiches you’ll make that week, only to find a head of wilted leaves waiting for you when you finally get around to it.

Enter Chef Charles Kim, better known as Chef Fatty on social media. He has an impressive knack for making me rethink my cooking. He’s already changed how I caramelize onions and make the juiciest chicken breasts, and now he’s apparently coming for my crisper drawer. His trick promises to keep lettuce fresh for an entire month using nothing more than aluminum foil—a claim I couldn’t resist investigating.

The idea is simple: Instead of leaving your head of lettuce in the plastic produce bag, loosely wrap it in aluminum foil before putting it in the refrigerator. That’s it. No special containers, paper towels or elaborate produce-preserving rituals required.

Chef Fatty recommends removing any yellowing or deteriorating leaves before wrapping the lettuce. If it’s dirty, you can wash it first, but make sure it’s completely dry. Then loosely fold the foil around the head and place it in the refrigerator’s crisper drawer.

The reasoning has to do with moisture and airflow. Lettuce loses its crispness as water escapes from its leaves, but trapping too much moisture can also encourage decay. A loose foil wrapping strikes just the right balance, protecting the leaves from drying out without sealing them inside an airtight container.

I wanted to see the difference for myself, so I bought two heads of romaine lettuce at the same time. I left one in the plastic produce bag from the grocery store and loosely wrapped the other in aluminum foil. Both went into the same crisper drawer in my refrigerator, where I left them undisturbed for a month. When I finally pulled them out, the difference was unmistakable.

After 30 days in the refrigerator, the foil-wrapped romaine was in dramatically better shape than its plastic-bag counterpart. The lettuce stored in its original bag had deteriorated considerably, while the foil-wrapped head had retained much more of its original appearance and crispness.

I had to peel away several of the outer leaves of the plastic-bag lettuce before I found anything resembling a crisp texture. The foil-wrapped head wasn’t perfect, but it was still pretty crisp, with leaves so fresh that I happily turned them into a Caesar salad for lunch. This was an entire month after I’d bought it. I’d call that a successful experiment.

While I tested the method with romaine, it’s also worth trying on other lettuce varieties. How long each stays fresh will depend on its condition when purchased, the refrigerator it’s stored in, and the variety itself. And lettuce isn’t the only vegetable that might benefit. Taste of Home senior editor Lindsay Mattison told me she uses the same aluminum foil trick to store celery, which makes sense given its tendency to lose moisture and go limp in the refrigerator.

I wouldn’t necessarily recommend buying lettuce with the intention of ignoring it for a month, and it’s still important to check for slime, mold or other signs of spoilage before eating it. But knowing I can give my produce a much longer window before it ends up in the compost is reason enough to keep an extra roll of foil handy.

#6540. Collard Greens Vinaigrette

For those who might shudder at the thought of eating raw hardy greens like collards or kale, this vibrant side inspired by the French bistro classic leeks vinaigrette is the answer. Simmered past squeaky-raw yet well short of meltingly braised, they offer substantial bite, like al dente pasta. The mustard dressing couldn’t be simpler to make—use it as a base for any salad you might serve this season. It’s punchy enough to stand up to winter vegetables or any sturdy bitter green.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Toast ½ cup raw walnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown, 10–12 minutes.

Meanwhile, cook 2 bunches collard greens, ribs and stems removed, leaves cut into 2" pieces, in a large pot of generously salted boiling water until just tender, 9–11 minutes. Using tongs, immediately transfer to a large bowl of ice water and let cool.

Whisk 2 garlic cloves, finely grated, ¼ cup white wine vinegar, 2 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, preferably country-style, ⅓ cup extra-virgin olive oil, ¼ cup (packed) coarsely chopped tarragon, 2 tsp. sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl to combine. Set dressing aside.

Transfer toasted walnuts to a small bowl and drizzle with remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Sprinkle with a generous pinch each of sugar and salt and toss to coat. Taste and add more sugar if needed (nuts should be more sweet than salty). Set seasoned walnuts aside.

Drain collard greens and squeeze gently to remove excess water. Transfer to bowl with reserved dressing and toss to coat evenly. Cover and chill at least 15 minutes and up to 2 hours.

Arrange greens in a shallow bowl or on a platter and spoon any dressing remaining in bowl over. Top with seasoned walnuts and tarragon leaves.

Do Ahead: Walnuts can be toasted and dressing can be made 1 day ahead. Store walnuts airtight at room temperature. Cover dressing and chill.

#6539. Best Kitchen Scales, Tested Over a Decade of Baking (2026)

I’ve been an avid home baker for well over a decade (my first stint in “food media” was a baking blog I started in middle school!), and I can confirm that there is no single tool quite as important to the outcome of your baked goods as a simple kitchen scale. Bon Appétit’s Test Kitchen team agrees, which is why you’ll see gram measurements in the baking recipes on our site.

Another bonus of a kitchen scale? In most cases, you can kiss measuring cups and spoons goodbye, which means far fewer utensils to clean once your bakes are in the oven.

Scales aren’t just for bakers, either. They make portioning burger patties and meatballs easier, streamline meal prep, and keep your Sunday morning pancake routine cleaner.

I’ve tested 16 models over several years and consulted Shilpa Uskokovic, former BA senior Test Kitchen editor and co-owner of Hani’s Bakery, to find the best kitchen scale for home cooks. The winner is just $27.

New in this update: I tested the new version of the Oxo Good Grips 11-Pound Digital Kitchen Food Scale. While it was easy to use and I appreciated the pull-out display, it was less accurate than the Escali—and over double the price. You can read my full review below.

Size: 8.5 x 6 x 1.5"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: 4 minutes 30 secondsPower: AA batteries (included)

This Escali Primo has held the top spot in our testing for over six years and has been a favorite in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen for far longer than that. “This scale has been with me for more than a decade of my career, staying faithfully by my side through 12-hour shifts in pastry kitchens, bouts of religious recipe testing, and weekly sessions of casual baking,” says senior Test Kitchen editor and resident baking whiz Shilpa Uskokovic.

It’s durable, accurate, intuitive to use, and affordable—pretty much everything we could ask of a kitchen scale.

What we love: The Escali Primo is lightweight, comes in a variety of fun colors, and has a simple two-button interface to turn it on, tare it, and toggle between ounces, pounds, and grams. In testing, it was responsive and precise, quick to tare, and delivered accurate readings every time. Its 4.5-minute auto shut-off is among the longest of any model we tested, so you won’t lose your measurements mid-bake. Plus, its 11-pound capacity is large enough to accommodate any task a home cook might ask of it.

Performance aside, the Escali Primo has several design features that helped it stand out. For one, the fact that the weighing platform is elevated and offset from the base means you can easily read the display or use the buttons even when measuring into a large, wide mixing bowl. The plastic body and sealed control panel make it a breeze to wipe down after a floury baking session and also keep stray crumbs from getting stuck in any crevices. Another detail we like? The four rubberized feet keep it stable on your kitchen counter.

The Escali Primo has proven quite durable as we’ve continued to test it long-term, another reason why it’s a perennial favorite among our Test Kitchen editors. Shilpa again: “It’s compact and easy to store, it’s easy to wipe clean, it toggles between grams and ounces seamlessly, and it’s reliably accurate."

What we’d leave: The Escali can only measure in 1-gram increments. While this was typical of most scales we tested, those looking to use their kitchen scale for dialing in their coffee routine will want something more precise (though coffee scales are kind of their own thing). Unlike some pricier models, the Escali’s display is not backlit, but we didn’t find this to be an issue. It’s also worth noting that the Escali is not a touchscreen device, so you’ll need to use a bit of pressure on the buttons.

Size: 8.3 x 7 x 1.3"Capacity: 11 lb.Gradation: 1 gAuto shut-off: NAPower: AAA batteries (included)

Amazon Basics products are not consistent across the board, but this scale is a certifiable hit. At about half the price of the Escali, it’s a good option if you’re not positive about this scale thing and want to spend as little as humanly possible to do so.

What we love: There are a lot of similarities between the Amazon Basics scale and the overall winner. The Amazon Basics scale has the same two-button setup, a similar elevated weighing platform that makes it easy to see the display, and the same 11-pound maximum capacity. It’s made of plastic with a stainless-steel platform that’s easy to wipe down and is just a touch larger than the Escali at 7 inches across.

In testing, I was impressed by the Amazon scale’s accuracy, considering its price point. It responded to weight addition or removal almost as quickly as the Escali and provided an accurate readout about 99% of the time. That 1% weight change inaccuracy happened when someone repeatedly added weight or switched back and forth between units of measurement, and when it did happen, the reading was off by a minor amount. The problem could be fixed by removing what was on the scale, taring it, and starting over. For $10 (at the time of writing), you’d be hard-pressed to find a better model.

What we’d leave: Unlike the Escali, the Amazon scale’s buttons lack any kind of laminated sealing to prevent crumbs or liquid from entering the crevices around them. As mentioned, this scale isn’t quite as accurate as the winner and it tended to overshoot an item’s actual weight at first (before correcting itself relatively quickly). And last, the stainless-steel platform is more prone to scratching or smudging than Escali’s plastic one.

You’ll notice there aren’t any other scales marketed as coffee scales on this list, and that’s because the Fellow Tally was the only coffee scale we thought could plausibly work as an all-purpose model too.

What we love: The Fellow Tally is one of our favorite coffee scales (especially for pour-over) thanks to features like a built-in timer and a “brew assist” that directs you on the proper ratio of coffee to water—but its 5.5-pound maximum capacity means it works for most home baking projects too. If you’re the kind of person who likes to nerd out over your brewing and baking techniques, this is your best bet unless you want to invest in two separate scales.

In testing, we quite liked the Tally’s design for its tactile controls and easy-to-read OLED display, and appreciated its ability to measure grams, ounces, pounds, and milliliters (that milliliter measurement is calibrated for water, so one milliliter equals one gram; if you're measuring a heavier liquid like milk it will be slightly off). The elevated 6-inch platform is large enough to comfortably hold a mixing bowl while allowing easy visibility of the display.

To find out how accurate each scale was, I used a set of calibration weights. I tested each scale’s ability to give an accurate reading for the minimum amount of weight it claimed to be able to accommodate (usually 1 or 2 grams), and its ability to detect small changes when there was already weight on the platform. I also placed weights in various places on each scale’s platform to determine whether they could give an accurate reading regardless of whether the weight was in the center or at the edge.

I coated each scale in a mixture of flour, water, and oil and let them sit overnight. I cleaned the residue off and noted which scales were easy to clean and resistant to any scratching or staining.

I distributed winning scales to staffers to see how they fared after long-term use in our homes and in the Test Kitchen and added any long-term testing notes to reviews as they came in.

I looked for consistently accurate measurements and a short response time when adding and removing items of varying sizes and materials from each scale. I took into account how weight distribution affected the readings, looking for scales that delivered spot-on results regardless of where on the platform we placed the weights. I also took note of how precise each scale could be in its measurements, but found our favorite all-around options tended to measure in 1-gram increments.

I looked for scales that were intuitive to use without picking up a manual.

I tested scales with weight capacities ranging from 1.65 to 16 pounds, but found that a maximum capacity of 11 pounds was more than enough for the tasks one might try to accomplish in a home kitchen.

I wanted a scale that felt durable, well-made, and stable on the counter and was also designed to be easy to clean.

Unlike a stand mixer, a scale isn’t the kind of kitchen gadget most home cooks are looking to keep permanently on their counter. Lightweight, compact models that could be easily stashed in a cabinet were better.

I took into account the relative price of each scale. After years of testing, we’ve found that you really don’t need to spend much to get a high-quality, highly accurate kitchen scale, so any models that were pricey needed to wow us with their design or extra features.

These scales didn’t quite make our list of top picks, but they still impressed us in testing and might fit your needs depending on what you’re looking for.

This is another scale from the makers of our top overall pick. It’s sleeker and slightly more advanced, with a four-button control panel that includes the typical on-off, unit change, and tare functions, plus a “hold” feature that keeps your measurement on the screen rather than automatically shutting off after a given amount of time.

We ultimately didn’t think the added feature and upgraded design merited spending an extra $10, but this is undoubtedly a good scale (and the rainbow of colorways available makes it easy to find a match for your kitchen decor).

This Oxo scale is a favorite among professional chefs for its easy-to-clean stainless-steel weighing platform and handy pull-out display design (great for measuring into extra-large bowls). I liked it a lot, but found it was often off by 1 gram, especially when the weight was placed in one of the platform’s corners. I ultimately didn’t feel its performance merited its price tag, which is more than double that of the winning Escali at the time of writing.

True to its name, this precision scale from Etekcity provides measurements in 0.1-gram increments as well as the option to measure in milliliters and fluid ounces (along with the typical grams and pounds/ounces). That said, we didn’t love that the instructions recommended using this scale with only the included plastic bowl and found that the stainless steel weighing platform scratched easily.

This rechargeable digital kitchen scale seemed promising, with its 22-pound maximum weight, easy-to-clean weighing platform, Bluetooth-enabled app connectivity, customizable auto-off function, and host of premium features. However, it was one of the least accurate scales we tested: Our 5-gram nickel weighed in at a low of 2 grams and high of 6. For that reason, we don’t recommend it unless you’re buying a scale primarily for meal tracking reasons.

The Zwilling Enfinigy Digital Food Scale was another promising option. It’s rechargeable via USB cord and has a sleek, buttonless design and 22-pound capacity. However, it wasn’t as accurate as we’d have liked, and despite how cool it looks, the lack of buttons turned out to be frustrating. We also disliked how the tab that switches the units of measurement is located underneath the scale.

MyWeigh KD-8000 Bakers Math Kitchen Scale

This scale is heavy-duty. It’s got a 16-pound max capacity, it can be charged with a plug-in A/C adapter, and it’s the size of a small kitchen appliance. It works well (and even allows you to measure using baker’s percentages), but unless you’re in a professional bakery setting, it’s overkill.

At less than 3-by-3 inches, this scale is truly tiny. It’s an impressive little kitchen tool, able to provide measurements in 0.1 gram increments, but its maximum capacity of 1.65 pounds is just too small for most cooking or baking projects besides making coffee.

This scale from Cuisinart has a glass weighing platform and removable stainless-steel bowl, but we ultimately didn’t love the idea of the bowl adding yet another piece of clutter to our kitchens. Besides that, this scale was less accurate than our top picks, had a short, 1-minute auto-off time, and was nearly double the price of the winning Escali.

This scale lost for a couple reasons: It was less accurate than our winners and one of the most difficult scales to clean in our most recent round of testing. The display panel was prone to trapping crumbs and bits of flour, and the scale itself required intensive scrubbing to remove leftover residue.

Joseph Joseph TriScale Compact Folding Digital Kitchen Food Scale

Like many of Joseph Joseph’s products, this scale has an interesting design. It’s made up of three prongs that fold into a small rectangle, making it easy to stash away when not in use. That said, this scale struggled in testing; it couldn’t detect small amounts of weight and was prone to reading the weight of your finger when you tapped its buttons.

I had high hopes for this dual platform scale from the makers of some of our favorite pizza ovens. It’s got a sleek, low-profile design, wide capacity range (0.1–22 grams if you take into account both platforms), and handy light-up display. Unfortunately, we found both the small and big platforms inaccurate: The small platform struggled with picking up small changes and was often off by multiple tenths of a gram, and the big platform was inconsistent, often fluctuating between two readings or off by a couple grams.

KitchenAid Dual Platform Digital Kitchen Scale

We noticed inaccuracies and inconsistencies with both of the KitchenAid’s platforms. The small scale is meant to be precise down to the hundredth of a gram, but it struggled to detect our .02-gram calibration weight and fluctuated between .19 and .20 when we weighed a 0.2-gram weight. The big scale was decidedly more inaccurate, off by 3–4 grams when we tested it with a 100-gram weight.

Like all of Smeg’s products, the brand’s take on a kitchen scale is very cute. Unfortunately, while the design is aesthetically pleasing, it didn’t prove to be very functional. The scale is very bulky because of the built-in bowl, which can’t be removed from the base (though the stainless-steel bowl insert can be removed for cleaning). The scale’s base itself is sensitive to weight, which means pressing on the buttons with force can cause a temporary spike in the reading—and, more important, if you drop any ingredients on the base, the weight of said ingredient will be added to the total. We also found that this scale struggled to accurately report small (1- or 2-gram) changes in weight.

ThermoWorks Gravitas Precision Kitchen Scale

I was very excited to test this scale from the brand behind our favorite cooking thermometers, but unfortunately it failed to impress me enough to merit a recommendation. The scale boasts the capability to measure down to the tenth of a gram, but according to ThermoWorks' product description, it does so with ±0.7 g accuracy. In testing, I found this to be true—readings were rarely accurate to the exact tenth. After testing the scale in his home kitchen for several weeks, senior commerce editor Noah Kaufman also noted that readings came in on the slow side, which made measuring ingredients that pour out quickly (like flour or liquids) tricky. I did appreciate the detachable display (helpful when using a large, wide bowl that might otherwise obscure the screen), but it wasn’t enough to outweigh the negatives—and besides, I’m of the opinion that there’s no reason for the average home cook to pay $120 for a scale when a $25 one performs incredibly well.

We also tested the Ozeri Pronto, Etekcity Multifunction Food Kitchen Scale, and GDealer Tempered Glass Kitchen Scale, all of which have been discontinued.

To use a kitchen scale, you’ll have to familiarize yourself with the concept of “tare.” Taring a scale allows you to reset the weight back to zero when you already have something on the weighing platform. This is particularly useful if you want to measure ingredients into a bowl (just place the bowl on the platform, click the tare button, and go on adding your ingredients), or if you want to measure multiple ingredients into that bowl without needing to add or subtract the existing weight in your head.

Baking is the obvious answer here, but the use cases for kitchen scales go far beyond the world of flour and butter. Use a scale to perfectly portion out meat for meatballs or burgers, aid in your meal prep for the week, or for any recipe where precise quantities are of the utmost importance.

Alaina Chou: Alaina has been testing products at Bon Appétit for over three years, which means she’s used dozens of air fryers, toasters, rice cookers, and—you guessed it—kitchen scales. She’s an avid baker who’s been a proponent of measuring by weight for the better part of a decade.

The best part? Because they’re tiny, the coloring books are perfect for holiday travels. Just pick up a pack of markers or crayons and you have a cozy activity to tap into all season long!

This seasonally-appropriate Winter Sports Advent calendar from KiwiCo includes 12 DIY wooden craft ornament kits, offering a new activity every couple of days. Each one is a different Christmas character participating in a winter sport. Editor Mary Henn enjoyed putting together the ornaments with her daughter as a cute holiday bonding activity.

“Okay, this Advent calendar is such a unique and fun idea,” raves Mary. “My kiddo loved helping assemble a few of the ornaments during testing. Although the suggested age range is 5+ (likely due to the small parts), the instructions were simple to follow, and the assembly was easy enough for her to help with some of the projects!”

The bright, bold colors also make it fun and appealing for kids. Each kit is also individually wrapped, so there’s no loose pieces or missing materials. The packaging is thoughtfully designed with hidden doors, colorful pictures, and descriptions on the back. While it’s a little pricey at $50, the ornaments are well-made and should last for years.

“Each little wooden craft ornament is adorable,” raves Mary. “I especially love that some have movable parts, like spinning tops and sliding limbs, which make them even more fun and interactive.”

For folks who still appreciate the art of sending letters and documenting memos on paper, the Papier stationery Advent calendar is well worth the splurge. This luxury countdown is loaded with 24 desk delights that make crafting snail mail a dream. It truly checks all the boxes: luxurious, cohesive, joyful and, a personal favorite, practical.

“I loved last year’s letter-shaped calendar, but the design of the 2026 countdown is even better,” says Deputy Editor Katie Bandurski. “It’s a little more streamlined yet still oh-so impressive.”

When you lift the lid, you’re greeted with three drawers of perfectly packaged mini presents to open each day until Christmas. Each gift is exquisitely wrapped in thick paper in an array of cohesive yet distinct patterns.

“If you want an Advent calendar that feels like you’re truly opening a gift, rather than just pulling open a drawer, this is the best option I’ve seen in my years of testing,” says Katie.

This luxury calendar sells out almost every year, so we recommend ordering it as soon as you can. And if you miss out on the full-sized version (or want to spend a little less), Papier offers a 12-day version new for 2026!

LEGO Advent calendars are some of the best Advent calendars, hands down—and that’s not just my nostalgia talking. Unpacking this year’s LEGO City Advent calendar offered me the same magical experience I remember as a kid.

Behind each door is a variety of buildable toys, figures and accessories. Each and every day was fun to open, especially the days with builds inside them. The instructions are printed on the inside of the doors, so they’re rather simplistic. However, I found them overall thorough enough to figure things out.

Both my notoriously hard-to-please nephew and my millennial husband worked on the projects together. Their verdict? This was the best Advent calendar either had ever received! Believe me—there’s no better endorsement than that.

Here’s a gift for crafters, young and mature. This DIY ornament Advent calendar includes all the bells and whistles for designing their own felt Christmas tree ornaments. While it’s not set up like a traditional calendar—you won’t be opening any doors—the numbered craft kids prove to be exciting enough on their own.

Tester Katie Bandurski tried this Advent calendar and confirms that it’s fun for almost any age, but tots especially will benefit from the easy instructions. Plus—and this is a big one for parents—there’s no mess!

Kids craft 25 ornaments using felt and stickers—no sewing or glue required at all. And while each ornament has its own set of picture instructions, crafters can follow their heart and create something truly unique. The only thing to consider? They might need their own mini Christmas tree to show off their creations!

At Taste of Home, we’ve tried more than 100 calendars over the years, so we already have experience with many of the Advent calendars on the market. To find the best crafting Advent calendars, we drew from this existing pool of tested options. We then scoured the internet to see if there were any others worth ordering and testing.

From there, we did exactly what you’re supposed to do with Advent calendars—we opened them! After noting our unboxing experience, we took a closer look, examining technical details like shipping, packaging and value. We then assembled our crafts and noted any observations, including instruction clarity,

Craft Advent calendars are for everyone who enjoys making things. While some are geared towards kids or adults, many of the options we’ve tested work for almost everyone!

What’s inside a craft Advent calendar depends on the calendar you choose! There are tons of options available, from picks for painters to finds for fiber art fans. A crafting Advent calendar typically offers a new bite-sized craft or new crafting tool each day leading up to Christmas.

From foodie Advent calendars to Advent calendars for kids, we’ve tried over 100 of the most popular Christmas countdowns in the past three years. This tiny inkwell contains an alphabetic inscription in ancient Etruscan, a language that has never been fully decoded.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The chicken-shaped, black-glazed vase has an abecedarium ‪—‬ an inscription with the 26 letters of the Etruscan alphabet in order.

What it is: A bird-shaped ceramic inkwell

This small terra-cotta vase, which is shaped like a cockerel or young male chicken with human feet, was discovered in central Italy and was made by the ancient Etruscans. The potter inscribed the Etruscan alphabet on the body of the chicken, giving modern researchers clues to a language that has never been fully deciphered.

The vase stands just over 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. The dark-black ceramic, known as bucchero, was made through a unique firing method that prevented the kiln from getting enough oxygen, which caused the clay to absorb carbon. Bucchero is considered the trademark Etruscan ceramic, and it was produced from the seventh to the fourth centuries B.C. by this pre-Roman society. It is unclear where the cockerel vase was originally found, but it may have been discovered in a grave in one of the many cemeteries that surround Viterbo, which was originally an Etruscan town about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northwest of modern-day Rome.

According to The Met, the vase may have been a portable inkwell used by an ancient Etruscan who was learning how to write. The cockerel's head was the stopper, and it was loosely attached to the body by a cord through a set of loops. The inscription on the body of the vase is known as an abecedarium ‪—‬ the sequential list of letters in an alphabet.

The Etruscan alphabet is well known, since it was adopted from a regional version of the Greek alphabet in the early eighth century B.C. There were 26 letters in the Etruscan alphabet, but one of them in this abecedarium is incorrect. A close look at the end of the alphabet shows that someone inscribed an S twice; the second one should look more like an X, according to The Met.

The terracotta cockerel vase was one of several ancient Etruscan artifacts that helped experts partially decode the mysterious ancient language, as it preserved the order of the letters in the early alphabet, archaeologist Gisela Richter wrote in a 1930 catalog of The Met's classical artifacts.

Thanks to the adoption of the Greek alphabet, it's possible to fully sound out the Etruscan language. But although more than 10,000 Etruscan inscriptions have been found, the language is still only partially understood because those inscriptions are short and any lengthy Etruscan literature that once existed has been lost.

#6536. A Quick and Dirty History of Honey Traps, From Mata Hari to Mozhno Girls

The honeypot—or honey trap—has re-entered the zeitgeist.

Ever since Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with Chinese intelligence asset Alice Huang became public, the term has been everywhere, calling to mind KGB sleeper agent Elizabeth Jennings (and her wide variety of wigs) on The Americans, Ingrid Bergman fraternizing with Nazi collaborators in Notorious, and Eva Marie Saint’s slick Eve Kendall in North by Northwest. (Espionage fiction author John le Carré is widely credited with coining the phrase “honey trap” in his 1974 novel Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy, later defining it for the BBC as when you “put a girl in a chap’s way. It’s a sexual enticement operation.”) But the real-life phenomenon has far deeper and more interesting roots.

Below, a roundup of some of the most famous honey traps in world history:

Dancer and espionage agent Mata Hari in 1906.

This Dutch exotic dancer and courtesan—who was born Margaretha Geertruida MacLeod in 1876— helped typify the concept of the femme fatale by seducing a wide variety of high-ranking military officers, including Prussian Crown Prince Wilhelm, German Major Arnold Kalle, Russian Captain Vadim Maslov, and former French Minister of War General Adolphe-Pierre Messimy. Hari was ultimately executed by a French firing squad in 1917 after a military court convicted her of spying for Germany during World War I, allegedly saying in her own defense: “A harlot? Yes, but a traitoress, never!”

Thorpe, also known as Betty Pack, Betty Thorpe, Elizabeth Pack, and Amy Brousse, was an Anglo-American spy who worked for MI6 (the British Secret Intelligence Service) and whose targets included the Polish foreign minister’s chief of staff Count Michał Łubieński, Italian naval attaché Admiral Alberto Lais, and Vichy French Embassy press attaché Charles Brousse. When a biographer asked Thorpe if she felt ashamed of using seduction as a means of gathering military intelligence, Thorpe responded: “Ashamed? Not in the least. My superiors told me that the results of my work saved thousands of British and American lives... It involved me in situations from which ‘respectable’ women draw back... [but] wars are not won by respectable methods.”

During the Cold War, the Soviet KGB deployed what it called “Mozhno girls” to befriend or seduce foreign targets in Moscow in order to gather intelligence. (Their name came from the Russian word mozhno, meaning “it is allowed”—a reference to the women’s special dispensation to break Soviet rules about intimate contact with foreigners; Jennifer Lawrence played one such figure in the 2018 spy thriller Red Sparrow.) Mozhno girls like Violetta Seina—the double agent who seduced Marine Security Guard Clayton Lonetree at the annual Marine Corps Ball in 1985—were most active under Joseph Stalin.

Actors Winfried Glatzeder and Erika Skrotzki in Schlüsselblumen, a 1987 German television program about a Romeo agent.

As it turns out, men can be honey traps too. The East German Stasi (or secret police and intelligence agency) proved as much when spymaster Markus Wolf masterminded the system of training select male agents between the ages of 25 and 35 to target lonely or vulnerable West German women—particularly secretaries, clerks, and translators—who worked in sensitive positions inside West German government. A CIA history notes that Wolf’s “Romeo” operation successfully compromised dozens of West German targets over four decades.

Earlier this year, newly declassified FBI documents provided additional information about former California Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell’s relationship with Christine Fang, a suspected Chinese intelligence operative also known as “Fang Fang.” Not only was Fang involved with fundraising for Swalwell’s 2014 re-election campaign, but the two also engaged in an affair before Fang fled the United States in 2015.

#6535. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#6534. Cranberry Brie Pull-Apart Bread

This cranberry Brie pull-apart bread recipe is bursting with melted cheese and sweet-savory cranberry butter. It's an interactive joy to eat.

I may be a year-round cranberry fan, but it’s hard to deny just how right it feels to feast on the ruby-colored fruit during the holiday season. Fresh and frozen cranberries are perfect for cranberry sauce and not-too-sweet cranberry desserts, but I also love using dried cranberries in everything from muffins to party appetizers. And my new favorite way to use dried cranberries is in cranberry Brie pull-apart bread, where they transform a loaf of cheesy bread into a holiday masterpiece.

Cranberry Brie pull-apart bread is what happens when you make a mashup of party cheese bread and cranberry butter. A crusty, round loaf of sourdough is cut in a grid pattern and stuffed with half a pound of cubed Brie. The cheese-stuffed loaf is then coated in a dried cranberry-honey butter (bolstered by orange zest, garlic and rosemary) and baked until it’s hot, crispy and melty. It’s hearty, decadent, sweet, salty and impossible to stop eating.

Preheat the oven to 350°F. In a small bowl, beat together the softened butter, finely chopped dried cranberries, honey, grated orange zest, minced garlic and salt until they’re blended.

Cut the bread into 1-inch slices to within 1/2 inch of the bottom of the loaf. Repeat cuts in the opposite direction. Insert the cubed Brie into the cuts.

Editor’s Tip: If your sourdough is crusty, a serrated bread knife will get the job done without too much elbow grease. The best bread knives slice cleanly without tearing the fluffy interior.

Spread the cranberry butter over the top of the bread. Wrap the loaf in foil and place it on a baking sheet.

Bake the bread for 20 minutes. Unwrap it and continue to bake it until the cheese is melted, about 10 minutes longer. If desired, drizzle it with hot honey before serving it.

Wrap leftover cranberry Brie pull-apart bread tightly, or transfer it to a food storage bag and refrigerate it for up to four days. To reheat it, wrap the bread in foil and bake it at 350º until it’s warm. Unwrap it and continue to bake until the cheese is melted and the bread is crisp. If the bread got pulled apart enough that it’s not really holding its shape anymore, transfer it to a baking dish, bake it until it’s melty, and eat it like stuffing.

Cranberry Brie pull-apart bread tastes best hot and crispy right out of the oven, but you can assemble the bread a few hours ahead of time, wrap it in foil, and refrigerate it until it’s ready to bake. You can also make and refrigerate the cranberry butter up to four days in advance and soften it at room temperature before using it. If you want to bring it to a party or Friendsgiving, follow good party etiquette and check with the host about whether the oven will be available to bake it when you arrive.

If your pull-apart bread is soggy, it might need to be baked longer or at a slightly higher temperature—especially if your bread is really fresh and soft. I use kitchen timers and oven thermometers to track my bakes and ensure my oven isn’t running cooler or hotter than I’d like. Don’t be afraid to bake the bread for a little longer than the recipe suggests if it hasn’t crisped on the outside or if the cheese isn’t fully melted.

Sourdough’s structure (and slightly sharp flavor) is perfect against the richness of the Brie and cranberry butter, but if sourdough isn’t for you, try a round, crusty loaf of rustic white bread. Get a loaf that weighs about 1 pound. Whole wheat and multigrain loaves can work as well, but they tend to have a denser texture and tighter crumb that won’t pull apart as easily. If you can’t find a round loaf, an oval-shaped loaf is the next best choice, but steer clear of sandwich loaves, which can’t be cut as easily into the necessary grid pattern.

Set cranberry Brie pull-apart bread out as a party appetizer next to a crudite platter, cocktail meatballs, and a selection of festive cocktails and mocktails. You can also add it to the holiday table as part of the main course, alongside a holiday ham, roast turkey or standing rib roast.

#6533. Puppy Chow Balls

Recipe by Margaret Knoebel, Milwaukee, Wisconsin

Puppy chow is our favorite Midwestern snack, and it’s the inspiration these holiday-ready truffles. You’ll find all the same ingredients—peanut butter, Chex, chocolate and confectioners’ sugar—but with a truffle redesign that’s sophisticated enough for a Christmas dessert table (and that keeps hands considerably less messy!).

Like puppy chow, Chex cereal (crushed for easier rolling) and peanut butter are melted together to make the crunchy truffle filling. Each truffle is enrobed in a thick layer of melted chocolate then coated generously with confectioners’ sugar. These puppy chow truffles are a two- to three-bite affair and totally remind me of those big puppy chow clusters everyone fights over.

In a large microwave-safe bowl, heat the peanut butter in 30-second increments until it’s completely melted, stirring occasionally. Add 2 tablespoons of confectioners’ sugar and stir until smooth. Add the crushed Chex and stir until everything is well combined.

Scoop the puppy chow truffles by the tablespoonful onto wax-paper-lined baking sheets. Freeze them until they’re firm, about 30 minutes.

In a microwave-safe bowl, melt the semisweet chocolate and shortening at 50% power, and stir until they’re smooth. Dip each puppy chow ball into the melted chocolate and shake off the excess. Place the puppy chow truffles on a waxed paper–lined baking sheet.

Place the confectioners’ sugar in a large airtight container or resealable bag. In batches, add the puppy chow balls and shake them in the bag until they’re well coated in confectioners’ sugar. Store the puppy chow truffles in an airtight container.

Store puppy chow truffles in an airtight container at room temperature for up to four days. They can also last in the fridge for up to one week.

Yes, you can freeze puppy chow truffles, but wait to coat them with confectioners’ sugar until after they’ve thawed. To freeze the puppy chow truffles, place them on a parchment-lined baking sheet and freeze them for one hour. Transfer them to a zip-top bag or airtight container, and freeze them for up to two months. Thaw them overnight in the fridge before enjoying them.

Your chocolate may not be smooth for a few reasons. The first is you may have burned it in the microwave. When you burn chocolate, it will seize and become clumpy. Unfortunately, this is unfixable. It’s also possible that you left out the shortening. Shortening makes the chocolate slightly less viscous, which makes it easier to evenly coat the truffles. It also makes it smooth and glossy. Don’t skip this ingredient!

To help puppy chow balls hold their shape, be sure to use a no-stir creamy peanut butter. It’s much thicker than the natural peanut butters you have to stir. Because their oils separate so easily, natural peanut butters will make the mixture softer and more malleable.

#6532. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)
